The Last Mile to the Real World: Agent-Native Primitives as Reusable Building Blocks for Solving Real-World Tasks
◊\lozenge Foundation ⋅\cdot Adaptation ⋅\cdot Composition ⋅\cdot Evolution ◊\lozenge

Haibo Jin1   Peng Kuang1   Xiaopeng Yuan1   Lucheng Fu2†   Jerry Wang1   Xucheng Yu1   Yaoning Yu1
Dehao Wu1   Runguo Li1   Colin Su1   Jingxuan Sun1   Xuyang Liu1   Haojing Luo3   Haohan Wang1
1University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign  2Georgia Institute of Technology  3heelo.dev
†Work done at UIUC    Corresponding Author
Abstract

Website: https://heelo.dev

1.  Introduction

A central objective of LLM agents is to complete real-world tasks end to end: to act on the world through tools, code, proofs, documents, and other agents until the task’s own acceptance criteria are met [1, 2, 3]. Recent advances in language models and in the harnesses built around them have improved this ability, as GPT acts through Codex [4] and Claude through Claude Code [5]. Through these harnesses an agent reaches tools and APIs [6, 7], code in large repositories [8, 9], formal proof libraries [10, 11], documents and memories [12, 13], and other agents [14, 15]. Meanwhile, benchmarks increasingly judge agents by whether the real task succeeds: the tool calls fulfil the request, the repository’s tests pass, the answer is correct [6, 16, 17, 18]. Existing studies have made resources easier to reach and to reuse through tool learning [2, 6, 19, 20], retrieval and memory [12, 21, 22, 23], skill and code libraries [24, 25, 26], and multi-agent frameworks, workflow search, and harness generators [15, 27, 28, 29, 30], providing an important foundation for agents that act in practical environments.

Despite this progress, frontier models in the harnesses built for them still fall short on public benchmarks of real-world tasks. On Terminal-Bench 4.0 at maximum reasoning effort, GPT-5.6 Sol with Codex resolves 37.3% of the tasks and Claude Opus 5 with Claude Code resolves 51.8%, and on the four stages of DevOps-Gym the same two pairs average 49.9% and 52.1% success. In the airline domain of τ2\tau^{2}-Bench [31], Claude-4.6-Sonnet succeeds in all four trials on half of the tasks. Tasks as ordinary as booking a flight under an airline’s policy or filling in a form whose later fields depend on earlier answers fail at the step from reaching a resource to applying it, which we call the last mile to the real world. Its difficulty shows in three aspects. Application in context: a reached resource must be applied to the task’s own objects, as a tool call must ground every argument, often in an earlier call’s output, and respect the rules of its environment [32, 33, 34], retrieved code must be adapted to its target and to the components that depend on it [35, 36], a proof method applies only where its conditions hold [37, 38], and an answer drawn from documents must stay faithful to its source [39, 40]. Composition: what one step returns or requires must reach the steps that consume it, in a form they can use. Evidence-driven revision: a failure observed in the task’s environment must be traced back to the work it implicates, so that only this work is redone. Together, these aspects extend the last mile from a single call to the whole harness. However, existing approaches keep the resource but leave the competence to apply it with the caller, or fold it into one monolithic agent, so the harness rebuilds this competence for every task: what the caller must read grows with the library, what it learns ends with the task, and its results are hard to check. This raises a natural question: how can an agent handle a real-world task end to end?

To address this gap, we argue that the competence to apply a resource should travel with the resource itself, and we introduce agent-native primitives, each a reusable resource equipped with a resident LLM. The primitive extends reusable software components, temporally extended options, and design by contract [41, 42, 43] to LLM-based units. The resident LLM is what makes the primitive agent-native: it gives the resource a natural-language interface, applies it to each request in context, and communicates requirements to other primitives. Passive artifacts thus become active participants that talk to one another, and the primitive’s interface lets a harness find and invoke it without reading the resource.

Primitives alone do not determine which of them a task needs, how their results reach one another, which to revise when the task fails, or which new primitives to admit. We therefore introduce HEELO (Harness Engineering around Evolving Agent-Native Primitives for the Last Mile to Real-WOrld Tasks), a harness engineering framework that builds each task’s harness, everything the task needs around the model, from an evolving library of primitives through three mechanisms. First, library selection and composition finds candidates through their interfaces or their own relevance assessments and composes the few the task needs into a task-specific graph that carries each result and message to its consumer. Second, evidence-based execution and improvement runs the graph in rounds, verifies the result against evidence from the task’s environment, and traces each failure to the primitives it implicates, so that revision redoes their work and keeps the rest. Third, validation and publishing improves the library between tasks, admitting a new or improved primitive once evidence such as tests, a compiler, or development runs confirms it. Results proved in our companion studies show that need-driven activation stays bounded by the task’s demand, however large the library grows, and identify when per-task composition beats the best fixed harness.

However, each task domain places its own demand on the last mile: cooperating agents must combine their work, a repository change must reach every component it affects, a search must follow what remains unresolved, and a harness must fit its task. We therefore instantiate HEELO with eight primitive families, each built as the solution to one kind of real-world task: Tool Primitives for LLM tool use [44], Code Primitives for repository construction [45], Math Primitives for formal theorem proving [46], Knowledge Primitives for knowledge-intensive tasks [47], Agent Primitives for multi-agent systems [48], Dev-Primitives for software engineering [49], Navigation Primitives for large information spaces [50], and Harness Primitives for agent harnesses [51]. Each family realizes the definition above and the mechanisms its task needs, so the eight companion studies become instances of one framework. For these families, we build 25,519 Tool Primitives, 16,464 of them wrapping live APIs; 1,424 Code Primitives, each validated against the tests it carries; and 82 Math Primitives whose Lean artifacts compile. We also introduce a benchmark of 522 repository-reconstruction tasks drawn from real Python projects in seven domains.

Extensive experiments on more than twenty benchmarks demonstrate that, on the same backbones, Dev-Primitives outperform Codex by 18.2 points on Terminal-Bench 4.0, and Harness Primitives composed per task exceed the mini-SWE-agent seed harness by 7.5 and 12.2 points and Codex by 1.5 and 15.5 points on 100 SWE-bench Verified and 45 Terminal-Bench 2.0 tasks, for a composition cost of 2.7% to 4.3% of one actor attempt. Code Primitives surpass Claude Code on its backbone by 56.2% in repository delivery and keep 95.1% of their delivery at 24.0% lower cost with GPT-OSS-20B adaptation and diagnosis. Tool Primitives on Qwen3-8B lead every reference model on τ2\tau^{2}-Bench at up to 7.7×7.7\times lower cost than GPT-5.4 and complete 2.62.6–3.8×3.8\times as many of 50 curated real-world tasks as GPT-5.4, Claude-4.6-Sonnet, and Gemini-3.1-Pro calling the same tools. Agent Primitives on Qwen3-8B exceed the strongest prior multi-agent system by 7.5 points with ∼3{\sim}3–4×4\times fewer tokens than a text-based one, Navigation Primitives lead the strongest GAIA-Text-103 baseline by 12.7 points, and with GPT-5.6 Luna, Knowledge Primitives gain 14.3 points over Hybrid RAG on average and Math Primitives lead the strongest reranker by 10.8 points in Putnam hit@5. Further analysis across families reveals that the gain lies inside the primitive and that the task decides which primitives run: Tool Primitives more than double the ToolBench pass rate of budget-matched self-refinement over raw schemas, and active Navigation Primitives grow 1.23×1.23\times while distractors grow the information space 16×16\times around the same evidence.

Beyond these research benchmarks, we build heelo.dev, a platform through which agents such as Claude Code, Codex, or Cursor invoke real-world actions as agent-native primitives, from publishing pages and sending outreach to reading invoices and scraping sources. Its 46 real-world tasks cover the 26 capabilities of four end-to-end loops, with the pass criteria of each task fixed before its first run. On their own, Claude Opus 5.5 with Claude Code and GPT-6.1 Sol with Codex, both at medium reasoning effort, complete 9 of the tasks each, with mean task scores of 28% and 25%. Connected to HEELO through our MCP server, Claude Code completes 39 and Codex 35, with scores of 90% and 83%. Per completed task, Claude Code with HEELO needs 3.4 minutes and $0.80 instead of 6.3 minutes and $1.24 on its own, and Codex with HEELO 3.5 minutes and $0.42 instead of 8.0 minutes and $0.65. HEELO thus provides a unified framework for handling real-world tasks end to end. Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

  • •

    We introduce agent-native primitives under one definition that pairs a reusable resource, from tools, code components, and proof methods to source models, multi-agent patterns, and repository files, with a resident LLM that applies it in context and messages other primitives. We further build libraries of 25,519 Tool Primitives, 1,424 validated Code Primitives, and 82 Math Primitives with Lean-checked scaffolds.

  • •

    We propose HEELO, one harness engineering framework that unifies the eight families: each task’s harness is a graph composed from an evolving library and revised where the task’s evidence implicates it, and the library grows between tasks with validated primitives, so that a new kind of task can join as a new primitive family.

  • •

    Experiments on more than twenty benchmarks across eight kinds of real-world tasks show that every family improves on its reference baseline: primitives lead Codex by 18.2 points on Terminal-Bench 4.0 and Claude Code by 56.2% in repository delivery, and cost up to 7.7×7.7\times less than GPT-5.4 on τ2\tau^{2}-Bench. Cross-family analyses locate the gain inside the primitive and show that the task decides which primitives run.

  • •

    We build heelo.dev, a platform that exposes real-world actions, from flights and calendars to email and browser automation, as agent-native primitives to agents such as Claude Code, Codex, or Cursor. On its 46 real-world tasks in four end-to-end loops, Claude Code and Codex complete 9 tasks each on their own and 39 and 35 when connected to HEELO through MCP, with 1.9×1.9\times and 2.3×2.3\times less time and 1.55×1.55\times lower cost per completed task.

2.  Related Work

Tool Learning and Interfaces. LLM agents learn to call tools from self-annotated data [2], large collections of real-world APIs [7, 6], and synthesized single- and multi-turn function-calling data [52, 19, 53], while compact models make function calling robust on device [54]. Benchmarks span structured calls and tool-augmented dialogue [20, 55], large-scale, compositional, and nested call sequences [56, 57, 32], and stateful, conversational environments [34, 31, 33, 58], while AgentDojo evaluates tool-using agents under adversarial prompt injection [59]. OpenAPI, the Model Context Protocol, Agent2Agent, and Agent Skills make services, tools, agents, and packaged instructions discoverable [60, 61, 62, 63]. Across these settings, the caller binds each call itself: it writes schema-compliant arguments and grounds each value in the intended object, often an earlier call’s output. Tool Primitives move schema binding into the tool, so that the caller states its need in natural language and a resident LLM conditioned on the tool’s schema produces the typed call.

Code Reuse and Repositories. Software reuse made interfaces, dependencies, and adaptation cost central to building systems from components [64, 41]. Learned systems discover libraries and abstractions [65, 66, 67], make tools for later tasks [26, 68, 69], retrieve code and documentation during generation [70, 71, 35], and distill reusable procedures from agent experience [72, 73]. Repository-level agents inspect, edit, and execute code [8, 9, 3], follow explicit localization and repair stages [74, 75], or divide work among task graphs, roles, and coordinated developers [76, 77, 78]. Evaluation ranges from cross-file and repository-level generation [36, 79] and issue repair [16] to long-horizon evolution [80], repository generation and whole-repository migration [81, 82], and terminal and DevOps workflows [17, 83]. In these systems, the reused artifact stays fixed while a central agent decides how to use it, and the units of reasoning and their connections are designed in advance or kept inside one trajectory [84, 85]. Code Primitives make adaptation an operation of the reused component, and Dev-Primitives route requirements along the repository’s own dependencies.

Retrieval, Memory, and Knowledge. Retrieval-augmented generation brings external content into model computation [86, 87, 12], adaptive methods decide when and what to retrieve [88, 89, 40, 90, 91], and long-context models use evidence unevenly across positions [39]. Reading-comprehension benchmarks ask a model to combine what it reads, through discrete reasoning over paragraphs in DROP [92] and multi-hop reasoning in HotpotQA [93]. Beyond flat passages, structured representations organize a source into summary trees [21], graphs [94, 95, 96], associative or global memories [97, 98, 99], and task-conditioned structures [100]. Agent memories keep interactions [101, 102, 13, 103, 104], feedback [22], insights [23], skills [24], and workflows or procedures [25, 105] across tasks. In large information spaces, retrieval chooses its next query from the remaining gaps [106, 107, 108], and multi-agent readers divide long inputs [109, 110] or retrieval, filtering, and planning [111, 112, 113] among workers. What persists in these methods is the corpus, a structure built from it, or experience from interaction, and when readers divide long inputs among workers, coordination grows with how the space is partitioned, regardless of what the query requires. By contrast, Knowledge Primitives keep a revisable model of one authoritative source and commit only the revisions that the source supports, and Navigation Primitives let unresolved information needs decide which primitives run.

Formal Theorem Proving. Lean and Mathlib give provers a checked proof language and a large reusable library [10, 11]. LLM provers generate whole proofs or repair them from verifier feedback [114, 115, 116], and agentic loops alternate generation with Lean-guided repair [117, 118]. Retrieval-augmented proving, premise selection, and declaration search supply formal facts [119, 120, 121], and lemma libraries grow across problems [122]. Such retrieval ranks a fact, a lemma, or a prior proof by relevance, and LLM rerankers that reason about fit report a score or an ordering [123, 124, 125, 126], leaving the prover to decide how to use a candidate. Proof planning describes methods by their conditions and effects [37, 38], and adaptation-guided retrieval prefers cases that adapt to a new problem [127, 128]. Math Primitives bring this view to LLM provers: a Method Contract carries a method’s required conditions, intended action, and residual obligations, and each contract proposes its use on the goal before ranking.

Multi-Agent Systems and Communication. Multi-agent frameworks organize LLMs by assigning predefined roles [15, 129], programming conversations among customizable agents [14], recruiting collaborators iteratively [130], or letting agents debate [131, 132]. Other methods design the team automatically: DyLAN selects agents by estimated value [133], GPTSwarm optimizes collaboration graphs [27], and MAS-GPT generates a configuration from the query [134]. Recent methods communicate below text by sharing a learned latent space [135], projecting or propagating key–value caches [136, 137], or aggregating experts through cross-attention [138]. For cache messages, rotary embeddings make a key’s position part of its meaning [139]. These systems take the agent or the team as the unit of design, and the latent methods mainly improve how information passes between agents. Agent Primitives make a recurring multi-agent computation pattern the reusable unit and implement its computation structure through latent KV cache communication, with all agents on one LLM so that their inputs and outputs stay aligned.

Agent Harnesses and Workflows. The harness around a model decides how observations, memory, retries, and checks shape its actions: ReAct interleaves reasoning with actions [1], Reflexion and Self-Refine feed verbal feedback into later attempts [22, 140], and DSPy compiles declarative pipelines of model calls [141]. Codex and Claude Code, the platform harnesses built for GPT and Claude, supply the tools and execution loop around these frontier models [4, 5]. Design methods search over agent programs and workflows [28, 29] or edit and evaluate candidate harnesses to select one for all tasks [142, 143]. Others adapt the harness at test time, specializing it for each case from retrieved execution experience [144] or rewriting harness code and generating task-specific modules [145, 30]. These methods fix one harness across tasks, specialize it through instructions that the actor must follow, or write new control code at test time, which must then be implemented, debugged, and validated. Harness Primitives validate each control operation when it enters the library, so that a task’s harness is selected and compiled from implemented parts before the actor runs.

Key Differences. Across these lines of work, the units (a function, a code component, a lemma, a passage or memory, a role or team, a harness) keep a resource but leave the competence to apply it with the caller or fix it in an agent design. An agent-native primitive keeps that competence with the resource by equipping it with a resident LLM: the primitive owns the resource, exposes an interface through which a harness finds and invokes it, applies the resource to a natural-language request in context, and communicates with other primitives; where a domain offers an exact procedure, a program replaces the resident LLM. HEELO selects and composes primitives per task, revises only what the evidence of a failure implicates, and publishes improved primitives through a validation path separate from task execution. Eight primitive families instantiate this design on eight kinds of real-world tasks. Overall, primitives let the harness of a real-world task be engineered around reusable, validated units.

3.  Methodology

Figure 2 gives an overview of HEELO. We first state the problem of building a harness for a real-world task and define the agent-native primitive from which the harness is built. We then describe the three mechanisms that build and run each task’s harness and improve the library between tasks, the eight primitive families that instantiate the method on eight kinds of real-world tasks, and three properties of the selection that decides which primitives run, each proved in a companion study.

3.1.  Problem Formulation

A real-world task qq arrives with a context cqc_{q}: its inputs, its environment, its constraints, and the acceptance criteria by which it is judged (the task request of Figure 2). An agent acts on the task through a harness HH, the control program between the model and the environment. The harness decides which operations run, with which inputs, in which order, and when the run stops. Running HH on qq produces a trajectory τ\tau. The task’s own acceptance procedure, such as its tests, its proof checker, or its answer key, scores the trajectory as Rq​(τ)∈[0,1]R_{q}(\tau)\in[0,1], and we write R⁡(q,H)=𝔼τ​[Rq​(τ)∣H]R(q,H)=\mathbb{E}_{\tau}[R_{q}(\tau)\mid H].

A fixed harness, such as one general-purpose coding agent, uses the same HH for every task. Following our companion study on Harness Primitives [51], we build the harness of each task from a library ℒ\mathcal{L} of reusable units:

Hq=F⁡(q,cq,ℒ)∈ℋ⁡(cq),Hq∗∈arg⁡maxH∈ℋ⁡(cq)⁡R⁡(q,H),H_{q}=F(q,\,c_{q};\,\mathcal{L})\in\mathcal{H}(c_{q}),\qquad H_{q}^{*}\in\arg\max_{H\in\mathcal{H}(c_{q})}\ R(q,H), (1)

where ℋ⁡(cq)\mathcal{H}(c_{q}) is the set of harnesses compatible with cqc_{q}. The construction procedure FF approximates Hq∗H_{q}^{*} from the units of ℒ\mathcal{L}, within a budget on model calls or revision rounds. While FF builds and runs HqH_{q}, it keeps a context 𝒞t\mathcal{C}_{t} for round tt, which starts as 𝒞0=cq\mathcal{C}_{0}=c_{q} and accumulates results and feedback.

The last mile lies inside Eq. (1) at two levels. Each unit of ℒ\mathcal{L} must be applied to the task’s own objects, and FF must decide which units the task needs and how their results combine. HEELO answers the first level with agent-native primitives and the second with the mechanisms that realize FF.

3.2.  Agent-Native Primitives

A unit of the library helps a task only once it is applied in context. A tool call must ground its arguments, a retrieved component must be adapted to its target, a proof method must be instantiated on the goal, and an answer must stay faithful to its source. A caller that applies every unit itself rebuilds this competence for each task and must hold the details of every unit it uses in one context [44, 49]. An agent-native primitive keeps this competence with the unit by equipping the unit with a resident LLM that applies it.

Definition 3.1 (Agent-native primitive).

An agent-native primitive PiP_{i} equips a reusable resource aia_{i} with a resident LLM ℳ\mathcal{M} and exposes an interface did_{i} through which a harness finds and invokes it. Invoked with a natural-language request xix_{i} in a context cic_{i}, the resident LLM, conditioned on the resource, applies aia_{i} and returns a result rir_{i} together with the messages mi={mi→j}jm_{i}=\{m_{i\to j}\}_{j} that the primitive addresses to other primitives PjP_{j}: the requirements that rir_{i} places on them, or task-relevant information they need, with mi=∅m_{i}=\varnothing when none is needed:

(ri,mi)=Pi​(xi,ci)=ℳ⁡([ai;ci;xi]),(r_{i},\,m_{i})=P_{i}(x_{i};\,c_{i})=\mathcal{M}\bigl([\,a_{i};\,c_{i};\,x_{i}\,]\bigr), (2)

where [⋅][\cdot] denotes the input context of the resident LLM.

The resident LLM is what makes the primitive agent-native. It reads the resource and serves as its natural-language interface, sparing the caller from holding the resource’s details in its own context. The primitive’s messages carry requirements and task-relevant information to other primitives. Resources that were passive artifacts thus become active participants that reason locally and communicate with one another. The resource aia_{i} can be anything the task relies on, from a tool’s schema and function to a repository component, a proof method, or a source model, and the interface did_{i} is what a harness reads in its place, such as a tool’s schema descriptor or the selection side of a Method Contract. One base model can serve as the resident LLM of every primitive of a library, conditioned on a different resource each time, so a primitive is defined by the resource it owns. Where a domain offers an exact procedure, as for the control operations of Harness Primitives, implemented code applies the resource and receives its request as parameters. A resource that a downstream prover or solver consumes, such as the execution side of a Method Contract or a source model, is applied by that model.

Relevance Assessment. Similarity between a request and an interface does not show that a primitive applies. A primitive can therefore assess its own relevance before it is selected [45, 46]:

(si,ui)=ℳassess​(Pi,x,𝒞t),(s_{i},\,u_{i})=\mathcal{M}^{\mathrm{assess}}(P_{i},\,x,\,\mathcal{C}_{t}), (3)

where sis_{i} judges whether PiP_{i} applies to a request xx derived from the task, and uiu_{i} proposes how PiP_{i} would be used. Run over the whole library at once, this assessment removes the dependence on a pool that similarity retrieval chooses first (Proposition 3.3).

Carried Validation. A resource may carry its own means of validation, such as tests or a schema. The primitive applies them before it returns and reports a structured failure when they fail. Carried validation shows that the primitive’s own step succeeded. Whether the result serves the task is for the harness to decide.

Library. Primitives form a library ℒ={Pi}i=1N\mathcal{L}=\{P_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N}. A library is either built ahead of the tasks that draw on it and reused across them, or induced from a task’s own data, such as a repository or an information space [49, 50]. A library built ahead of its tasks does not change while a task runs. An induced library follows the task’s data and can change as the task edits that data.

3.3.  Harness Engineering around Agent-Native Primitives

Primitives determine how each resource is applied. They do not determine which primitives a task needs, how their results reach one another, or what to change when the task still fails. Two mechanisms realize the construction procedure FF of Eq. (1): library selection and composition builds the harness, and evidence-based execution and improvement runs and revises it. A third mechanism, validation and publishing, improves the library between tasks (Figure 2).

Library Selection and Composition. A primitive sees only the request it is handed, so it cannot decide alone whether the task needs it. A library also usually holds more primitives than one task uses. COMPOSE therefore finds candidates through their interfaces, either by retrieval or by reading every interface at once. It reads their relevance assessments where primitives provide them and builds a plan

Πt=COMPOSE⁡(q,𝒞t,ℒ)=({(i,xi)}i∈𝒜t,ℰt),\Pi_{t}=\operatorname{COMPOSE}(q,\,\mathcal{C}_{t};\,\mathcal{L})=\bigl(\{(i,\,x_{i})\}_{i\in\mathcal{A}_{t}},\ \mathcal{E}_{t}\bigr), (4)

where 𝒜t⊆{1,…,N}\mathcal{A}_{t}\subseteq\{1,\dots,N\} is the activation set, xix_{i} is the local request of PiP_{i}, and ℰt⊆𝒜t×𝒜t\mathcal{E}_{t}\subseteq\mathcal{A}_{t}\times\mathcal{A}_{t} holds the dependencies along which results and messages flow. The plan is the task-specific graph of Figure 2. Only the activated primitives run, so the cost of applying primitives follows |𝒜t||\mathcal{A}_{t}|, however large NN is. A dependency carries an earlier result to the request that consumes it, a message to the primitive that must act on it, or internal state between models that share parameters. A plan may also hand a selected resource to the prover or solver that consumes it. A need that no primitive covers is left to the harness itself.

Evidence-Based Execution and Improvement. A primitive can succeed at its own step while the task still fails, and the task’s environment reports such a failure without naming the primitive that should change. HEELO therefore runs the plan in rounds that end in evidence and revises what the evidence implicates. In round tt, the activated primitives act, and verification judges the integrated result:

(ri,mi)\displaystyle(r_{i},\,m_{i}) =Pi(xi;cit),i∈𝒜t,\displaystyle=P_{i}\bigl(x_{i};\,c_{i}^{t}\bigr),\qquad i\in\mathcal{A}_{t}, (5)
ot\displaystyle o_{t} =EXECUTE(St),(vt,ϕt)=VERIFY(q,Πt,St,ot),ϕt=(et,ℐt,ut).\displaystyle=\operatorname{EXECUTE}\bigl(S_{t}\bigr),\qquad(v_{t},\,\phi_{t})=\operatorname{VERIFY}(q,\,\Pi_{t},\,S_{t},\,o_{t}),\qquad\phi_{t}=(e_{t},\,\mathcal{I}_{t},\,u_{t}).

Here citc_{i}^{t} holds what the plan routes to PiP_{i}: the results of its predecessors in ℰt\mathcal{E}_{t}, the messages m→i={mj→i}j∈𝒜tm_{\to i}=\{m_{j\to i}\}_{j\in\mathcal{A}_{t}} addressed to it, and the part of the task state it needs. Each primitive changes only what it owns. Messages reach their recipients before the round ends, so a requirement found while one primitive works can still be met in the same round by the primitives that depend on it. The task state StS_{t} integrates the round’s results into the task’s artifacts, such as a repository, a proof, or an answer. EXECUTE runs what the task can run and records evidence oto_{t}, such as build status, test outcomes, compiler messages, and traces. Where nothing runs, the results themselves are the evidence.

VERIFY turns the integrated state and its evidence into a verdict vt∈{pass,fail}v_{t}\in\{\textup{{pass}},\textup{{fail}}\} and structured feedback ϕt\phi_{t}. The feedback names the observed failures ete_{t}, the primitives ℐt⊆{1,…,N}\mathcal{I}_{t}\subseteq\{1,\dots,N\} that they implicate, and revision guidance utu_{t}. A failed build or test sets vt=failv_{t}=\textup{{fail}}, and no model judgment overrides it. Verification can also judge each step as soon as it completes, or run inside the plan as a primitive of its own. On a failure, the feedback enriches the context, and COMPOSE revises the plan:

𝒞t+1=𝒞t∪{ϕt},Πt+1=COMPOSE⁡(q,𝒞t+1,ℒ,Πt,ϕt).\mathcal{C}_{t+1}=\mathcal{C}_{t}\cup\{\phi_{t}\},\qquad\Pi_{t+1}=\operatorname{COMPOSE}\bigl(q,\,\mathcal{C}_{t+1};\,\mathcal{L},\,\Pi_{t},\,\phi_{t}\bigr). (6)

Revision changes only what ϕt\phi_{t} implicates. It re-plans the affected steps, reactivates the implicated primitives or activates those the evidence newly implicates, or redirects an unresolved need. It keeps the work that the new evidence does not contradict. Revision can also precede execution: a plan that can be checked before it runs is corrected from its own diagnostics within a bounded number of attempts, and a fallback plan is kept if correction fails. The loop ends when vt=passv_{t}=\textup{{pass}} or after BB revision rounds and returns the current result.

Validation and Publishing. A library built ahead of its tasks is reused across them, so what enters it must be validated first, independently of the tasks it will serve. New and improved primitives may be mined from existing artifacts, harvested from runs whose results were verified in context, or proposed from failed trajectories. They enter the library only on the separate path of Figure 2:

ℒk+1=ℒk⊕{P~∈𝒫~k:VALIDATE⁡(P~)=pass},\mathcal{L}_{k+1}=\mathcal{L}_{k}\oplus\bigl\{\tilde{P}\in\tilde{\mathcal{P}}_{k}:\ \operatorname{VALIDATE}(\tilde{P})=\textup{{pass}}\bigr\}, (7)

where 𝒫~k\tilde{\mathcal{P}}_{k} holds the candidates of stage kk, and ⊕\oplus adds a new primitive or replaces the one that P~\tilde{P} revises. VALIDATE checks each candidate with the evidence that its domain affords, such as its tests, a compiler, its source, or matched runs on development tasks. An output produced inside a task, such as an adapted component, enters the library only through this path. Together, Eqs. (4)–(7) define the per-task harness and the evolving library that make up HEELO.

3.4.  Eight Primitive Families

The method above is shared across tasks, but each task domain places its own demand on the last mile: cooperating agents must exchange their intermediate state, a repository change must reach the components that depend on it, a search must follow the needs that remain unresolved, and a harness must fit its task. We therefore instantiate HEELO with eight primitive families, each built as the solution to one kind of real-world task, and the primitives of a family own the resource that its task applies, from the tools of LLM tool use and the components of repository construction to the proof methods of formal theorem proving and the control operations of agent harnesses. The families differ in how they specialize the method, as summarized below in each family’s own terms and notation, so that a symbol such as FF, MM, or RR keeps the meaning of its own study within its paragraph. We provide the full framework of each family, with its overview figure, in Appendix B.

Tool Primitives. A Tool Primitive [44] wraps one ToolFace tool: its resource aia_{i} is the schema–function pair (si,fi)(s_{i},f_{i}), and its interface did_{i} is the schema descriptor. The shared model conditioned on the schema, 𝒫i​(x,c)=ℳ⁡([si;c;x])\mathcal{P}_{i}(x;c)=\mathcal{M}([s_{i};c;x]), maps the request xx to the arguments of sis_{i} and invokes fif_{i}, returning the result with a summary or a structured failure. HEART is the harness engineering framework around Tool Primitives, and its COMPOSE has three parts: request decomposition asks the user for missing details and writes an invocation plan, semantic search over schema descriptors retrieves candidate tools for each step, and value resolution grounds each step’s values in the query and earlier results; each step’s result is the context cc of the next. VERIFY is per-step result validation on four criteria, and targeted revision re-plans from its feedback within B=3B=3 rounds. ToolFace holds 25,519 tools with manually authored schemas, each inducing a Tool Primitive.

Code Primitives. A Code Primitive [45] owns an executable component ai=(Ci,Ii,Di,Vi,Xi)a_{i}=(C_{i},I_{i},D_{i},V_{i},X_{i}) of implementation, contract, dependency closure, carried tests, and provenance; the contract IiI_{i} is its interface did_{i}, and a resident LLM MiM_{i} assesses and adapts the component. LEGO constructs repositories from these primitives and task-specific code, with Retrieval and Activation over the CodeFace library as its COMPOSE: DECOMPOSE writes capability requirements, the top two candidates for each requirement assess their relevance (Eq. (3)), and MATCH activates the smallest mutually compatible set. In Primitive Adaptation and Collaboration, each activated primitive adapts its own component into a target-specific variant P~i\widetilde{P}_{i}, reruns ViV_{i}, and sends its consumers the requirements μi→j\mu_{i\to j} the rewrite imposes. Execution Feedback extends the target’s tests with synthesized ones, DIAGNOSE realizes VERIFY, and revision reactivates the implicated primitives within five rounds per module. CodeFace, mined from repositories and validated in isolation, grows with implementations harvested from verified construction runs.

Math Primitives. A Math Primitive [46] packages a reusable proof method as a Method Contract aia_{i} with parameters xcx_{c}, required conditions Prec\operatorname{Pre}_{c}, a target GcG_{c} with its action, a Lean scaffold ScS_{c}, and residual obligations Oblc\operatorname{Obl}_{c}. The contract’s selection side is the interface did_{i}, and its execution side goes to the prover. COMPOSE is self-advertised method selection: in one batched call, each contract in the library proposes its use on the goal as a target, an action, and required facts (Eq. (3)). A commitment gate demotes a contract that claims the main role with a vague or unsupported proposal to a supporting role, a tiered ranking then orders the contracts, and an optional runoff re-ranks the top ten. The prover applies the top-ranked contract; Lean compiles each attempt, and its errors drive whole-proof repair within ten compilations. The 82 contracts are built once from Putnam 2000–2014 solutions and admitted after their Lean artifacts compile (Eq. (7)).

Knowledge Primitives. Each authoritative source DD has one Knowledge Primitive [47], whose resource aia_{i} is the source model MM of DD, organized around its entities with units citing DD, and a task grounded in DD invokes it. SourceLearn constructs and progressively refines these source models, and at task time it realizes COMPOSE as source-model activation AB​(M,q)A_{B}(M,q), the whole model if it fits B=24B=24k tokens and its task-relevant regions otherwise; the solver FF applies the activated model beside evidence retrieved from DD, y^=F⁡(q,R⁡(D,q),AB​(M,q))\hat{y}=F\bigl(q,R(D,q),A_{B}(M,q)\bigr). The source model stays fixed during testing and improves on the publishing path of Eq. (7): Self-Directed Source Learning deepens unresolved aspects of the initial model and connects knowledge fragmented across entities, and Task-Guided Source Learning revises the regions implicated by incorrectly answered guidance tasks and recalibrates MM under a learned representation policy. Grounded source reconstruction realizes VALIDATE, rejecting a rewrite unless the source supports it and previously supported meaning is preserved.

Agent Primitives. An Agent Primitive owns a recurring multi-agent computation pattern as its resource aia_{i} and encapsulates it as a reusable latent operator behind the interface of a standard LLM agent [48]; the three primitives are Review, Voting and Selection, and Planning and Execution. An LLM Organizer performs COMPOSE: guided by a Knowledge Pool of 45 query–MAS-structure pairs, it maps each query to a primitive composition plan in code, and executing the plan forms a primitive-based MAS. Internal agents follow task-agnostic role prompts on one shared LLM and exchange KV caches within and across primitives, re-indexing the sender’s keys for RoPE. Verification and revision happen inside the primitives, where a Critic’s feedback drives the Solver’s refinement in Review and a Selector judges candidates in Voting and Selection. The primitives come from decomposing existing MAS designs into recurring computation patterns, and the library stays fixed.

Dev-Primitives. A Dev-Primitive [49] wraps a repository component aia_{i}, by default a file, with a resident LLM, and activation reads the repository in place of an interface did_{i}. The primitive edits its own artifact where needed and sends directed messages to the components its reasoning implicates, (ai′,mi)=ℳ⁡([ai;xi;𝒞i])(a_{i}^{\prime},m_{i})=\mathcal{M}([a_{i};x_{i};\mathcal{C}_{i}]), where 𝒞i\mathcal{C}_{i} holds the messages it receives. HERMES, the harness engineering framework for software engineering via Dev-Primitives, instantiates them on demand: its COMPOSE, Dynamic Primitive Activation, localizes the relevant components, expands along their dependencies, and assigns each a local objective xix_{i}. The activated primitives collaborate in one round, and task-visible checks run on the modified repository. VERIFY is Bug Diagnosis, which traces a failure to the components it implicates, and activation re-plans from this feedback within B=3B=3 revision rounds. The repository induces the library, and a persistent file created during the task becomes a new Dev-Primitive.

Navigation Primitives. A Navigation Primitive [50] is a scope-specialized worker whose resource aia_{i} is one territory of the information space and whose interface did_{i} is the territory’s WorkerCard. The library is induced per query: a deterministic partition splits the space into territories, bounded searchable regions fixed during execution. ANTMAN, an adaptive coordination framework for these workers, keeps the context 𝒞t\mathcal{C}_{t} as a revisable Need Graph GtG_{t} holding each need’s status, evidence, attempts, and progress, and composes one need at a time: WorkerCard retrieval and an orchestrator decision over GtG_{t} route an unresolved need to at most one worker, which searches its territory and reports evidence, progress, and uncertainty. Need-resolution assessment in the update Gt+1=U⁡(Gt,rt)G_{t+1}=U(G_{t},r_{t}) realizes VERIFY, judging the need resolved, partial, or unresolved, and task-local recovery reframes a stalled need, reroutes it, or sends it to a fallback path, within ρ\rho routings per need.

Harness Primitives. In a Harness Primitive [51], the resource aia_{i} is an implemented control operation, fixed at test time, and the interface did_{i} combines an application scope, stating when it helps, with a composition contract of inputs, outputs, setup, and dependencies. The framework that composes these primitives is STITCH, and its COMPOSE acts before the harness sends its first request to the actor, the task-solving model: the harness composer π\pi reads the whole catalog and either keeps the seed graph or returns a composition intent, whose primitives the deterministic compiler KK wires into GseedG_{\mathrm{seed}} with their contract dependencies, Π0=K⁡(Gseed,π⁡(q,cq,Gseed,ℒ),ℒ,cq)\Pi_{0}=K\bigl(G_{\mathrm{seed}},\pi(q,c_{q};G_{\mathrm{seed}},\mathcal{L});\mathcal{L},c_{q}\bigr). An invalid candidate returns its diagnostics to the composer for bounded correction, and the seed harness is kept if correction fails. During the run, verification and repair primitives return failed checks to the actor. A development agent mines the library from failed trajectories, accepting candidates that pass mechanism tests and improve matched runs (Eq. (7)).

3.5.  Theoretical Analysis

COMPOSE decides which primitives run, so it governs both what a harness costs and what it gains. The companion studies prove three properties of this choice, which we restate in the notation of this section: how many primitives a task activates, what choosing them per task gains over a fixed harness, and what limits a shortlist. We give the proofs, with the correspondence to each study’s notation, in Appendix A.

Demand-Bounded Activation. Suppose that COMPOSE activates a primitive only by routing one unresolved need of the task to it, and routes each need at most ρ\rho times, reroutes included. Let D⁡(q)D(q) count the needs realized while qq runs, with a reframed or newly introduced need counted as new. Let K⁡(q)K(q) count the routing events, 𝒜q=⋃t𝒜t\mathcal{A}_{q}=\bigcup_{t}\mathcal{A}_{t} be the set of primitives activated during the run, and ℒq\mathcal{L}_{q} be the library available to qq.

Proposition 3.1 (Demand-bounded activation [50]).

Under these conditions,

|𝒜q|≤K⁡(q)≤ρ​D​(q),and consequently|𝒜q|≤min⁡{|ℒq|,ρ​D​(q)}.|\mathcal{A}_{q}|\leq K(q)\leq\rho\,D(q),\qquad\text{and consequently}\qquad|\mathcal{A}_{q}|\leq\min\bigl\{|\mathcal{L}_{q}|,\ \rho\,D(q)\bigr\}. (8)

The companion study on Navigation Primitives proves the bound for workers that each search one territory of an information space. If realized demand stays bounded, D⁡(q)≤D¯D(q)\leq\bar{D}, and ρ\rho does not depend on the library, then |𝒜q|≤ρ​D¯|\mathcal{A}_{q}|\leq\rho\bar{D}: growth of the library alone does not force the active part of such a harness to grow.

Task-Conditioned Composition. The companion study on Harness Primitives asks, under a simplified additive model, when choosing primitives per task beats one fixed harness. Tasks qq follow a distribution 𝒬\mathcal{Q}, and each primitive PiP_{i} helps on a scope Ωi\Omega_{i} of tasks with prevalence μi=Prq∼𝒬⁡(q∈Ωi)\mu_{i}=\Pr_{q\sim\mathcal{Q}}(q\in\Omega_{i}). Activating PiP_{i} yields a gain gi​(q)>0g_{i}(q)>0 on Ωi\Omega_{i} and a penalty κi​(q)>0\kappa_{i}(q)>0 off it, with conditional means g¯i\bar{g}_{i} and κ¯i\bar{\kappa}_{i}. Under valid execution, the harness with activation vector 𝐳∈{0,1}N\mathbf{z}\in\{0,1\}^{N} attains R⁡(q,𝐳)=R0​(q)+∑i=1Nzi​Δi​(q)R(q,\mathbf{z})=R_{0}(q)+\sum_{i=1}^{N}z_{i}\Delta_{i}(q), where R0​(q)R_{0}(q) is the performance without primitives and Δi​(q)\Delta_{i}(q) is gi​(q)g_{i}(q) on Ωi\Omega_{i} and −κi​(q)-\kappa_{i}(q) otherwise. All combinations are admissible, and RR lies in [0,1][0,1]. A harness HH earns J⁡(q,H)=𝟏​[H​ executes validly]⋅R⁡(q,H)J(q,H)=\mathbf{1}[H\text{ executes validly}]\cdot R(q,H), with R⁡(q,H)R(q,H) as in Section 3.1. For a composer whose harnesses HcompH_{\mathrm{comp}} execute validly, with final activations ziz_{i}, the utility-weighted false-positive and false-negative rates are αi=𝔼⁡[zi​κi​(q)∣q∉Ωi]/κ¯i\alpha_{i}=\mathbb{E}[z_{i}\kappa_{i}(q)\mid q\notin\Omega_{i}]/\bar{\kappa}_{i} and βi=𝔼⁡[(1−zi)​gi​(q)∣q∈Ωi]/g¯i\beta_{i}=\mathbb{E}[(1-z_{i})g_{i}(q)\mid q\in\Omega_{i}]/\bar{g}_{i}.

Proposition 3.2 (Fixed versus task-conditioned composition [51]).

Assume μi∈(0,1)\mu_{i}\in(0,1), g¯i>0\bar{g}_{i}>0, and κ¯i>0\bar{\kappa}_{i}>0 for all ii, and let zi∗(q)=𝟏[q∈Ωi]z_{i}^{*}(q)=\mathbf{1}[q\in\Omega_{i}] be the oracle task-conditioned activation. (i) The best task-independent activation 𝐳fixed∗∈arg⁡max𝐳​𝔼q​[R⁡(q,𝐳)]\mathbf{z}^{*}_{\mathrm{fixed}}\in\arg\max_{\mathbf{z}}\mathbb{E}_{q}[R(q,\mathbf{z})] falls short of 𝐳∗​(q)\mathbf{z}^{*}(q) by the positive gap Γfixed\Gamma_{\mathrm{fixed}} below. (ii) Task-conditioned composition outperforms the best fixed harness Hfixed∗H^{*}_{\mathrm{fixed}}, which activates 𝐳fixed∗\mathbf{z}^{*}_{\mathrm{fixed}}, if and only if its utility-weighted selection loss is smaller than this gap:

Γfixed=𝔼q​[R⁡(q,𝐳∗​(q))]−𝔼q​[R⁡(q,𝐳fixed∗)]=∑i=1Nmin⁡(μi​g¯i,(1−μi)​κ¯i)>0,𝔼⁡[J⁡(q,Hcomp)]>𝔼⁡[J⁡(q,Hfixed∗)]⇔∑i=1N[μi​βi​g¯i+(1−μi)​αi​κ¯i]<Γfixed.\begin{gathered}\Gamma_{\mathrm{fixed}}=\mathbb{E}_{q}\bigl[R(q,\mathbf{z}^{*}(q))\bigr]-\mathbb{E}_{q}\bigl[R(q,\mathbf{z}^{*}_{\mathrm{fixed}})\bigr]=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\min\bigl(\mu_{i}\bar{g}_{i},\ (1-\mu_{i})\bar{\kappa}_{i}\bigr)>0,\\[2.0pt] \mathbb{E}\bigl[J(q,H_{\mathrm{comp}})\bigr]>\mathbb{E}\bigl[J(q,H^{*}_{\mathrm{fixed}})\bigr]\iff\sum_{i=1}^{N}\bigl[\mu_{i}\beta_{i}\bar{g}_{i}+(1-\mu_{i})\alpha_{i}\bar{\kappa}_{i}\bigr]<\Gamma_{\mathrm{fixed}}.\end{gathered} (9)

A fixed harness that includes PiP_{i} pays its expected out-of-scope penalty (1−μi)​κ¯i(1-\mu_{i})\bar{\kappa}_{i}, and one that excludes it forgoes its expected in-scope gain μi​g¯i\mu_{i}\bar{g}_{i}; Γfixed\Gamma_{\mathrm{fixed}} sums the smaller of the two. The composer need not be perfect: under the additive model and valid execution, building each task’s harness from the library beats the best fixed harness built from the same primitives if and only if its selection loss stays below this gap.

Coverage and Retrieval Ceiling. Let 𝒰q⊆ℒ\mathcal{U}_{q}\subseteq\mathcal{L} be the nonempty set of primitives that serve task qq, which the study of self-advertised method selection takes to be the annotated reference methods of a goal. The set is random given the information XX that a selector reads: the task with its context and the interfaces of the library. With information ZZ, the best achievable expected hit@kk of a size-kk shortlist S⊆ℒS\subseteq\mathcal{L} is Vk​(Z)=𝔼⁡[max|S|=k⁡Pr⁡(S∩𝒰q≠∅∣Z)]V_{k}(Z)=\mathbb{E}\bigl[\max_{|S|=k}\Pr(S\cap\mathcal{U}_{q}\neq\varnothing\mid Z)\bigr].

Proposition 3.3 (Coverage and retrieval ceiling [46]).

(i) If TT holds the features that a similarity-only selector computes from XX, then Vk​(X)≥Vk​(T)V_{k}(X)\geq V_{k}(T); the inequality can be strict when distinct tasks share the same similarity representation but need different shortlists, and the full interfaces distinguish them. (ii) Consider a two-stage selector that takes the top mm primitives 𝒮m​(q)\mathcal{S}_{m}(q) under a similarity-only selector and then orders them by any procedure, placing the remaining primitives after them. For every k≤mk\leq m and every task qq,

hit@k≤𝟏[𝒮m(q)∩𝒰q≠∅],recall@k≤|𝒮m​(q)∩𝒰q||𝒰q|,\text{hit@}k\leq\mathbf{1}\bigl[\mathcal{S}_{m}(q)\cap\mathcal{U}_{q}\neq\varnothing\bigr],\qquad\text{recall@}k\leq\frac{|\mathcal{S}_{m}(q)\cap\mathcal{U}_{q}|}{|\mathcal{U}_{q}|}, (10)

for any model in the second stage. (iii) The expected hit@kk objective S↦Pr⁡(S∩𝒰q≠∅∣X)S\mapsto\Pr(S\cap\mathcal{U}_{q}\neq\varnothing\mid X) is monotone and submodular, and greedy selection with the true marginal gains attains at least 1−(1−1/k)k≥1−1/e1-(1-1/k)^{k}\geq 1-1/e of the best size-kk coverage.

The study of self-advertised method selection proves these results for selecting proof methods. An assessment run over the whole library, as in Eq. (3), escapes the ceiling of Eq. (10); its coverage is then limited by the information in XX and by how accurately the model judges applicability. Expected hit@kk is submodular: once a shortlist holds a primitive that is likely to serve the task, a near-duplicate adds little, so the best size-kk shortlist need not consist of the kk individually most likely primitives.

4.  Experiments

We evaluate HEELO through its eight primitive families, each on the benchmarks of its own task and against the baselines of its companion study. Three families use the terms of their own studies: the resource of a Math Primitive is a Method Contract, that of a Knowledge Primitive is a source model, and a Navigation Primitive is a territory-backed worker. We order the families by the demand that their tasks place on the last mile, from calling a tool that needs no change to fitting the harness itself to the task. Each family keeps the notation of its paper; the budget BB, for instance, counts revision rounds in HEART and HERMES, Lean compilations for Math Primitives, and tokens in SourceLearn. In every table, a shaded row marks the primitive system under study, and differences between rates are in percentage points (pp).

4.1.  Experimental Setup

Tasks and Datasets. The eight families cover the following tasks and benchmarks. (i) LLM tool use: ToolBench, which evaluates the use of a large catalogue of real APIs [6]; NESTFUL, whose call sequences feed one call’s output into the next [32]; τ2\tau^{2}-Bench, which extends the tool–agent–user setting of τ\tau-bench to dual control [31, 34]; ACEBench, which targets robustness and fine-grained tool use across complex multi-tool workflows [58]; BFCLv4, which covers agentic web search and memory function calling [20]; and 50 end-to-end real-world tasks in five domains [44]. (ii) Repository construction: the 522 frozen tasks of LEGO-REPO, across seven domains and five difficulty bands [45], and the external repository benchmarks RepoZero, RepoGenesis, and RepoCraft under their published protocols. (iii) Formal theorem proving: 120 Putnam 2015–2025 problems and 60 IMO ProofBench problems in Lean 4 with Mathlib [10, 11], held out from the Putnam 2000–2014 solutions from which the contract library was built [46]. (iv) Knowledge-intensive tasks: MultiDoc2Dial, NarrativeQA, SWE-QA, APIBench, and AppWorld [146, 147, 148, 7, 149]. (v) Multi-agent systems: AIME25, AIME24, MATH, GSM8K, HumanEval+, MBPP+, MedQA, and GPQA-Diamond [150, 151, 152, 153, 154, 155, 156]. (vi) Software engineering: SWE-bench Verified [16], Terminal-Bench 4.0 [17], DevOps-Gym [83], and whole-repository migrations from SWE Refactor Bench [82]. (vii) Large information spaces: multi-document QA over HotpotQA [93], 2WikiMultiHopQA [157], and MuSiQue [158]; RepoProbe-Python, SWE-QA-Pro, and GAIA-Text-103 [159, 160, 18]; controlled spaces of 32K to 512K tokens built on LongAgent’s multi-needle setting [109]; and a demand intervention in a fixed 512K space. (viii) Agent harnesses: sampled subsets of 100 SWE-bench Verified and 45 Terminal-Bench 2.0 tasks, with two attempts per task and development tasks disjoint from evaluation [51]. Additional details on each study’s subsets, versions, and changes to the evaluation interface are in Appendix D.

Baselines. We compare each family with established methods of its task and with controls that remove or replace its primitives while the rest of the pipeline stays fixed. (i) LLM tool use: ReAct [1], retrieval-only selection, a planner–executor, and DFSDT, ToolLLM’s depth-first search over a decision tree [6], all on the backbone and tool catalogue of the Tool Primitives, together with the reference systems of its benchmarks. (ii) Repository construction: construction paradigms from single-shot generation through execution feedback, diagnosis, and retrieval to retrieval with a generic code editor, and the independently developed repository agents OpenHands, Claude Code, SWE-agent, and Agentless, each under its own harness [9, 5, 8, 74]. (iii) Formal theorem proving: for method selection, random order, BM25 [161], TF-IDF [162], and three embedding retrievers, two from OpenAI [163] and Qwen3 Embedding [164], with each embedding retriever used alone and with listwise reranking of its top ten by the selector backbone [123]; for proving, one attempt without retrieval (Base), pass@20 with twice the compilation budget, APOLLO [117], and the same AxProverBase loop without a contract [118]. (iv) Knowledge-intensive tasks: Hybrid RAG, RAPTOR [21], HippoRAG 2 [98], and Agent Workflow Memory [25]. (v) Multi-agent systems: a single agent, TextMAS with natural-language communication, LatentMAS [137] in its sequential configuration, and each single primitive applied to every query, the last three with four agents each; on Llama-3-70B-Instruct, eight existing MAS methods, among them LLM-Debate [131] and MAS-GPT [134], and the prompting baselines Chain-of-Thought [165] and Self-Consistency [166]. (vi) Software engineering: Codex [4], Claude Code [5], OpenHands [9], mini-SWE-agent [8], Grok Build, SageAgent, and Aider with the same backbones. (vii) Large information spaces: direct, iterative sparse, and dense retrieval, ChainRAG [106], S2G-RAG [108], ReAct, OWL [113], the repository agents ReAct with RepoGraph [167] and RepoDistill [168], the benchmark-specific SWE-QA-Pro Agent [160], and, for long contexts, LongAgent [109] and Chain of Agents [110]. (viii) Agent harnesses: the mini-SWE-agent seed harness, SWE-agent [8], Codex, MemoHarness [144], and MetaHarness [143].

Models. Each family keeps the backbones of its companion study, and its controls hold the backbone fixed across arms unless the control varies the model itself. Tool Primitives and HEART’s request decomposition, value resolution, and result validation all run Qwen3-8B [169]. Code Primitives adapt with GPT-5.6 Terra, which also fills the backbone and diagnosis positions, and a model-allocation study varies all three. Math Primitives are selected by GPT-5.6 Luna [170], GPT-5.6 Terra, or DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash [171], and GPT-5.6 Luna drives the prover. SourceLearn learns and applies Knowledge Primitives with GPT-5.6 Luna, GPT-OSS-120B [172], or DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, one backend per configuration performing every LLM step of every method. Agent Primitives run Qwen3-8B and two DeepSeek-R1-Distill models [173] as worker backbones, three of the study’s five, and Llama-3-70B-Instruct [174] in the comparison with existing MAS methods; they are composed per query by a GPT-5.2 Organizer, which Claude-4 [175] replaces in an ablation. The controls of Dev-Primitives run GPT-5.6 Sol, and their harness comparisons run each baseline’s own backbone in both arms. Navigation Primitives and the rest of their system run on GPT-4.1, and ANTMAN-H keeps the GPT-4.1 orchestrator and runs every other component, the Navigation Primitives included, on Qwen3-8B. Harness Primitives are developed with GPT-5.6 Sol and composed for a GPT-5.6 Luna actor at medium effort, whose backbone the composer shares; GPT-5.6 Terra, DeepSeek-V4-Flash, and Claude-4.5-Haiku serve as actors not used in development.

4.2.  Tool Primitives for LLM Tool Use

LLM tool use places the smallest demand on the last mile: each tool does what the task needs, and what remains is to call it correctly. In function calling, the model writes schema-compliant arguments for each call [2, 7, 20] and maps one tool’s output into the next tool’s input schema, a step that nested and multi-turn calls make brittle, while a large catalogue in context degrades performance [39]. Tool Primitives reverse this burden: instead of requiring models to speak the language of APIs, they make tools speak the language of models [44]. Each Tool Primitive resolves the schema of its own tool, and HEART, a harness engineering framework, decomposes each query into an invocation plan, grounds each step’s arguments, and validates every returned result (Section 3.4).

Setup. We evaluate HEART on the five benchmarks of its study and report three of them in full: the six single- and multi-tool splits of ToolBench [6], NESTFUL [32], and the retail, airline, and telecom domains of τ2\tau^{2}-Bench [31]. The baselines are each benchmark’s reference systems: on ToolBench, models from Vicuna [176] and Alpaca [177] to ToolLLaMA [6] and GPT-4 [178] under ReAct [1] and DFSDT; on NESTFUL, function-calling models such as xLAM [52], Hammer [54], ToolACE [19], and Granite [179] and general models from Llama-3.1 [174] and Mixtral [180] to DeepSeek-V3 [181] and GPT-4o [182]; and on τ2\tau^{2}-Bench, GPT-4.1, GPT-4.1-mini, GPT-o4-mini, and Claude-3.7-Sonnet. GPT-5.4, Claude-4.6-Sonnet, and Gemini-3.1-Pro appear on all five. HEART runs Qwen3-8B [169] in request decomposition, value resolution, result validation, and the Tool Primitives, with revision budget B=3B=3 and retrieval over the 25,519 tools of ToolFace; results average three runs, and eight on τ2\tau^{2}-Bench.

Main Results. On ToolBench (Table 1), HEART reaches an average pass rate of 75.1% and win rate of 75.7%. Without tree search, it leads Claude-4.6-Sonnet with DFSDT, the strongest commercial baseline, by 1.7 and 1.9 pp, and ToolLLaMA with DFSDT and its retriever, the strongest fine-tuned baseline, by 7.8 and 12.6 pp. The lead is largest on I3-Inst., the hardest split, whose multi-tool instructions require cross-API dependencies: 77.2% pass and 89.4% win rates, 3.4 and 2.9 pp above Claude-4.6-Sonnet with DFSDT. On the same Qwen3-8B backbone and ToolFace catalogue, HEART leads DFSDT, the strongest of four scaffolds on ToolBench, by 19.3 pp pass rate, 75.1% against 55.8%, and by 0.31 NESTFUL full accuracy (Table 25).

On NESTFUL (Table 2), HEART is best on all five metrics under both one- and three-shot demonstrations. Its full-sequence accuracy is 0.44 and 0.47, against 0.40 and 0.42 for GPT-5.4, the strongest baseline, and its win rate 0.75 and 0.79, against 0.66 and 0.68. Fine-tuning on flat tool-use trajectories does not carry over to nested sequences: with one-shot demonstrations, the xLAM models up to 8B and both ToolACE models reach 0.00 full accuracy. Nor does scale close the gap, as DeepSeek-V3, with 685B parameters, reaches 0.09.

On τ2\tau^{2}-Bench (Table 3), HEART has the highest Passk in each domain for each kk. Its Pass1 margins over Claude-4.6-Sonnet, the strongest baseline model, are small, 0.82, 0.73, and 0.63 against 0.80, 0.72, and 0.58 on retail, airline, and telecom, and they widen with kk: in the airline domain, whose tasks include booking a flight under the airline’s policy, HEART succeeds in all four trials on 0.63 of the tasks against 0.50, and in telecom on 0.50 against 0.33. Although each invocation step adds a Tool Primitive’s model call and HEART uses 20,887 to 24,531 tokens per task, it costs $0.0146 to $0.0172 per task on Qwen3-8B, against $0.1098 to $0.1219 for GPT-5.4, up to 7.7×7.7\times less.

Component Ablation. Removing one component at a time locates the gain in the natural-language interface (Table 4). Without ToolFace and its Tool Primitives, value resolution resolves arguments against raw schemas and dispatches calls itself; ToolBench pass rate then falls from 75.1% to 16.1% and NESTFUL full accuracy from 0.44 to 0.06. Removing result validation, which drives revision, gives the second-largest drop, to 47.6% and 0.15, and removing request decomposition or value resolution gives 57.2% and 62.4%. Removing the primitives also removes one model call per step; given that budget to self-refine its schema-compliant arguments at matched backbone, calls, and tokens, value resolution without primitives reaches 34.2% (Table 26), so the interface carries most of the gain.

On the other two benchmarks, HEART has the highest ACEBench Overall score, 86.9, and the highest BFCLv4 Web Search and Memory Overall scores, 86.0 and 69.38 [58, 20]. On 50 end-to-end real-world tasks in five domains, it completes 84%, against 20% to 24% for GPT-5.4, Claude-4.6-Sonnet, and Gemini-3.1-Pro in their product interfaces and 22% to 32% when they call the ToolFace tools through native function calling. We provide the full framework of HEART, its overview figure, the matched-backbone and budget-matched controls, and further diagnostics in Appendix B.1. A Tool Primitive invokes its function as it is; a component that must itself change to fit its target calls for a primitive that adapts the resource it owns, the step a Code Primitive takes.

\WF@box

4.3.  Code Primitives for Repository Construction

Repository construction asks an agent to deliver a complete project whose modules, interfaces, configuration, tests, and dependencies work together [81]. When the project reuses code, the last mile lies in making that code fit its target. A component reused from another repository becomes part of the delivered source, so its signatures, data representations, and dependencies must be reconciled with the target. Retrieval-augmented code generation finds related code [35, 70, 71] but leaves this reconciliation to the caller. Code Primitives assign it to the component itself: each Code Primitive adapts the implementation it owns to the target and checks the result against the tests it carries, while LEGO retrieves, coordinates, and verifies these primitives during construction [45].

Setup. LEGO-REPO poses the task as reconstruction. Each of its 522 frozen tasks removes the implementation of an installable Python package, keeps the package’s interfaces, native tests, and environment, and grades the delivered repository with those tests. The tasks span seven domains and five difficulty bands, D1–D5, which combine module count with the number of native tests the original passes. Let Π⁡(X)\Pi(X) denote the number of native tests passed using source set XX. For task TT, the original sources OO define the identity ceiling c⁡(T)=Π⁡(O)c(T)=\Pi(O) and an empty reconstruction tree the floor f⁡(T)=Π⁡(∅)f(T)=\Pi(\varnothing), and generated sources GG score

s⁡(G,T)=clamp[0,1]⁡(Π⁡(G)−f⁡(T)c⁡(T)−f⁡(T)),Sdelivery=1522​∑T=1522s~T,s~T={s⁡(GT,T),admissible,0,otherwise,s(G;T)=\operatorname{clamp}_{[0,1]}\left(\frac{\Pi(G)-f(T)}{c(T)-f(T)}\right),\qquad S_{\mathrm{delivery}}=\frac{1}{522}\sum_{T=1}^{522}\widetilde{s}_{T},\qquad\widetilde{s}_{T}=\begin{cases}s(G_{T};T),&\text{admissible},\\ 0,&\text{otherwise},\end{cases} (11)

where a run is admissible when c⁡(T)−f⁡(T)≥5c(T)-f(T)\geq 5, execution completes, and provenance confirms that the tests exercised the generated target code. The zero-score rate is the fraction of tasks assigned 0. The baselines are construction paradigms, from single-shot generation to retrieval with a generic code editor, and independently developed repository agents, among them OpenHands and Claude Code [9, 5], each under its own harness with tasks, environment, and grading held fixed. Unless a configuration varies them, GPT-5.6 Terra fills the backbone, adaptation, and diagnosis positions, retrieval returns the top two of 1,424 CodeFace entries per requirement, and revision runs at most five rounds per module.

Main Results. Construction from scratch weakens as repositories grow: under execution feedback, GPT-5.6 Terra is the strongest of the study’s 13 backbones, and the mean delivery of the 13 falls from 0.393 on D1 to 0.038 on D5. Table 5 compares the construction paradigms on all 522 tasks with GPT-5.6 Terra. LEGO reaches a delivery score of 0.5134 against 0.3180 for execution feedback, a gain of 0.1954 or 61.4%, and lowers the zero-score rate from 41.0% to 18.8%. Retrieval adds 0.0172 to execution feedback, whereas primitive adaptation adds 0.1154 to retrieval with diagnosis; RAG with a generic editor, the strongest paradigm without primitive adaptation, reaches 0.4093. The strongest independent repository agents stay near the feedback baseline: OpenHands reaches 0.3263 with GPT-5.6 Terra and Claude Code 0.3170 with Claude Sonnet 5, while SWE-agent and Agentless, run with GPT-5.6 Terra through an issue-to-patch adapter, reach 0.2750 and 0.2181 [8, 74]. LEGO leads OpenHands and Claude Code on the same backbones by 57.3% and 56.2%, at 0.5134 and 0.4953. Across the 13 backbones of the study, with adaptation and diagnosis on GPT-5.6 Terra, LEGO improves all 13 and raises mean delivery from 0.1926 to 0.3400, a gain of 0.1474 [45].

Access versus Adaptation. Access to the retrieved components adds little; the gain comes from adapting them. The consumption controls of Table 6 keep LEGO’s retrieval and diagnosis and vary how the components are used. As read-only context with their contracts and tests, they reach 0.3544, and vendored and called unchanged they reach 0.3430, against 0.3469 for diagnosis without a library; on D5, unchanged invocation falls to 0.060 against 0.135 for that reference. Structured-schema adaptation keeps primitive adaptation but replaces the natural-language request with a typed field mapping, and it scores 0.4974 against 0.5134. Most of LEGO’s 0.1041 margin over generic editing lies in the primitive’s fields: given the carried tests, the interface contract and provenance, and the dependency closure, a generic editor over the same components recovers 0.0946 of it.

Cost and Model Allocation. Spending LEGO’s recorded-call budget on more repair attempts does not close the gap: execution feedback with eight attempts per module costs $2.07 per task and reaches 0.3437, against 0.5134 at $2.08 for LEGO. The locally scoped models can also be small. With GPT-OSS-20B as the resident LLM MiM_{i} of each primitive and as the diagnosis model, LEGO keeps 95.1% of its delivery, 0.4880, at 24.0% lower cost; replacing the backbone with DeepSeek-V3.2 keeps 48.1%. Delivery thus depends more on the backbone, which plans and integrates the repository, than on these models.

The gain holds across repository sizes, library restrictions, and benchmarks. Over the five bands, the absolute gain stays between 0.161 and 0.209, so the relative gain rises from 30.7% on D1 to 162.0% on D5 as feedback falls. Excluding same-repository donors lowers delivery to 0.4743, and a library re-mined from a corpus disjoint from the benchmark repositories gains 0.1348 over feedback. Under the published protocols of three external repository benchmarks, LEGO with GPT-5.6 Terra raises the RepoZero (Python to Python) pass rate from 53.8% to 62.9%, the RepoGenesis resolved rate from 41.0% to 48.2%, and the RepoCraft normalized score from 0.436 to 0.501 over execution feedback, relative gains of 16.9%, 17.6%, and 14.9%. With the CodeFace entries traced to these targets removed, the library covers 29.6–34.8% of their target modules, against 61.4% on LEGO-REPO.

We provide the full framework of LEGO, its overview figure, the field-by-field decomposition of the primitive, and the full model-allocation table in Appendix B.2, with breakdowns by band and domain, donor-provenance controls, attempt budgets, and seed uncertainty in Appendix C. A Code Primitive checks its adaptation against the tests it carries and leaves the integrated result to the repository’s build and tests. When an exact checker judges the final result, the open step moves earlier, to deciding which method to apply.
