4.4.  Math Primitives for Formal Theorem Proving

In formal theorem proving with Lean 4 and Mathlib [10, 11], the kernel checks each completed proof, and LLM provers generate and revise proofs against this check [114, 115, 117], aided by premise selection, Mathlib search, and lemma libraries [119, 120, 121, 122]. Here the last mile is deciding whether a method applies: which part of the goal it targets, what action it takes there, and which conditions that action requires. For n​∑iai2≥(∑iai)2n\sum_{i}a_{i}^{2}\geq(\sum_{i}a_{i})^{2} over the reals, similarity retrieval proposes AM–GM, which needs ai≥0a_{i}\geq 0, a condition the goal does not give, while Cauchy–Schwarz applies. Math Primitives let the library speak instead: each holds a proof method as a Method Contract, and under self-advertised method selection every contract proposes how it would be used on the goal before the contracts are ranked [46].

Setup. We evaluate on 120 Putnam problems from 2015–2025 and 60 IMO ProofBench problems, held out from the Putnam 2000–2014 solutions behind the 82 contracts. Each problem is labeled with the contracts whose method appears in its official solution; GPT-5.6 Sol proposed the labels, and a human checked each one before any selector ran. The baselines are random ordering, BM25, TF-IDF cosine, and three embedding retrievers, each also paired with a listwise LLM reranker over its top ten candidates. The LLM-based selectors within a block of Table 7 share one backbone, GPT-5.6 Terra, GPT-5.6 Luna, or DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash.

Main Results. Self-advertisement gives the broadest shortlist coverage (Table 7). Lexical matching reaches at most 0.525 Putnam hit@5, dense embeddings 0.775, and LLM reranking of an embedding pool 0.858. Self-advertisement attains the highest recall@5 in all six backbone–benchmark settings, and on Putnam it also leads at hit@3, hit@5, and MRR under each backbone. With GPT-5.6 Luna, the prover’s backbone, it reaches 0.950 Putnam hit@5 against 0.842 for the strongest reranker, and 0.917 IMO ProofBench hit@5 against 0.883, a difference of two of the 60 problems. Its lead grows with the backbone while the rerankers plateau: from DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash to GPT-5.6 Luna to GPT-5.6 Terra, its Putnam hit@5 rises from 0.900 to 0.950 to 0.975, and the best reranker stays at 0.842, 0.842, and 0.858. The lead under DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash shows that it does not depend on the model family that drafted the contracts and labels. On IMO ProofBench, whose problems come from different competitions than the Putnam-derived library, self-advertisement keeps its recall@5 lead, at 0.494, 0.554, and 0.493 under GPT-5.6 Terra, GPT-5.6 Luna, and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, against at most 0.469, 0.468, and 0.449 for the rerankers.

Rerankers remain more precise at rank one in most settings; under GPT-5.6 Luna, the best reaches 0.692 Putnam hit@1 against 0.658 for self-advertisement. The runoff targets this gap: with the same backbone, it re-ranks self-advertisement’s top ten by comparing the leading proposals. Under GPT-5.6 Terra, it raises Putnam hit@1 from 0.625 to 0.725, above the strongest reranker’s 0.675, and IMO ProofBench hit@1 from 0.517 to 0.600, with the best MRR on both benchmarks (0.831 and 0.736). Under DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, it gives the best Putnam hit@1 and MRR (0.608 and 0.735), and under GPT-5.6 Luna it changes each hit metric by at most three problems.

Downstream Proving. The selected contract also helps the prover (Table 8). AxProverBase is an Ax-Prover whole-proof repair loop driven by GPT-5.6 Luna with ten Lean compilations per problem [118], and the contract arm adds the execution side of the top-ranked contract to its initial prompt. The contract more than doubles AxProverBase’s success on Putnam, from 5.8% to 12.5%, and raises it from 10.0% to 15.0% on IMO ProofBench. On Putnam the gains come from analysis (3.3% to 10.0%) and discrete problems (4.3% to 17.4%), while algebra stays at 9.1%; on IMO ProofBench the contract adds Basic problems (20.0% to 26.7%) and the one Advanced problem that any arm solves. Base and pass@20 solve almost no problems, although pass@20 has twice the budget, and APOLLO [117] trails both AxProverBase arms. Since the two arms share the prover, its backbone, and its budget, the gain reflects selection and contract content together.

Applicability Beyond Similarity. The coverage gains of Table 7 come largely from methods that similarity overlooks. We place each problem by the rank of its highest-ranked annotated method under self-advertisement with GPT-5.6 Luna and by that method’s rank under BM25 and each embedding retriever (Figure 17 in Appendix C). Under all four retrievers, annotated methods that similarity ranks outside its top five enter the top five of self-advertisement, and many of them lie outside the top ten that the rerankers receive. This is the candidate-pool ceiling of Proposition 3.3(ii) at work: a reranker reorders the pool that similarity retrieved, so no reranking backbone recovers a method that the pool omits. Self-advertisement judges all 82 contracts, and each method it brings into the shortlist arrives with a target, an action, and required conditions that can be checked against the goal.

We provide the full method of self-advertised method selection, its overview figure, the theory behind the commitment gate and the runoff, and the experimental configuration in Appendix B.3. A Method Contract stays fixed once built, whereas a Knowledge Primitive’s source model changes as the agent studies its source.

\WF@box

4.5.  Knowledge Primitives for Knowledge-Intensive Tasks

When many tasks draw on one persistent, authoritative source, such as a document collection, a code repository, or API documentation, the last mile is understanding that source: how its knowledge is structured, interpreted, and applied, beyond the passages that one task retrieves. Retrieval brings such passages into each task [12, 86], structured indexes organize the source’s content [21, 94, 98], and agent memories keep experience from earlier tasks [22, 23, 25], yet repeated use of a source is still treated as repeated access. Knowledge Primitives turn this repeated use into source learning: the resource of a Knowledge Primitive is a persistent source model that holds reusable source-specific competence, while the source itself remains the authority for factual content. SourceLearn [47] develops this source model in two ways. Before future tasks are known, Self-Directed Source Learning studies what the source model does not yet explain well, and Task-Guided Source Learning uses guidance tasks to expose local gaps and recurring needs in how the source is represented. We provide the full framework of SourceLearn in Appendix B.4, together with its overview figure, the benchmark and baseline settings, and the comparison at a matched context budget.

Setup. We evaluate SourceLearn on question answering over document collections, stories, and code repositories with MultiDoc2Dial [146], NarrativeQA [147], and SWE-QA [148]; tool use with APIBench [7]; and interactive tasks with AppWorld [149]. Each document collection, story, repository, or API library is one source. Guidance and test tasks are disjoint, with three fixed 30%/70% splits and AppWorld’s official training and test-normal splits. GPT-5.6 Luna judges QA answers against the references, and APIBench and AppWorld use their official evaluators. The baselines are task-local retrieval with Hybrid RAG, persistent source representations with RAPTOR [21] and HippoRAG 2 [98], and experience-based memory with AWM [25], which learns workflows from the same guidance tasks. Each configuration uses a single backbone, GPT-5.6 Luna [170], GPT-OSS-120B [172], or DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash [171], for the LLM operations of all methods, which share the embedding model, the answer or agent prompt, and, on AppWorld, the ReAct-style code agent [1]. SourceLearn adds the activated source model to the Hybrid RAG evidence R⁡(D,q)R(D,q), which AWM also receives, so the comparison with Hybrid RAG isolates the contribution of the source model.

Main Results. Across the 15 settings of Table 9, SourceLearn is the best method in 13 and the second best in one more. It improves on Hybrid RAG in 14 settings, and its average gain over the five benchmarks is 14.3 pp with GPT-5.6 Luna, 4.9 pp with GPT-OSS-120B, and 13.4 pp with DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash. The gains span document, code, and API sources and exceed 10 pp on four of the five benchmarks with GPT-5.6 Luna and with DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash; with GPT-5.6 Luna, MultiDoc2Dial rises from 64.9% to 77.6% and APIBench from 47.8% to 70.4%. The two settings in which it is not the best both use GPT-OSS-120B: HippoRAG 2 leads on SWE-QA (56.7% against 53.4%), and on AppWorld SourceLearn falls below Hybrid RAG (27.4% against 30.4%). The baselines help unevenly. RAPTOR’s summary tree falls below Hybrid RAG on SWE-QA under all three backbones, where HippoRAG 2 is the strongest baseline, and AWM, the strongest baseline on APIBench, moves question-answering accuracy by at most 3.9 pp. Learning the source transfers across benchmarks more evenly than structuring its content or retaining task experience. SourceLearn also leads on three of the four sources tested with GPT-5.6 Luna at a matched context budget, where each retrieval baseline fills SourceLearn’s per-question budget by reading further down its own ranking; HippoRAG 2 leads on Sphinx (73.5% against 72.5%; Table 29).

Analysis. Both learning mechanisms contribute and complement each other. We remove each in turn with GPT-5.6 Luna on two sources of each QA benchmark, with the splits and task-time source access of the main results (Figure 9). The full model MTM_{T} is the most accurate on all three benchmarks, omitting Self-Directed or Task-Guided Source Learning lowers accuracy, and the initial model M0M_{0} is the lowest. Within Task-Guided Source Learning, removing failure-guided local refinement or cross-task representation learning lowers accuracy on all three benchmarks, and removing both, which recovers the self-directed model MSM_{S}, lowers it further. The two pathways thus carry different information from the same guidance tasks: concrete failures repair local gaps, while recurring representation lessons change how the whole model represents the source. Learning also does more than compress the source (Figure 19). From M0M_{0} to MTM_{T}, the model shifts from isolated look-up content toward rules and procedures, and the share of units with an explicit applicability condition rises from roughly 30% to 65–82% on the four MultiDoc2Dial sources. The share of the claims required by test questions that the model represents rises from 23.2% to 40.0%, and questions with all of their required claims represented are answered correctly 86.6% of the time, against 67.5% when none are.

The Tool, Code, Math, and Knowledge Primitives each own a resource that a single model applies; Agent Primitives own a recurring multi-agent computation pattern, whose agents run on one LLM and exchange KV caches.

\WF@box

4.6.  Agent Primitives for Multi-Agent Systems

Where several agents share one problem, the last mile lies in how they combine their work. Multi-agent systems (MAS) let LLM agents critique, vote, and plan together, but they are usually designed task by task, with handcrafted roles and interaction prompts, so their complexity grows with the task, and no reusable abstraction amortizes it. Their agents also communicate in natural language, which degrades over long, multi-stage interactions. In two stress tests with Qwen3-8B, an instruction injected at the midpoint of a long context is followed in 15.6% of cases through text and in 73.3% through KV caches, and after ten unrelated sentences are injected into solved GSM8K traces, 47% of the problems stay solved through text and 93% through KV caches. Agent Primitives [48] address both problems with three reusable latent building blocks, Review, Voting and Selection, and Planning and Execution, whose internal agents communicate through KV caches and which an LLM Organizer composes into a primitive-based MAS for each query.

Setup. The evaluation covers mathematical problem solving on AIME24, AIME25, MATH, and GSM8K [151, 150, 152, 153], code generation on HumanEval+ and MBPP+, which extend the tests of HumanEval and MBPP [154, 183, 184], and question answering on MedQA and GPQA-Diamond [155, 156]. The baselines are a single agent, a text-based MAS (TextMAS), LatentMAS [137] in its sequential configuration, and each primitive applied alone to all queries; the last three use four agents each, whereas the Organizer, GPT-5.2 by default, sets the number of agents per query. KV cache communication assumes that the communicating agents share parameters and positional encoding, so all agents of a run use one worker backbone: Qwen3-8B [169], DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B, or DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-70B [173], abbreviated R1/Qwen-32B and R1/Llama-70B.

Main Results. Composing primitives gives the highest mean accuracy with each backbone (Table 10). With Qwen3-8B, the primitive-based MAS reaches 75.3%, against 58.8% for a single agent, 66.1% for TextMAS, 67.8% for LatentMAS, and 71.3% for Voting and Selection, the strongest single primitive. With R1/Qwen-32B and R1/Llama-70B, it improves on a single agent by 6.6 and 6.3 pp. Across the three backbones, it is best or tied for best on each benchmark except GSM8K with R1/Qwen-32B, where LatentMAS reaches 95.2% against 95.0%. Each primitive used alone also improves on the mean accuracy of a single agent, and composing them adds 4.0, 2.6, and 1.9 pp on the three backbones over the strongest one, Voting and Selection. TextMAS improves on a single agent by 2.4 to 7.3 pp. LatentMAS is the strongest baseline with R1/Qwen-32B, at 75.9%, but falls to 60.0% with R1/Llama-70B, 10.1 pp below a single agent, which the study attributes to its aggressive chunking of latent reasoning steps; the more conservative KV cache communication of Agent Primitives improves on a single agent with each backbone.

Existing MAS Methods. Table 11 compares the primitive-based MAS on Llama-3-70B-Instruct [174] with eight MAS methods, LLM-Debate [131], Self-Refine [140], Quality-Diversity [185], SPP [186], AgentVerse [130], GPTSwarm [27], DyLAN [133], and MAS-GPT [134], and with two prompting baselines, Chain-of-Thought [165] and Self-Consistency [166]. It is the most accurate method on MATH, HumanEval+, and GPQA, with 72.4%, 82.3%, and 53.2%. On MATH and HumanEval+, it leads MAS-GPT, the strongest prior method, by 3.7 and 3.4 pp, and on GPQA the other methods reach 33.6 to 40.2%. Self-Consistency leads on GSM8K, with 95.0% against 93.8%. These gains come at moderate cost. Across the study’s five worker backbones, the primitive-based MAS reduces token usage and inference latency by about 3–4×\times relative to TextMAS, with 1.3–1.6×\times overhead relative to single-agent inference, and on Llama-3-70B-Instruct it uses fewer output tokens than each MAS baseline, the Organizer’s 200–400 tokens per query included.

Analysis. The ablations attribute the gain to per-query composition and to KV cache communication. Replacing the Organizer’s choice with a random structure from the Knowledge Pool lowers accuracy by 4.9 to 6.6 pp with Qwen3-8B and by up to 12.4 pp with R1/Llama-70B, and removing the pool costs up to 11.9 pp. Replacing GPT-5.2 with Claude-4 [175] as the Organizer keeps accuracy within 1.8 pp, so the main benefit comes from problem-aware structure selection and not from a particular Organizer model (Tables 47 and 47). KV cache communication in turn depends on re-indexing the sender’s keys for RoPE. Without the re-indexing, the primitive-based MAS on R1/Llama-70B falls from 85.3% to 31.1% on HumanEval+ and from 81.9% to 36.6% on MedQA, and each primitive alone falls to between 16.7% and 34.7%, so the loss arises within the primitives; with Qwen3-8B, the largest drop is 13.3 pp (Table 30). With text communication, the three primitives reach 50.0, 56.7, and 53.3% on Qwen3-8B AIME25, above the 46.7% of a single agent, and KV caches raise them to 60.0, 66.7, and 66.7%, so the primitive abstraction and KV cache communication each contribute.

We provide the full framework of Agent Primitives, its overview figure, and additional results in Appendix B.5. The agents of an Agent Primitive share one LLM inside the primitive; when the units that must coordinate are the components of a repository, Dev-Primitives make each component a primitive of its own.

\WF@box

4.7.  Dev-Primitives for Software Engineering

The last mile of software engineering runs through the repository. The program state that a change must respect is spread over interdependent sources, configurations, and tests, and each edit changes the repository that the next step reads, so a single agent repeatedly reconstructs this distributed state within one trajectory, whose growing history leads to context explosion and semantic drift. Dev-Primitives [49] let individual software components reason about their own responsibilities and communicate relevant information directly to one another, and HERMES instantiates them through dynamic activation, localized collaboration, environment execution, and diagnosis-driven revision.

Setup. We evaluate HERMES on four benchmarks: SWE-bench Verified [16], 500 human-validated GitHub issues; SWE Refactor Bench [82], 20 whole-repository migrations scored by a composite; Terminal-Bench 4.0 [17], 66 terminal tasks run five times each; and DevOps-Gym [83], scored by the unweighted mean over its build and configuration, monitoring, issue-resolving, and test-generation stages. The baselines are the harnesses of published configurations, among them mini-SWE-agent [8], Claude Code [5], Codex [4], and OpenHands [9], and HERMES runs on the backbone and reasoning effort of each, so that the comparison isolates the harness. The backbones include GPT-5.6 Sol, Terra, and Luna, Claude Opus 5 and Sonnet 5, DeepSeek-V4, and Qwen3-8B [169], with medium reasoning effort unless stated otherwise and B=3B=3 revision rounds.

Main Results. With GPT-5.6 Sol at medium effort, HERMES improves on the matched baseline harnesses by 12.4 pp on average over the four benchmarks. On SWE-bench Verified (Table 12), it raises the resolved rate over mini-SWE-agent for 19 of the 20 backbones, ties on Claude Opus 5 at 97.00%, and improves on Claude Code and Codex by 5.20 and 9.20 pp. The gains are largest where the baseline is weakest, 19.40 pp for GPT-5-mini, from 60.80% to 80.20%, and smallest on frontier backbones: with GPT-5.6 Sol, HERMES resolves 97.00±0.7697.00\pm 0.76% against 96.20±0.8696.20\pm 0.86%, at $1.80 against $1.15 per task. Coordination need not cost time, since with Claude Sonnet 5 HERMES gains 6.20 pp while average latency falls from 962.37 s to 824.63 s. With Qwen3-8B in all roles, it resolves 80.60%.

The largest gain with GPT-5.6 Sol at medium effort is on whole-repository migration: on SWE Refactor Bench (Table 31), HERMES raises the composite by 24.5 pp, from 6.5% under Codex to 31.0%, and at high effort from 19.0% to 36.5%; three repetitions of the default configuration give 31.0±1.331.0\pm 1.3. On Terminal-Bench 4.0 (Table 13), HERMES with GPT-5.6 Sol resolves 51.8% against 33.0% under Codex at medium effort and 55.5% against 37.3% at maximum effort, and GPT-5.6 Terra gains 26.3 and 26.7 pp. The smallest gains, 1.5 and 1.2 pp, are for Claude Opus 5, whose Claude Code configurations are the two strongest baselines. Most configurations spend more tokens, but with Claude Sonnet 5 at maximum effort, HERMES raises resolution by 27.6 pp, from 12.4% to 40.0%, while total cost falls from $9.6k to $7.4k. On DevOps-Gym (Table 14), the stage mean rises with GPT-5.6 Sol from 49.89% under Codex to 55.41%, with gains in all four stages. Across all baseline harnesses, HERMES raises the mean by 4.78 to 31.70 pp, and with Claude Opus 5 it reaches the highest mean, 57.10%.

Analysis. Removing one mechanism at a time shows where the gain arises (Table 15). Among the four removals, diagnosis feedback matters most: without it, Terminal-Bench 4.0 resolution falls from 51.8% to 41.2% and the SWE Refactor composite from 31.0 to 20.0, the largest drop on each benchmark. Once edits are artifact-local, a failure observed at the repository level must be routed back to the component that owns the responsible implementation, and diagnosis provides this routing. Execution feedback ranks second. Removing inter-primitive communication lowers the Refactor composite to 23.5 and Terminal-Bench resolution to 46.1%, larger losses than on SWE-bench Verified (97.0 to 94.2), in line with its role in coordinating changes that span files. Keeping all initially identified Dev-Primitives active lowers the scores by 1.2 to 3.0 points at 1.61 to 1.88 times the cost (Table 52). The primitives add value beyond the choice of components: one editor given the same plan and components resolves 38.8% of Terminal-Bench tasks, below each single-mechanism removal, and 45.5% at matched compute, against 51.8% for HERMES (Table 32).

The Dev-Primitives also run well on a small model. With GPT-5.6 Sol for activation and diagnosis, Qwen3-8B Dev-Primitives stay within 4.5 points of the homogeneous Sol configuration on all four benchmarks, at 26.2% lower Terminal-Bench cost, and a stronger model pays off more in diagnosis than in activation (Tables 50 and 52). We provide the full framework of HERMES, its overview figure, and additional results on component selection, the revision budget, and related multi-agent frameworks in Appendix B.6. HERMES chooses its Dev-Primitives before each round; when what a query needs changes as the search proceeds, the choice of primitives must follow the needs that remain open.

\WF@box

4.8.  Navigation Primitives for Large Information Spaces

In a large information space, the requirements of a query change as evidence arrives: new evidence can resolve or refine a requirement, reveal another, and redirect the search [187]. At the last mile, coordination must therefore follow what remains unresolved, whereas partition-driven multi-agent systems such as LongAgent [109] and Chain of Agents (CoA) [110] assign one member to each chunk of the input, so their coordination grows with the space. Navigation Primitives are workers that each search one territory of the space, and ANTMAN [50] coordinates them through a revisable Need Graph that tracks a query’s unresolved information needs and decides which primitives take part in the search (Section 3.4).

Setup. Three benchmarks require navigation in structured spaces: RepoProbe-Python, 108 questions over eight Python repositories [159]; a frozen 80-question set of SWE-QA-Pro [160]; and GAIA-Text-103, the text subset of GAIA for tool-using information seeking [18]. Two controlled interventions grow the space and the demand separately, and multi-document QA over HotpotQA [93], 2WikiMultiHopQA [157], and MuSiQue [158] checks answer quality on standard tasks. The baselines include direct, iterative sparse, and dense retrieval, S2G-RAG [108], the tool-using agents ReAct [1] and OWL [113], the repository agents ReAct with RepoGraph [167] and RepoDistill [168], and the benchmark-specific SWE-QA-Pro Agent. ANTMAN runs all components on GPT-4.1, as do the other methods in its evaluation harness, and ANTMAN-H runs all components except the orchestrator, the Navigation Primitives included, on Qwen3-8B [169].

Main Results. ANTMAN obtains the best overall score on all three structured benchmarks (Table 16): 38.21 on RepoProbe against 33.15 for iterative sparse retrieval, 79.78 on SWE-QA-Pro against 77.58 for the SWE-QA-Pro Agent and 67.38 for ReAct with RepoGraph, and 58.3% on GAIA-Text-103 against 45.6% for iterative sparse retrieval. On GAIA, a web-and-tool substrate with one territory-backed worker, unresolved needs decide only where the search continues, so the gain is not tied to repository-specific navigation machinery. ANTMAN-H scores 34.10, 74.60, and 57.3%, above all baselines on RepoProbe and GAIA-Text-103, and its GAIA gap to ANTMAN lies at Level 3, 25.0% against 41.7%.

Space Scaling. The space intervention tests Proposition 3.1, which bounds participation by realized demand whatever the number of territories, |ℒq||\mathcal{L}_{q}|. In LongAgent’s multi-needle Needle-in-a-Haystack PLUS setting, filler grows the distractor space around the preserved evidence of ten questions from 32K to 512K tokens, at approximately fixed demand. Under this 16×16\times growth, the mean number of Navigation Primitives that participate per query, the active coordination, grows 1.23×1.23\times, against 15.29×15.29\times for LongAgent and 15.33×15.33\times for CoA, whose members multiply with the partitions (Table 17). ANTMAN’s calls grow 1.21×1.21\times and its cost 6.90×6.90\times, against cost growth of 14.22×14.22\times and 16.11×16.11\times for the baselines, while its F1 rises by 0.065.

\WF@box

Demand Scaling. The reverse intervention fixes the 512K space, with its distractors, evidence locations, and eight territories, and raises the required evidence from 1 to 4 to 16 units (Table 18). The answer combines all required values, so omitting one unit leaves it ambiguous. Calls rise from 35.5 to 86.2 per query and cost from $0.107 to $0.293, and ANTMAN recovers the complete evidence and answers correctly at all three levels. Active coordination dips from 5.0 workers at one unit to 4.3 at four units and reaches 8.0 at 16 units; at one unit, most worker activity is exploration that finds no required evidence. Coordination thus stays nearly flat when the space grows and rises when the query needs more.

Evolving Need State. The ablations in Table 19, all under a budget of 100 LLM calls per query, separate the explicit need state from generic adaptive control. Graph-free Adaptive keeps adaptive worker selection, rerouting, and recovery but replans from the accumulated evidence and interaction history, without any explicit Need Graph. Its 512K F1 falls from 84.03 to 64.01 while it activates a comparable number of distinct workers, 3.20 against 3.17, so the gap does not come from wider participation; on the 40-question GAIA subset, its accuracy falls from 60.00 to 50.00. Static ANTMAN freezes the initial Need Graph and routing plan, and its 512K F1 falls to 40.32. Single removals play complementary roles: removing recovery gives 60.12 at 512K, removing need revision gives 42.50 on GAIA, and removing adaptive rerouting gives 72.13 against 81.43 on SWE-QA-Pro and leaves single-worker GAIA unchanged.

Further Results. On standard multi-document QA (Table 33), ANTMAN has the best macro average of nine methods, 0.711 EM and 0.814 F1, against 0.700 and 0.799 for S2G-RAG; it is best on HotpotQA and MuSiQue, and S2G-RAG leads on 2WikiMultiHopQA. Narrowing the context searched per need also makes it robust to evidence position: its Middle F1 minus the mean of its Early and Late F1 is +0.015+0.015, against −0.181-0.181 for direct full-context inference, which shows the lost-in-the-middle pattern [39]. We provide the full method of ANTMAN with its overview figure, implementation details, and these results in Appendix B.7. Across these experiments, unresolved needs decide which Navigation Primitives run, under a control program that is the same for all queries; Harness Primitives compose that program itself for each task.

\WF@box

4.9.  Harness Primitives for Agent Harnesses

For a fixed task-solving model, the actor, an agent’s success depends on its harness: the control program that constructs the actor’s requests, executes its actions through the available tools, returns observations, and decides when to terminate [143, 51]. The last mile then reaches the harness itself, which must fit the task. Hand-designed harnesses such as SWE-agent [8] and Codex [4], and the harnesses that optimizers such as MetaHarness find, apply one design to all tasks, yet a mechanism that improves one task can impose overhead or context distraction on another. Generating harness code for each task avoids this mismatch but adds generation and debugging cost, with execution risks that compound as more mechanisms are generated. Harness Primitives make task-specific harnesses possible without generating or repairing mechanism code at test time. They are control operations implemented and validated during development, each with an application scope and a composition contract, and STITCH [51] selects the primitives that suit each task and compiles them into its harness before the actor starts.

Setup. We evaluate on 100 randomly sampled tasks of SWE-bench Verified [16], which asks for repairs of real repository issues, and on 45 randomly sampled tasks of Terminal-Bench 2.0 [17], which covers tasks in a terminal environment; results are broken down by repository (Django, SymPy, and the others) and by difficulty. Both samples are disjoint from the 100 SWE-bench and 44 Terminal-Bench development tasks on which the primitives were developed. Each task gets two attempts, and we report Pass@1, the fraction of successful attempts; Pass@2, the fraction of tasks solved in at least one attempt [183]; and Pass2, the fraction solved in both. GPT-5.6 Luna at medium reasoning effort [170] serves as both the actor and the composer, and GPT-5.6 Sol is the development model. The baselines are the mini-SWE-agent 2.4.6 seed harness [8], SWE-agent, Codex, and the harness optimizers MemoHarness [144] and MetaHarness [143], which start from the same seed. Two controls keep the primitive implementations and vary the composition alone: a fixed harness that applies one focused primitive, with its required dependencies and shared supporting operations, to all tasks, and a random composer.

Main Results. STITCH attains the highest overall Pass@1, Pass@2, and Pass2 on both benchmarks (Tables 20 and 21). On SWE-bench Verified it reaches 80.5% Pass@1, 7.5 pp above the seed harness, 1.5 pp above Codex, and 7.0 pp above MetaHarness, the stronger harness optimizer. On Terminal-Bench 2.0 it reaches 72.2%, 12.2, 15.5, and 16.6 pp above the same three baselines. The gains extend to repeated success: Pass2 rises over the seed from 68.0% to 76.0% on SWE-bench Verified and from 51.1% to 66.7% on Terminal-Bench 2.0.

The controls attribute the gain to the choice made for each task. STITCH exceeds the best fixed primitive by 4.5 pp on SWE-bench Verified and by 5.5 pp on Terminal-Bench 2.0, whereas the random composer, at 73.3% and 63.5%, stays within the range of the fixed primitives. The breakdowns show why a fixed choice falls short: the same primitive can help on some tasks and hurt on others. Contract-case Explorer raises Pass@1 above the seed on the other repositories, 77.9% against 69.1%, but lowers it on Django, 69.2% against 75.0%, and on SymPy no fixed primitive reaches the seed’s 75.0%, which STITCH matches. On Terminal-Bench 2.0, State Guard leads the fixed arms on medium tasks but lowers easy-task Pass@1 from 100.0% to 83.3%, while Execution Supervisor leads them on hard tasks; STITCH reaches 81.0% on medium and 46.2% on hard tasks and keeps 100.0% on easy ones. This is the task-mechanism mismatch behind Proposition 3.2: a fixed harness either pays a primitive’s penalty outside its application scope or forgoes its gain inside it.

Composition also scales with the library. Growing the test-time library along one order of addition, from the seed harness (size 0) to eight entries on SWE-bench Verified and six on Terminal-Bench 2.0, raises Pass@1 from 73.0% to 80.5% and from 60.0% to 72.2% (Figure 15).

Transfer and Cost. The primitives and the composer carry over to actors not used in development. With implementations and contracts unchanged and the scopes adjusted on development tasks, STITCH averages 84.0% Pass@1 on SWE-bench Verified over GPT-5.6 Terra, DeepSeek-V4-Flash, and Claude-4.5-Haiku, against 75.2% for the seed, 78.5% for Codex, and 79.5% for the best fixed primitive (Table 34); with the GPT-5.6 Terra actor, Codex leads at 88.0% against 86.5%. Each fixed primitive also stays above the seed on this average, so the primitives encode control mechanisms that generalize across actors. Composition is cheap and reliable. It costs 4.3% of one actor attempt on SWE-bench Verified and 2.7% on Terminal-Bench 2.0; a lower bound for writing the complete harness at test time, which counts an oracle coder’s output tokens alone, is about 543×543\times and 638×638\times the cost of composition. Each selected primitive activated and executed without runtime errors (Figure 16): the selected primitives take effect during the actor’s execution, free of the reliability risk of generated harness code.

We provide the full framework of STITCH, its overview figure, and the per-actor, library-size, and composition-cost results in Appendix B.8.

5.  Analysis

We further analyze the gains of Section 4 by setting the controls of the eight companion studies side by side. The analysis asks four questions: where the benefit of a primitive comes from, what the channels between agents and primitives carry, what decides which primitives run and what is revised after a failure, and what a task costs and where a strong model pays off. Each question draws on more than one family, so its answer concerns the method that the eight families share.

5.1.  Where the Benefit Comes From

With the backbone and the reused resources fixed, the controls below vary how a primitive applies the resource it owns (Definition 3.1), what it carries, and how much of the library its assessment reaches.

Application versus Access. At matched backbone, calls, and tokens, the gain comes from the primitive, which extra inference does not replace. HEART’s budget-matched control reallocates the calls of the Tool Primitives to value resolution, which self-refines its arguments over raw schemas; with Qwen3-8B, it reaches 34.2% ToolBench pass rate, against 75.1% with Tool Primitives (Table 26). Nor does access to the same components suffice. When LEGO shows the caller the retrieved components with their contracts and tests as read-only context, delivery reaches 0.3544, close to the 0.3469 of diagnosis without any library and below the 0.5134 of Code Primitives (Table 6).

Primitive Fields. Most of the margin over generic editing lies in the fields of PiP_{i} (Table 28). A generic editor over the same retrieved components scores 0.4093, and adding the carried tests ViV_{i}, the interface contract and provenance Ii,XiI_{i},X_{i}, and the dependency closure DiD_{i} raises it to 0.5039, within 0.0095 of primitive adaptation (p=0.49p=0.49) [45]. Withholding ViV_{i} from an otherwise complete primitive lowers delivery to 0.4796.

Source-Model Content. A source model adds more than context. When each retrieval counterpart receives SourceLearn’s per-question context budget, filled from further down its own ranking, SourceLearn leads on three of the four sources tested with GPT-5.6 Luna (Table 29). On the QA benchmarks with Luna, its gain over Hybrid RAG is 12.1 pp on regions that no guidance task touched and 14.9 pp on touched regions (Table 45).

Reach of Assessment. Assessment over the whole library reaches what reranking of a retrieved pool misses. By Proposition 3.3(ii), the hit@kk of any reranker of a similarity pool is capped by whether the pool holds an annotated contract (Eq. (10)). Across three selector backbones, the best reranker of a top-10 pool plateaus between 0.842 and 0.858 Putnam hit@5, while self-advertisement over all 82 contracts (Eq. (3)) reaches up to 0.975 (Table 7). Tool Primitives are found by similarity retrieval and so face the same ceiling, which is high here: retrieval over the 25,519 schema descriptors of ToolFace places 95.8% of ToolBench and 97.2% of NESTFUL gold tools in its top ten (Table 36).

Validation and Grounding Audits. HEART’s result validation agrees with human labels on 200 sampled ToolBench and NESTFUL decisions at 0.97 precision and 0.96 recall, with an 8% false-pass rate (Table 36), so the failures it reports can drive revision (Section 5.3) [44]. SourceLearn’s grounding audit finds 13.3% and 3.3% of the sampled units of the final StudentAid and pytest source models unsupported by the source elements they cite, while the fully supported share of the HuggingFace model rises from 65.0% to 84.2% (Table 44). The source model therefore complements the source, which stays authoritative and directly accessible [47].

Together, these controls place the benefit in what the primitive owns and in applying it where it lives. What a primitive returns must then reach the agents and primitives that use it.

5.2.  Communication Within and Between Primitives

What crosses between agents and primitives carries part of the result (Section 3.3). Two families each disrupt one channel while keeping backbones, primitives, and components fixed.

KV Cache Communication. Agent Primitives run all agents on one LLM, so that one agent’s cache is readable by another. When a receiver reads a sender’s cache after its own system-level cache, the sender’s keys are re-indexed to their new positions to preserve RoPE semantics [139]. Without this re-indexing, the composed MAS on R1/Llama-70B falls from 85.3% to 31.1% on HumanEval+, and on Qwen3-8B it loses 13.3 pp on AIME25 (Table 30). Each primitive used alone on R1/Llama-70B also loses 26.7 to 59.7 pp, so the loss already arises in the KV cache communication inside each primitive, before any composition [48].

Messages Between Dev-Primitives. A Dev-Primitive’s directed message mim_{i} carries the task-relevant information or requirements that it communicates to other components (Section 3.4). With GPT-5.6 Sol, removing these messages while keeping each Dev-Primitive’s local reasoning and edits lowers the SWE Refactor Bench composite from 31.0 to 23.5 and Terminal-Bench 4.0 resolution from 51.8% to 46.1%, larger drops than on SWE-bench Verified (97.0 to 94.2), consistent with messages coordinating changes that span files (Table 15). On Terminal-Bench 4.0, one editor given the same plan and components resolves 38.8%, and 45.5% at matched compute, against 51.8% for HERMES (Table 32), so component-local reasoning with direct communication leads at equal compute.

In both families, a cache read at the wrong positions or a requirement that never reaches its component costs accuracy, although each agent and Dev-Primitive performs its own step as before.

5.3.  Activation and Revision

With the primitives and their channels fixed, COMPOSE decides which primitives run (Eq. (4)), and revision decides what changes after a failure (Eq. (6); Figure 2, middle and bottom). For ANTMAN and STITCH, the interventions below examine the behaviour that Propositions 3.1 and 3.2 predict.

Space and Demand. ANTMAN satisfies the premises of Proposition 3.1: each step routes one unresolved need to at most one territory-backed worker (Eq. (48)), and each need is routed at most ρ\rho times. Participation accordingly follows demand and changes little with the size of the space: it grows 1.23×1.23\times when distractors grow the space 16×16\times around the same evidence, against 15.29×15.29\times and 15.33×15.33\times for the members of LongAgent [109] and CoA [110] (Table 17), and it reaches 8.0 workers when the required evidence grows to 16 units in a fixed space (Table 18).

Excess Activation. Activating more than the task needs costs accuracy as well as calls. Keeping all Dev-Primitives identified in HERMES’s initial analysis active throughout raises primitive calls from 9.6 to 28.7 per SWE-bench Verified task and lowers the score on each of the four benchmarks by 1.2 to 3.0 points (Tables 15 and 52).

Task-Conditioned Choice. Per-task composition beats the best fixed choice, and a random composition falls to the level of the fixed choices. STITCH’s fixed primitives raise Pass@1 on some repositories and difficulty levels and lower it on others (Section 4.9), the heterogeneity that Proposition 3.2 needs. With the GPT-5.6 Luna actor, per-task composition reaches 80.5% Pass@1 on SWE-bench Verified, against 76.0% for the best primitive applied to all tasks and 73.3% for a random composer (Table 20), and Terminal-Bench 2.0 keeps this order (Table 21). The Organizer of Agent Primitives composes per query and reaches 73.3% on Qwen3-8B AIME25 (Table 10). Random structures from its Knowledge Pool reach 66.7%, the level of the best single primitives, and the Organizer without its pool reaches 63.3%. With Claude-4 as the Organizer, composition also reaches 73.3% (Tables 47 and 47). For Agent Primitives, the benefit thus comes mainly from problem-aware structure selection and not from a particular Organizer model [48]. For Harness Primitives, it comes from choosing complementary primitives for each task [51].

Library Size. Growing STITCH’s test-time library of accepted primitives along one order of addition raises Pass@1 from 73.0% for the seed harness (size 0) to 80.5% at size 8 on SWE-bench Verified and from 60.0% to 72.2% at size 6 on Terminal-Bench 2.0 (Figure 15).

Drivers of Revision. Removing the mechanism that turns evidence from the run into revision (Eq. (6)) lowers the result in each family that ablates it. Result validation is HEART’s sole judgment of whether a step’s result answers the query; without it, ToolBench pass rate falls from 75.1% to 47.6%, the same value as with no revision rounds (Tables 4 and 37). Without the diagnosis feedback that names the components that revision reactivates (Eq. (45)), HERMES’s Terminal-Bench 4.0 resolution falls from 51.8% to 41.2%, the largest drop among its four mechanism removals (Table 15). Without task-local recovery of stalled needs, ANTMAN’s 512K F1 falls from 84.03 to 60.12 (Table 19).

Across these interventions, the task decides what runs and what is revised: its unresolved needs bound participation, its features select the composition, and the evidence of its failures and stalled needs decides what changes.

5.4.  Cost and Model Allocation

What runs and what is revised also sets what a task costs, which each study records in its own unit.

Per-Task Cost. At matched cost, reuse delivers more: execution feedback with eight attempts reaches 0.3437 delivery at $2.07 per task, against 0.5134 at $2.08 for Code Primitives, which lead at each attempt limit (Tables 27 and 40). Composing Harness Primitives costs 4.3% of one actor attempt on SWE-bench Verified and 2.7% on Terminal-Bench 2.0, while the output-token lower bound for an oracle that writes the complete harness is about 543×543\times and 638×638\times the cost of composition (Figure 16). As the space grows 16×16\times, ANTMAN’s calls grow 1.21×1.21\times and its cost 6.90×6.90\times, against cost growth of 14.22×14.22\times for LongAgent and 16.11×16.11\times for CoA (Table 17).

Strong-Model Placement. For Dev-Primitives, whose LLM can differ from the activation and diagnosis models, a strong model pays off most in diagnosis (Table 50). With GPT-5.6 Sol in activation and diagnosis, Qwen3-8B Dev-Primitives resolve 50.6% of Terminal-Bench 4.0 tasks, against 27.6% with Qwen3-8B in all three roles. A stronger diagnosis model alone raises resolution to between 44.5% and 47.9%, and a stronger activation model alone to at most 38.2%. Sol activation with Qwen3-8B Dev-Primitives and GPT-5.5 diagnosis reaches 49.7% at $2.13k, against 51.8% at $3.40k with Sol in all three roles, a 2.1-pp loss for 37.4% lower expenditure (Table 52).

Smaller Models Inside Primitives. With GPT-OSS-20B as the resident LLM of all Code Primitives and as the diagnosis model, LEGO keeps 95.1% of its delivery (0.4880) at 24.0% lower recorded-call cost (Table 27). ANTMAN-H, which runs all components except the GPT-4.1 orchestrator on Qwen3-8B, reaches 57.3% against 58.3% on GAIA-Text-103 and 25.0% against 41.7% on its hardest level (Table 16). With GPT-5.4 in decomposition, value resolution, and result validation and Qwen3-8B in the Tool Primitives, HEART reaches τ2\tau^{2}-Bench Pass1 of 0.84, 0.75, and 0.67 on retail, airline, and telecom, close to the 0.86, 0.78, and 0.68 of GPT-5.4 in all roles (Appendix B.1) [44]. In these three families, as in Dev-Primitives, a smaller model takes the work inside the primitives while a stronger model coordinates.

Summary. Across the four questions, the analyses locate the benefit in applying each resource inside its primitive, in what the primitive carries, in channels that keep their meaning, and in activation and revision controlled by the task. At matched budgets the primitives deliver more, and smaller models inside them keep most of the result at lower cost while a stronger model coordinates. The end-to-end outcome of a real-world task thus depends both on the competence that each primitive keeps with its resource and on the mechanisms that HEELO builds around the primitives (Section 3.3), which each family realizes as its task needs.

6.  The heelo.dev Platform for Real-World Tasks

On the research benchmarks of Section 4, as in the cross-family protocol of Appendix E, the environment is frozen and the grader is fixed in advance. Real-world tasks also run against live services, accounts, and people. To test HEELO under these conditions, we built heelo.dev (https://heelo.dev), a platform that exposes real-world actions as agent-native primitives (Figure 3), and we compared agents with and without HEELO on 46 such tasks.

6.1.  Platform Overview

heelo.dev is a tool execution backend for AI agents. It exposes third-party actions, such as flights, calendars, email, social posting, company research, and browser automation, as tools behind one invocation endpoint, and each tool follows the agent-native design of Section 3.2. A tool accepts the fields of its input schema or a natural-language request and encapsulates its own execution strategy, from LLM calls to browser automation and third-party APIs, and it keeps its state in a session. When a request lacks a detail, the tool returns a clarification question with the session’s identifier, and the caller continues the session until the tool returns a result or an error. Callers reach the tools in four ways: direct invocation; a natural-language router that selects a tool from the descriptions and examples of all registered tools; a ReAct loop that chains tools step by step, each result informing the next action; and an MCP server through which external agents, such as Claude Code, connect to HEELO. Tool calls are recorded in a shared log.

6.2.  Four Real-World Loops

The real-world tasks of the platform are organized as four loops, each with one end-to-end task (Table 22). Each loop adds three tool families to the platform, such as mail.read, doc.extract, and doc.render for the assistant, and draws on tools that the platform already has, such as calendars, Notion, and the posting tools of single platforms. Distribution publishes a campaign’s content to several channels, each under its own platform rules, and hosts the pages that capture visitors. Acquisition finds people and companies with a matching need and sends them multi-step outreach from an authenticated domain. The assistant turns an invoice email into checked fields, approved writes, and a receipt, and validation mines the problems that people report and tests the demand for one of them. The loops also feed one another: distribution attributes each click from acquisition’s outreach to the contact who clicked and stops that contact’s sequence once the contact is captured, and validation reaches real people through acquisition. A loop’s task is therefore solved only when the tools compose within a loop and across loops, each tool’s result reaching the tool that consumes it. The four tasks need 26 capabilities: distribution, for instance, needs page publishing, click attribution, safety and input checks, multi-platform posting, budget control, share-card rendering, and the launch pipeline that chains them.

6.3.  Evaluation Protocol

The acceptance criterion RqR_{q} of a loop’s task (Section 3.1) is met only when the whole chain runs live: the assistant loop’s live runner, for instance, checks the chain against real accounts link by link, each link reported as passed, failed, or not run, and a link that has not run never counts as passed. To measure what the primitives add, we pose the 26 capabilities as 46 tasks that name no heelo.dev tool. The pass criteria of each task are fixed before its first run as facts that a person can check, such as an invoice total, the pages of a PDF, or a refused channel, and the tasks include failure paths, such as a wrong contact identifier that must return a clean error or a page that robots.txt disallows. The tasks also serve as acceptance tests of the primitives: when a run exposes a defect in a primitive, the primitive is fixed and the task runs again, and we report the runs after the fix.

We run two agents, Claude Opus 5.5 with Claude Code and GPT-6.1 Sol with Codex, both at medium reasoning effort, in two arms each: on their own, and connected to HEELO through the MCP server of heelo.dev, which gives the agent HEELO’s primitives as tools; in five validation tasks, Codex with HEELO is also prompted to use them. Each agent keeps the built-in tools that a task allows, from web search and web fetch to file editing and a sandboxed shell. On its own, an agent receives no credentials, and each run starts in an empty directory outside the heelo.dev repository, in a new session unless it follows up an earlier task; Claude Code cannot read this repository, and Codex, whose shell can read outside its directory, runs with its user configuration and connected apps turned off. A task with side effects uses test accounts and allowlisted recipients only, and an agent on its own, which cannot act on any account, is scored by the pass criteria that its work meets, from a ready draft to a script that needs only a credential. A connected agent calls the staging deployment of heelo.dev, or a local build where a task needs what staging lacks, such as a sandbox channel, a second tenant, a CMS site, or a browser for Lighthouse, and the validation tasks run on a local build with the loop’s latest fixes. Most tasks run three times per arm under a fixed time limit.

In distribution and the assistant loop, Claude Sonnet 5.5, which is not one of the tested agents, grades the answers blind, with the arm names and heelo.dev’s tool names removed, and a person reviews its grades against the run records; acquisition and validation runs are checked against their criteria from the answers or tool results, the artifacts they link, and the request logs. Each run records whether it passes, its wall-clock time and tokens, and its cost at API prices, which for each model call is its tokens multiplied by the model’s price per token, with cached input tokens at the cache price. A run scores 1 when it passes. A run that does not pass scores the share of its pass criteria that it meets, or of its target that it reaches, where a task measures one, as in distribution, lead discovery, problem mining, and the six-stage end-to-end validation, and 0 otherwise; a task’s score averages its runs. A capability’s score averages its tasks, a loop’s score the loop’s tasks, and the overall score all 46 tasks. A task is done when all its runs pass. An arm’s time and cost per completed task are its time and cost summed over 43 tasks, which leave out three tasks whose runs another task already counts, divided by the number of tasks it completes out of 46. In the six-stage end-to-end validation, only the time of the agent’s sessions counts, not that of the launch, which runs on without the agent.

6.4.  Results

Overall Results. Connected to HEELO, Claude Code completes 39 of the 46 tasks instead of 9, and Codex 35 instead of 9, and their overall scores rise from 28% to 90% and from 25% to 83%; Figure 1(c) and Table 24 give the score of every capability, and Table 23 the scores by loop. Of the 26 capabilities, Claude Code completes every task in 2 on its own and in 21 with HEELO, and Codex in 3 and in 19. On their own, both agents score zero in 12 capabilities, most of which act on an account or a service: publishing a page, sending a sequence, finding a contact, reading a mailbox, or holding an invoice’s writes for a person’s approval.

Distribution and Acquisition. In distribution, Claude Code scores 98% with HEELO and Codex 90%, against 23% and 14% on their own. Claude Code with HEELO completes every task except the card check over four templates and four sizes, in which one of three runs stops at the time limit, and Codex with HEELO every task except two of the three multi-platform posts. In acquisition, both agents score 84% with HEELO, against 41% and 34% on their own, and with HEELO they complete every task in all capabilities but lead discovery. On their own, the agents score mainly where the open web and their own code suffice, as in multi-platform posting (56% and 39%) and source coverage within robots.txt (100%). Lead discovery, which asks for people who state a matching need on public platforms, is the only capability in which no arm scores above 20%: both connected agents reach 20%, and Claude Code and Codex on their own 6% and 3%.

Assistant. On their own, both agents score 0% in the assistant loop, because an agent on its own cannot read the mailbox, the calendar, or Notion. With HEELO, Claude Code completes every assistant task and passes all 15 runs behind them, from an invoice email to its planned writes, through an invoice whose total does not add up and is held for correction, to the receipt of an approved invoice. Codex with HEELO completes five of the seven tasks and scores 83%: in the three runs that end with the receipt of an approved invoice, heelo.dev returns the receipt, but Codex’s answer leaves it out. Every link of the loop’s chain also passes live against real accounts: the invoice email is read, its eight fields are extracted by the rule-based tier, the arithmetic checks pass, nothing is written until a person approves, and the approval then produces the calendar event, the Notion page, and the PDF receipt.

Validation. In validation, Claude Code scores 81% with HEELO and Codex 73%, against 35% and 46% on their own, and they complete 7 and 6 of the 10 tasks, against 2 and 3. Only the connected agents record the status code of every request in a scrape. On a self-contained version of the mining task that asks for problems ranked with their trends, Codex completes the task with and without HEELO; for Claude Code with HEELO, heelo.dev’s problem miner gives a trend for 8 of the 14 mined problems. On its own, Codex also completes the hand-off of 100 people with a draft of 100 candidate contacts; with HEELO, it passes two of its three runs, and Claude Code with HEELO stops at the time limit, because the agent resolves the contacts one at a time, with a call for each. Codex scores zero on the funnel math with and without HEELO: its answers compute the rate but leave out the caveat of a small sample. Of the two end-to-end tasks, Claude Code with HEELO passes all 12 runs of the shorter one and Codex with HEELO 7. In the six-stage end-to-end validation, Claude Code with HEELO passes stages two to four, up to a launch that finds 110 people at 77 companies, and Codex with HEELO stops before the assessment, because its fresh scans return no assessable problem.

Time and Cost. In most tasks, a connected run costs more than a run on its own, because it reads more tokens, from the tool menu to the structured results of the primitives: the median assistant run of Claude Code with HEELO reads 160,701 tokens and takes 23.4 seconds, against 19,456 tokens and 9.4 seconds on its own. Because the connected agents complete most of their tasks, they need less time and lower cost per completed task: Claude Code with HEELO needs 3.4 minutes and $0.80, against 6.3 minutes and $1.24 on its own, and Codex with HEELO 3.5 minutes and $0.42, against 8.0 minutes and $0.65, which is 1.9×1.9\times and 2.3×2.3\times less time and 1.55×1.55\times lower cost. Per completed task, Codex with HEELO is the cheapest of the four arms. Repeated work also costs less with HEELO: when a task revisits a JavaScript page whose extraction recipe heelo.dev stored on the first visit, the second visit costs less than half the first in every run of both connected agents, against one of three runs of Codex on its own.

Across the four loops, the gap between an agent on its own and the same agent connected to HEELO opens where a task must act on an account or a service: an agent on its own can find a page, draft a message, or write a script, but a published page, a sent sequence, or an invoice read from a mailbox takes a primitive that holds the account, applies its resource in the task’s context, and verifies the outcome before it reports success.

7.  Conclusion

How can an agent handle a real-world task end to end? Our answer is to engineer each task’s harness around agent-native primitives, which address the last mile to the real world by keeping the competence to apply a resource with the resource itself. An agent-native primitive equips a resource with a resident LLM that applies it to a natural-language request in context and sends other primitives the requirements that its result places on them; where the domain offers an exact procedure, a program takes the place of the resident LLM. HEELO builds each task’s harness from a library of such primitives through three mechanisms. Library selection and composition retrieves and assesses candidates and composes the few that the task needs into a task-specific graph. Evidence-based execution and improvement runs the graph, verifies its result against evidence from the task’s environment, and after a failure revises only the primitives that the evidence implicates, within a budget of revision rounds. Validation and publishing admits new or improved primitives into the library only after validation, on a path separate from any task.

Each of the eight primitive families comes from the solution we built for one kind of real-world task, realizes the mechanisms that its task needs, and improves on the reference baseline of its companion study. On the tasks where frontier harnesses fall short, Dev-Primitives lead Codex by 18.2 points on Terminal-Bench 4.0 with GPT-5.6 Sol at maximum effort, and composing Harness Primitives per task raises Terminal-Bench 2.0 Pass@1 from 60.0% for the seed harness to 72.2%, above the 56.7% of Codex. The analyses show that binding inside a Tool Primitive beats budget-matched self-refinement over raw schemas and that the fields a Code Primitive carries account for most of its margin over generic editing. What crosses between agents and primitives must keep its meaning: exchanged KV caches need positional re-encoding, and requirements must reach the components they concern. The task, in turn, decides which primitives run, as active Navigation Primitives grow 1.23×1.23\times while distractors grow the information space 16×16\times around the same evidence.

The families share one method, so a new kind of task can join HEELO as a new primitive family that realizes the same definition and mechanisms. Beyond the research benchmarks, heelo.dev exposes real-world actions to agents as agent-native primitives. On its 46 real-world tasks, Claude Code and Codex complete 9 tasks each on their own and 39 and 35 when connected to HEELO through MCP, with 1.9×1.9\times and 2.3×2.3\times less time and 1.55×1.55\times lower cost per completed task. Overall, primitives let the competence developed for one task outlast that task: once validated and published, the primitive that carries this competence becomes a building block that later tasks compose.

Appendix A Proofs for Section 3.5

Section 3.5 states three results that the companion studies prove about selection: demand-bounded activation in ANTMAN, the comparison of fixed and task-conditioned composition in STITCH, and the coverage and retrieval ceiling in self-advertised method selection [50, 51, 46]. This appendix proves them in that order. Each proof follows the proof of its study and uses the study’s notation, which holds only within the subsection of that result, and a closing paragraph records what each premise contributes. Section 3.5 states the same results in the notation of the model, with the following correspondence. For demand-bounded activation, ANTMAN’s territory-backed workers are the primitives, its information needs are the needs that COMPOSE routes, its realized need count H⁡(q)H(q) is D⁡(q)D(q), and its number of territories MM is |ℒq||\mathcal{L}_{q}|. For task-conditioned composition, STITCH’s task xx, task distribution 𝒟\mathcal{D}, primitive pip_{i}, and library size MM are qq, 𝒬\mathcal{Q}, PiP_{i}, and NN; its utility uiu_{i} and penalty cic_{i} are gig_{i} and κi\kappa_{i}; its activation vector 𝐚\mathbf{a} is 𝐳\mathbf{z}; and its validity indicator V⁡(H)V(H) is 𝟏​[H​ executes validly]\mathbf{1}[H\text{ executes validly}]. For the coverage results, the study’s Lean goal gg with its local context, its contract descriptions, and its contract library 𝒞\mathcal{C} are the task qq with its context, the interfaces, and ℒ\mathcal{L}; its set A⁡(g)A(g) of annotated reference contracts is 𝒰q\mathcal{U}_{q}; its information variable FF is ZZ; and its top-mm similarity pool Pm​(g)P_{m}(g) is 𝒮m​(q)\mathcal{S}_{m}(q).

A.1.  Demand-Bounded Activation

The proof follows ANTMAN’s proof of its Proposition 1 [50], in ANTMAN’s notation (Appendix B.7). At coordination step tt, ANTMAN selects one unresolved need ntn_{t} of the Need Graph Gt=(Nt,Δt)G_{t}=(N_{t},\Delta_{t}) and routes it to the territory-backed worker iti_{t} (Eq. (48)). The realized need set ℋ⁡(q)=⋃t=0TqNt\mathcal{H}(q)=\bigcup_{t=0}^{T_{q}}N_{t} of Eq. (49), with H⁡(q)=|ℋ⁡(q)|H(q)=|\mathcal{H}(q)|, collects every need that the graph holds during execution, and a reframed or newly introduced need counts as a new member; it is distinct from the attempt history ℋt​(n)\mathcal{H}_{t}(n) that each need carries in Eq. (47). For a realized need nn, a⁡(n)a(n) counts its routing attempts, its initial routing and every rerouting caused by recovery, with a⁡(n)≤ρa(n)\leq\rho under the execution budget, and 𝒜⁡(q)=⋃t=0Tq−1{it}\mathcal{A}(q)=\bigcup_{t=0}^{T_{q}-1}\{i_{t}\} is the set of distinct workers activated (Eq. (50)).

Proof of Proposition 3.1.

Every worker activation in Algorithm 2 occurs through a routing decision at Line 7, and each such decision is associated with the one need ntn_{t} selected at that step, which belongs to Nt⊆ℋ⁡(q)N_{t}\subseteq\mathcal{H}(q). Summing the routing events of all needs encountered during execution therefore counts every worker-dispatch event once:

K⁡(q)=∑n∈ℋ⁡(q)a⁡(n).K(q)=\sum_{n\in\mathcal{H}(q)}a(n).

A single routing event activates at most one territory-backed worker. Mapping each activated worker to the first routing event that activated it therefore sends distinct workers to distinct events, so the number of distinct workers activated cannot exceed the number of routing events, |𝒜⁡(q)|≤K⁡(q)|\mathcal{A}(q)|\leq K(q). Each need is routed at most ρ\rho times, so

K⁡(q)=∑n∈ℋ⁡(q)a⁡(n)≤∑n∈ℋ⁡(q)ρ=ρ​|ℋ⁡(q)|=ρ​H​(q).K(q)=\sum_{n\in\mathcal{H}(q)}a(n)\ \leq\ \sum_{n\in\mathcal{H}(q)}\rho\ =\ \rho\,|\mathcal{H}(q)|\ =\ \rho\,H(q).

Combining the two inequalities gives |𝒜⁡(q)|≤K⁡(q)≤ρ​H​(q)|\mathcal{A}(q)|\leq K(q)\leq\rho H(q). ANTMAN contains only MM territory-backed workers, so |𝒜⁡(q)|≤M|\mathcal{A}(q)|\leq M, and together |𝒜⁡(q)|≤min⁡{M,ρ​H​(q)}|\mathcal{A}(q)|\leq\min\{M,\rho H(q)\}, which is Eq. (8). ∎

Role of the Premises. MM enters only as the size of the available candidate pool and not as a factor of the demand-dependent bound ρ​H​(q)\rho H(q), so enlarging the information space and increasing MM does not by itself force additional workers to become active. If realized demand stays bounded, H⁡(q)≤H¯H(q)\leq\bar{H}, and ρ\rho does not depend on MM, then |𝒜⁡(q)|≤ρ​H¯=O⁡(1)|\mathcal{A}(q)|\leq\rho\bar{H}=O(1) with respect to MM, which is ANTMAN’s Corollary 1. A harder query can still produce more needs, revisions, or recovery attempts and so raise H⁡(q)H(q) or K⁡(q)K(q); the proposition attributes this growth to task demand. The argument uses three properties of ANTMAN’s coordination: every activation goes through a routing decision on one selected need, a routing event activates at most one worker, and each need is routed at most ρ\rho times, with a reframed need counted as a new need. These are the properties that Section 3.5 requires of a COMPOSE that activates a primitive only by routing an unresolved need to it. The bound concerns active coordination, that is, whether worker participation is structurally coupled to the number of available territories; the retrieval stage that ranks WorkerCards for each routing decision is a separate cost, which can grow with the information space.

A.2.  Fixed versus Task-Conditioned Composition

The proof follows STITCH’s proofs of its Proposition 1 and of part 1 of its Proposition 2 [51], in STITCH’s notation (Section 3.5 and Appendix B.8). Expectations include task sampling and any randomness in primitive selection. Because the additive expression lies in [0,1][0,1] for every task and activation vector, Δi​(x)=R⁡(x,𝐞i)−R⁡(x,𝟎)\Delta_{i}(x)=R(x,\mathbf{e}_{i})-R(x,\mathbf{0}), where 𝐞i\mathbf{e}_{i} activates pip_{i} alone and 𝟎\mathbf{0} activates no primitive, lies in [−1,1][-1,1], and every expectation below exists.

Proof of Proposition 3.2.

Part (i). Under the pointwise sign assumptions, Δi​(x)=ui​(x)>0\Delta_{i}(x)=u_{i}(x)>0 for x∈Ωix\in\Omega_{i} and Δi​(x)=−ci​(x)<0\Delta_{i}(x)=-c_{i}(x)<0 otherwise. Since R⁡(x,𝐚)R(x,\mathbf{a}) is additive and every combination is admissible, one oracle activation that maximizes R⁡(x,𝐚)R(x,\mathbf{a}) on each task is

ai∗​(x)=𝟏​(x∈Ωi).a_{i}^{*}(x)=\mathbf{1}(x\in\Omega_{i}).

The expected performance of the oracle task-adaptive harness is

𝔼x∼𝒟​[R⁡(x,𝐚∗​(x))]=𝔼⁡[R0​(x)]+∑i=1M𝔼x​[𝟏​(x∈Ωi)​ui​(x)]=𝔼⁡[R0​(x)]+∑i=1Mμi​u¯i.\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}}\bigl[R(x,\mathbf{a}^{*}(x))\bigr]=\mathbb{E}[R_{0}(x)]+\sum_{i=1}^{M}\mathbb{E}_{x}\bigl[\mathbf{1}(x\in\Omega_{i})\,u_{i}(x)\bigr]=\mathbb{E}[R_{0}(x)]+\sum_{i=1}^{M}\mu_{i}\bar{u}_{i}.

For a fixed harness 𝐚∈{0,1}M\mathbf{a}\in\{0,1\}^{M}, 𝔼x∼𝒟​[R⁡(x,𝐚)]=𝔼⁡[R0​(x)]+∑i=1Mai​𝔼x​[Δi​(x)]\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}}[R(x,\mathbf{a})]=\mathbb{E}[R_{0}(x)]+\sum_{i=1}^{M}a_{i}\,\mathbb{E}_{x}[\Delta_{i}(x)], and the law of total expectation gives, for each ii,

𝔼x​[Δi​(x)]=Pr⁡(x∈Ωi)​𝔼​[ui​(x)∣x∈Ωi]−Pr⁡(x∉Ωi)​𝔼​[ci​(x)∣x∉Ωi]=μi​u¯i−(1−μi)​c¯i.\mathbb{E}_{x}[\Delta_{i}(x)]=\Pr(x\in\Omega_{i})\,\mathbb{E}[u_{i}(x)\mid x\in\Omega_{i}]-\Pr(x\notin\Omega_{i})\,\mathbb{E}[c_{i}(x)\mid x\notin\Omega_{i}]=\mu_{i}\bar{u}_{i}-(1-\mu_{i})\bar{c}_{i}.

The sum separates over ii, so the optimal fixed harness sets ai,fixed∗=1a^{*}_{i,\mathrm{fixed}}=1 if μi​u¯i>(1−μi)​c¯i\mu_{i}\bar{u}_{i}>(1-\mu_{i})\bar{c}_{i} and ai,fixed∗=0a^{*}_{i,\mathrm{fixed}}=0 otherwise, and

𝔼x∼𝒟​[R⁡(x,𝐚fixed∗)]=𝔼⁡[R0​(x)]+∑i=1Mmax⁡(0,μi​u¯i−(1−μi)​c¯i).\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}}\bigl[R(x,\mathbf{a}^{*}_{\mathrm{fixed}})\bigr]=\mathbb{E}[R_{0}(x)]+\sum_{i=1}^{M}\max\bigl(0,\ \mu_{i}\bar{u}_{i}-(1-\mu_{i})\bar{c}_{i}\bigr).

Subtracting this from the expected performance of the oracle gives Γfixed=∑i=1M(μi​u¯i−max⁡(0,μi​u¯i−(1−μi)​c¯i))\Gamma_{\mathrm{fixed}}=\sum_{i=1}^{M}\bigl(\mu_{i}\bar{u}_{i}-\max(0,\ \mu_{i}\bar{u}_{i}-(1-\mu_{i})\bar{c}_{i})\bigr), and the identity y−max⁡(0,y−z)=min⁡(y,z)y-\max(0,y-z)=\min(y,z) with y=μi​u¯iy=\mu_{i}\bar{u}_{i} and z=(1−μi)​c¯iz=(1-\mu_{i})\bar{c}_{i} gives the first line of Eq. (9). Because μi∈(0,1)\mu_{i}\in(0,1), u¯i>0\bar{u}_{i}>0, and c¯i>0\bar{c}_{i}>0, each term of the sum is strictly positive, so Γfixed>0\Gamma_{\mathrm{fixed}}>0.

Part (ii). Write A=𝔼x​[R⁡(x,𝐚∗​(x))]A=\mathbb{E}_{x}[R(x,\mathbf{a}^{*}(x))] and B=𝔼⁡[J⁡(x,Hcomp)]B=\mathbb{E}[J(x,H_{\mathrm{comp}})]. The final activation aia_{i} of pip_{i} in HcompH_{\mathrm{comp}} depends on the task and on the composer’s randomness. Conditioning on the application scope and using the definitions of αi\alpha_{i} and βi\beta_{i},

𝔼⁡[ai​Δi​(x)]=μi​𝔼​[ai​ui​(x)∣x∈Ωi]−(1−μi)​𝔼​[ai​ci​(x)∣x∉Ωi]=μi​(1−βi)​u¯i−(1−μi)​αi​c¯i,\mathbb{E}\bigl[a_{i}\Delta_{i}(x)\bigr]=\mu_{i}\,\mathbb{E}\bigl[a_{i}u_{i}(x)\mid x\in\Omega_{i}\bigr]-(1-\mu_{i})\,\mathbb{E}\bigl[a_{i}c_{i}(x)\mid x\notin\Omega_{i}\bigr]=\mu_{i}(1-\beta_{i})\,\bar{u}_{i}-(1-\mu_{i})\,\alpha_{i}\,\bar{c}_{i},

because 𝔼⁡[ai​ui​(x)∣x∈Ωi]=u¯i−𝔼⁡[(1−ai)​ui​(x)∣x∈Ωi]=(1−βi)​u¯i\mathbb{E}[a_{i}u_{i}(x)\mid x\in\Omega_{i}]=\bar{u}_{i}-\mathbb{E}[(1-a_{i})u_{i}(x)\mid x\in\Omega_{i}]=(1-\beta_{i})\,\bar{u}_{i}. The compositions execute validly, V⁡(Hcomp)=1V(H_{\mathrm{comp}})=1, so J⁡(x,Hcomp)=R⁡(x,𝐚)J(x,H_{\mathrm{comp}})=R(x,\mathbf{a}) at the final activations, and summing over ii under the additive model gives

B=A−∑i=1M[μi​βi​u¯i+(1−μi)​αi​c¯i].B=A-\sum_{i=1}^{M}\bigl[\mu_{i}\beta_{i}\bar{u}_{i}+(1-\mu_{i})\alpha_{i}\bar{c}_{i}\bigr].

As in STITCH, the best static harness Hfixed∗H^{*}_{\mathrm{fixed}}, which activates 𝐚fixed∗\mathbf{a}^{*}_{\mathrm{fixed}} on every task, executes validly, so part (i) gives 𝔼⁡[J⁡(x,Hfixed∗)]=A−Γfixed\mathbb{E}[J(x,H^{*}_{\mathrm{fixed}})]=A-\Gamma_{\mathrm{fixed}}. Comparing the two expressions, B>A−ΓfixedB>A-\Gamma_{\mathrm{fixed}} if and only if the utility-weighted selection loss is smaller than Γfixed\Gamma_{\mathrm{fixed}}, which is the second line of Eq. (9). ∎

Role of the Premises. Additivity is the modeling assumption: it abstracts away interactions between primitives, so it excludes primitives that help only together or that interfere. Admissibility of every combination lets the maximum over fixed harnesses separate over primitives, and the range [0,1][0,1] keeps every expectation finite. Part (i) compares two oracle values. Part (ii) adds valid execution, V⁡(Hcomp)=1V(H_{\mathrm{comp}})=1, which STITCH assumes for compositions of validated primitives built by its deterministic compiler; every selected primitive activated and executed without runtime errors, an activation rate of 100% that STITCH reads as support for part 2 of its Proposition 2 (Figure 16). The composer need not be perfect, since its selection loss need only stay below Γfixed\Gamma_{\mathrm{fixed}}. Each aia_{i} is the final activation of mechanism pip_{i}, after selection, bounded correction, and fallback to the seed harness, and the dependencies that the compiler supplies belong to the mechanism that requires them, as in STITCH’s fixed arms. Part 2 of STITCH’s Proposition 2, the comparison with raw code generation under independent implementation failures, is Eq. (53), proved in Appendix B.8. Each fixed arm of Section 4.9 applies one focused primitive with its required dependencies and shared supporting operations to every task. It is one of the fixed activations over which the maximum in Eq. (9) ranges, so the best fixed arm bounds the value of the best fixed harness from below.

A.3.  Coverage and Retrieval Ceiling

The three parts of Proposition 3.3 restate the information bound (Proposition 2), the candidate-pool ceiling (Corollary 1), and the multi-method coverage result (Proposition 4) of the study of self-advertised method selection [46]. The proofs follow the study’s appendix, in its notation (Section 3.5 and Appendix B.3). A Method Contract makes its own guarantee conditional on explicit premises, as program contracts do [188, 43]: once Prec⁡(θ)\operatorname{Pre}_{c}(\theta) and Oblc⁡(θ)\operatorname{Obl}_{c}(\theta) are proved for a binding θ\theta, its action yields Gc​(θ)G_{c}(\theta) (Proposition B.1). The three parts proved here concern selection instead, that is, which contracts a selector can place in its shortlist. Throughout, X=(g,Γ,contract descriptions)X=(g,\Gamma,\text{contract descriptions}) is the selector’s input, the nonempty annotated set A=A⁡(g)A=A(g) is random given XX, and T=ϕ⁡(X)T=\phi(X) holds the features available to a similarity-only selector.

Proof of Proposition 3.3.

Part (i). For each value tt of TT, choose a set S⁡(t)S(t) with |S⁡(t)|=k|S(t)|=k that attains the maximum in the definition of Vk​(T)V_{k}(T); a maximizer exists because 𝒞\mathcal{C} is finite. Then

Role of the Premises. Part (i) is a statement about information and leaves open whether a particular model extracts it. An LLM reranker reads full descriptions, but only of the contracts that a similarity stage passes to it, so similarity still determines what the reranker can consider. Part (ii) requires only that the second stage reorder the pool and place the remaining contracts after it, so it holds for every reranking backbone. The study’s rerankers follow this design with m=10m=10, and every reported kk satisfies k≤mk\leq m, so an annotated contract that similarity ranks low cannot be recovered by any of them (Figure 17). Self-advertisement judges all 82 contracts from their proposals, and its coverage is limited instead by the information in XX and by how accurately the model judges applicability. Part (iii) concerns expected hit@kk. Expected recall@kk is additive over contracts, Rx​(S)=∑c∈Swc​(x)R_{x}(S)=\sum_{c\in S}w_{c}(x) with wc(x)=𝔼[𝟏[c∈A]/|A||X=x]w_{c}(x)=\mathbb{E}\bigl[\mathbf{1}[c\in A]/|A|\bigm|X=x\bigr], so sorting by wc​(x)w_{c}(x) maximizes it, and the two objectives coincide when a goal has a single reference contract. When several methods apply, a near-duplicate of a contract that is likely to apply adds little to expected hit@kk, so sorting per-contract scores need not maximize it. The study sorts per-contract scores, which is optimal for expected recall@kk, and part (iii) identifies the objective that a diversity-aware selector would target.

Appendix B Framework Details of the Eight Primitive Families

This appendix gives the full framework of each primitive family, one subsection per family and in the order of Section 4: Tool Primitives and HEART [44], Code Primitives and LEGO [45], Math Primitives and self-advertised method selection in Lean [46], Knowledge Primitives and SourceLearn [47], Agent Primitives [48], Dev-Primitives and HERMES [49], Navigation Primitives and ANTMAN [50], and Harness Primitives and STITCH [51]. Each subsection gives one family’s framework in the notation of its own paper, with the paper’s equations, its algorithm where the paper has one, and its implementation specifics, such as models, budgets, and retrieval sizes. The symbols of a subsection hold only within that subsection, and each subsection ends with a short mapping of its framework to the method of Section 3.

B.1.  Tool Primitives: Natural-Language Invocation and Harness Engineering

Tool Primitives give each tool a natural-language interface [44], and HEART, a Harness Engineering framework via Agent-native, Reusable Tool Primitives, makes these primitives practical at repository scale. With ToolFace storing the tools, the primitives representing them, and the harness supplying what this abstraction leaves open, HEART decouples tool storage, representation, and invocation, which prior methods couple by exposing raw schemas in the model’s context. In Figure 4, an illustrative request to freeze the cards in a stolen wallet passes through these parts, from the clarification that request decomposition asks for to the validation of each step.

ToolFace. ToolFace is a centralized registry 𝒯={(si,fi)}i=1N\mathcal{T}=\{(s_{i},f_{i})\}_{i=1}^{N} of schema–function pairs. Each manually authored schema sis_{i} gives the parameter types, constraints, and return specifications of tool ii, and fif_{i} is its executable implementation. The 25,519 tools comprise 16,464 live APIs from ToolBench [6], 40 mathematical reasoning and 4,348 coding tools from NESTFUL [32], 68 tools from τ2\tau^{2}-Bench [31], 4,538 bilingual APIs from ACEBench [58], 2 web-search and 5 memory tools from BFCLv4 [20], and 54 manually crafted interaction tools such as form filling. Semantic search over schema descriptors retrieves tools on demand, so the model need not know the catalogue upfront and context pressure follows the number of candidates retrieved per step. A Tool Primitive is defined by the tool it wraps, so the set of primitives is induced by ToolFace and grows with it, and invocations chain along the data dependencies between calls.

Tool Primitives. A Tool Primitive is an LLM-based wrapper around one ToolFace tool, and all Tool Primitives share one base LLM ℳ\mathcal{M}, conditioned on different schemas:

𝒫i​(x,c)=ℳ⁡([si;c;x]),\mathcal{P}_{i}(x;\,c)=\mathcal{M}\bigl([\,s_{i};\,c;\,x\,]\bigr), (12)

where xx is the natural-language request of the upstream caller, cc is optional context such as a prior primitive’s result, empty when there is none, and [⋅][\cdot] denotes prompt concatenation. 𝒫i\mathcal{P}_{i} maps each value that the request describes to the argument space of sis_{i}, with type coercion, enum matching, unit conversion, required-field, range, and format checks, schema defaults, and binding of fields referenced in the upstream context; it then invokes fif_{i} and returns the execution result rir_{i}. On success, rir_{i} holds the tool name, the bound arguments, the function’s result, and a one-sentence summary that lets it serve as the context cc of a downstream primitive. A failed schema resolution or a runtime error is not retried silently but returned as a structured failure of type SCHEMA_RESOLUTION, CONSTRAINT_VIOLATION, or RUNTIME_ERROR, with the parameter or constraint that failed. The resulting properties are natural-language invocation, inter-tool communication, and execution isolation; under the last, a primitive never calls another tool, modifies the plan, or recovers from a failure on its own.

Harness Engineering. HEART supplies what the abstraction leaves undetermined with three mechanisms.

Request decomposition is needed because a primitive answers the request it is handed and cannot ask what the user wants. Intent analysis identifies the target task and its objective, the relevant tool categories, and the user’s explicit constraints or preferences. Information sufficiency checking then decides whether the context 𝒞t\mathcal{C}_{t} of query, acquired information, and execution history supports a fully specified plan:

δt=Decompose​(q,𝒞t)∈{sufficient,insufficient}.\delta_{t}=\textsc{Decompose}(q,\,\mathcal{C}_{t})\in\{\texttt{sufficient},\,\texttt{insufficient}\}. (13)

While δt=insufficient\delta_{t}=\texttt{insufficient}, decomposition returns to the user a targeted clarification request ctc_{t} for the missing information, and the reply enters the context. It then writes the invocation plan Π=(π1,…,πK)\Pi=(\pi_{1},\dots,\pi_{K}), whose steps give a tool category, a tool hint, the step’s objective, and the steps it depends on.

Value resolution is needed because a step’s values come from the user query and from earlier results, which the primitive does not see. It resolves the values of step πk\pi_{k} from 𝒞t\mathcal{C}_{t} into a natural-language invocation request xkx_{k} that names the target Tool Primitive and embeds the values inline, together with execution hyperparameters:

βk=Resolve​(πk,𝒞t)=(xk,H-Paramsk).\beta_{k}=\textsc{Resolve}(\pi_{k},\,\mathcal{C}_{t})=\bigl(x_{k},\,\texttt{H-Params}_{k}\bigr). (14)

Values may come from the query, earlier clarifications, or the result of any upstream step, referenced as $step_j.<field>.
