Value resolution never invents an ungrounded value, never overrides the primitive chosen by decomposition, and resolves a value shared by several steps once. H-Paramsk\texttt{H-Params}_{k} sets retry in [1,5][1,5], priority to low, normal, or high, and timeout_s, 30 seconds by default. The step’s primitive then runs with the previous result as its context, rk←𝒫k​(βk∣rk−1)r_{k}\leftarrow\mathcal{P}_{k}(\beta_{k}\mid r_{k-1}).

Result validation is needed because a primitive reports whether its own call executed, not whether the result answers the query. It decides

vk=Validate​(rk,πk,sk)∈{pass,fail}v_{k}=\textsc{Validate}(r_{k},\,\pi_{k},\,s_{k})\in\{\texttt{pass},\,\texttt{fail}\} (15)

on four criteria, each assessed independently: task completion of the step’s objective, argument consistency with the user’s intent and the constraints of sks_{k}, execution validity, without runtime errors and with output of the expected schema, and constraint satisfaction of task-level or domain-specific constraints such as rate limits, access permissions, or business rules. A step passes if all four hold and fails otherwise; execution then proceeds to πk+1\pi_{k+1} or, after πK\pi_{K}, returns the final result. On a failure, ϕk←Validate.Feedback​(rk,πk,sk)\phi_{k}\leftarrow\textsc{Validate}.\textsc{Feedback}(r_{k},\pi_{k},s_{k}) names each failed criterion and why, with the root cause first.

Targeted revision returns this feedback to decomposition, which re-plans from the enriched context:

𝒞t+1=𝒞t∪{ϕk},Π′=Decompose​(q,𝒞t+1).\mathcal{C}_{t+1}=\mathcal{C}_{t}\cup\{\phi_{k}\},\qquad\Pi^{\prime}=\textsc{Decompose}(q,\,\mathcal{C}_{t+1}). (16)

The revised plan addresses the diagnosed failure, so a failed call is re-planned instead of terminating the trajectory, and recovery stays confined to the step that failed validation. Revision repeats for at most BB rounds, after which the current result is returned (Algorithm 1).

Implementation. HEART is training-free, unlike tool-calling models fine-tuned on curated trajectories [54, 19, 52]. Qwen3-8B [169] runs decomposition, value resolution, result validation, and the Tool Primitives, which share its weights and differ in their system prompts. All experiments use B=3B=3 and retrieval over the full repository, with results averaged over three runs, and over eight on τ2\tau^{2}-Bench. A backbone study on τ2\tau^{2}-Bench separates the orchestration layer of the three mechanisms from the execution layer of the Tool Primitives: with GPT-5.4 in the first and Qwen3-8B in the second, HEART reaches Pass1 of 0.84, 0.75, and 0.67 on retail, airline, and telecom, close to the 0.86, 0.78, and 0.68 of GPT-5.4 in all roles, so the two layers can be scaled independently. The default Qwen3-8B configuration reaches 0.82, 0.73, and 0.63 at more than 12×12\times lower cost than GPT-5.4 in all roles.

Matched Backbone and Budget. HEART pairs its harness with a small backbone, so its gains could come from the scaffold, the backbone, or the tool catalogue. Holding the backbone at Qwen3-8B and the catalogue at ToolFace, we compare HEART with ReAct, retrieval-only tool selection, a planner–executor pipeline, and DFSDT (Table 25). HEART reaches 75.1% ToolBench pass rate against 55.8% for DFSDT, the strongest of the four there, and 0.44 NESTFUL full accuracy against 0.19 for the planner–executor, the strongest on that metric.

Removing ToolFace and the Tool Primitives also removes one model call per invocation step. The budget-matched control of Table 26 gives these calls to value resolution, which self-refines its schema-compliant arguments with backbone, total call count, and token budget matched to full HEART. It raises the 16.1% pass rate and 0.06 full accuracy of the plain ablation to 34.2% and 0.15, against 75.1% and 0.44 with Tool Primitives.

Further Benchmarks. HEART reaches the highest ACEBench Overall score, 86.9, and the highest BFCLv4 Web Search and Memory Overall scores, 86.0 and 69.38; outside HEART, the same Qwen3-8B reaches 12.0 on BFCLv4 Web Search. The 50 real-world tasks, 10 in each of travel planning, healthcare, e-commerce, finance, and local services, are grounded in user personas, range from a single-tool lookup to a multi-tool workflow of search, comparison, and conditional booking, and are scored by human annotators on whether the system completes the task. Through their product interfaces and built-in tools, GPT-5.4, Claude-4.6-Sonnet, and Gemini-3.1-Pro complete 20% to 24% of these tasks; given the ToolFace tools through native function calling, they complete 22% to 32%, a gain of at most 8 pp, against 84% for HEART.

Validation and Revision. Because the recovery loop is conditioned on result validation, HEART’s study compares 200 sampled validation decisions from ToolBench and NESTFUL trajectories with human pass/fail labels (Table 36): precision is 0.97, recall 0.96, and the false-pass and false-fail rates are 8% and 4%. Most false passes fall on the task-completion criterion for partially satisfied objectives, and fewer than 3% of trajectories end on a false pass; false fails trigger at least one redundant revision round in 10–15% of trajectories without changing outcomes. ToolBench pass rate grows from 47.6% without revision to 51.4%, 65.9%, and 75.1% with one to three rounds and saturates at 75.3% with five (Table 37), a plateau indicating that the loop terminates because validation converges.

Retrieval and Robustness. Over the full repository, Recall@5 is 92.4 on ToolBench and 94.7 on NESTFUL, and the top ten hold 95.8% and 97.2% of the gold tools (Table 36). Retrieval misses account for 15–20% of HEART’s residual end-task failures, and validation-triggered revision recovers part of the first-pass misses by reformulating the tool query. On subsampled repositories, ToolBench Recall@5 is 94.6 at 5k tools and 93.7 at 10k, against 92.4 at 25,519. Because tool schemas stay in each primitive’s own prompt and never enter the caller’s, HEART’s attack success rate on ToolBench is 0.0% when a malicious tool document is injected into the retrieved candidates following ToolHijacker [190], under both gradient-free and gradient-based attacks, against 66.0–82.2% for GPT-5.4, Claude-4.6-Sonnet, and Gemini-3.1-Pro.

Mapping to the Method. Schema resolution with its structured failure is the carried validation of a Tool Primitive (Section 3.2), and running 𝒫k​(βk∣rk−1)\mathcal{P}_{k}(\beta_{k}\mid r_{k-1}) is the act step of Eq. (5), in which the summary in rk−1r_{k-1} carries the earlier result along a dependency of the plan.

B.2.  Code Primitives: Adaptation with Carried Tests

Code Primitives are reusable software components that adapt their implementations, interfaces, and dependencies to target repositories [45]. Tool Primitives and Agent Primitives expose tools and reusable behaviours through interfaces that support invocation; a Code Primitive instead provides an interface for adaptation, because it becomes part of the delivered repository. LEGO, Large-scale repository Engineering via aGent-native reusable cOde primitives, builds repositories with Code Primitives drawn from CodeFace, a library mined once from real repositories. Adaptation is performed by the component that owns the implementation, while constraints that cross components are resolved at the repository level. In Figure 5, CodeFace is mined offline, and a single illustrative OAuth request then passes through adaptation, execution, and diagnosis.

Code Primitives. A Code Primitive is a reusable executable software component equipped with a resident LLM, Pi=(Ci,Ii,Di,Vi,Xi,Mi)P_{i}=(C_{i},I_{i},D_{i},V_{i},X_{i},M_{i}), and the resident LLM is its natural-language interface. Its boundary follows functional coherence and the dependencies required for independent execution, so its granularity is induced by mining: entries have a median of 214 implementation lines (p25 96, p75 468) across 2 files (p75 4), and they export 4 symbols and carry 9 tests at the median. Given a requirement rr and construction context 𝒞\mathcal{C}, MiM_{i} runs in two modes:

(si,ui)=Miassess​(Pi,r,𝒞),(P~i,μi)=Miadapt​(Pi,r,𝒞),(s_{i},u_{i})=M_{i}^{\mathrm{assess}}(P_{i},r,\mathcal{C}),\qquad(\widetilde{P}_{i},\mu_{i})=M_{i}^{\mathrm{adapt}}(P_{i},r,\mathcal{C}), (17)

where sis_{i} is the relevance assessment, uiu_{i} the usage proposal, and μi={μi→j}j\mu_{i}=\{\mu_{i\to j}\}_{j} is empty for locally contained changes. ASSESS never modifies the primitive, and it answers UNSUITABLE when the capability does not support the request or when meeting the request would require replacing the capability itself. ADAPT may change the implementation, exported signatures, data representations, dependencies, and configuration while preserving the selected capability. The primitive then updates its interface and dependency records and reruns ViV_{i}, and this carried validation distinguishes primitive adaptation from generic editing.

Prompt Contract. A primitive receives a fixed four-part input: its own state (Ci,Ii,Di,Vi,Xi)(C_{i},I_{i},D_{i},V_{i},X_{i}) verbatim; the requirement rr as the backbone wrote it; a context slice naming the target module path, the symbols the module must export, and the signatures of the sibling components it binds to; and the diagnostics ee of a previous attempt, if any, with the incoming requirements μ→i\mu_{\to i} in a construction round. It sees no native test, no other module’s source, and neither the repository-level plan nor its diagnosis. ADAPT returns a complete replacement implementation, the updated exports, behavioural contract, and dependencies, the outgoing requirements μi→j\mu_{i\to j}, a mapping that marks each carried test kept, rewritten, or dropped, and the execution log of ViV_{i} on the rewritten component. A test may be dropped when it checks donor-specific behaviour, never because the adapted implementation fails it. A return that cannot be parsed, misses a field, or leaves a retained test failing is re-requested with the failure attached up to 3 times and then returns to repository-level handling as an unsuccessful adaptation.

CodeFace and Mining. CodeFace organizes the validated primitives as a library ℱ={Pi}i=1N\mathcal{F}=\{P_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N}. The evaluated snapshot holds 1,424 entries: 871 mined, 343 harvested from construction runs whose repository-level suite verified the component in context, and 210 web-sourced for capabilities that the mined corpus lacked, all admitted under the same requirements. Mining parses a source repository ℛ\mathcal{R} into program entities and relations and proposes component boundaries by weighted community discovery,

Gℛ=(V,Ecall∪Edata∪Estruct),𝒮ℛ(0)=COMMUNITY⁡(Gℛ)={S1(0),…,Sm(0)},G_{\mathcal{R}}=(V,E_{\mathrm{call}}\cup E_{\mathrm{data}}\cup E_{\mathrm{struct}}),\qquad\mathcal{S}^{(0)}_{\mathcal{R}}=\operatorname{COMMUNITY}(G_{\mathcal{R}})=\{S^{(0)}_{1},\ldots,S^{(0)}_{m}\}, (18)

whose edges capture calls, data and type dependencies, and structural relations such as imports, configuration references, and implementation–test associations. Semantic refinement then splits separable functions or merges entities that serve one capability into a component SiS_{i}. Across its dependency boundary ∂Si\partial S_{i}, local helpers and configuration state are internalized into CiC_{i}, external requirements are recorded in DiD_{i}, and the exposed interactions, associated tests, and documentation with provenance supply IiI_{i}, ViV_{i}, and XiX_{i}. Each candidate is validated in isolation, and its build, runtime, and test diagnostics eite_{i}^{t} refine it,

∂Si={v∉Si∣∃u∈Si,(u,v)∈E},(Cit+1,Dit+1,Iit+1)=REFINE(Cit,Dit,Iit,eit),\partial S_{i}=\{v\notin S_{i}\mid\exists u\in S_{i},\;(u,v)\in E\},\qquad(C_{i}^{t+1},D_{i}^{t+1},I_{i}^{t+1})=\operatorname{REFINE}(C_{i}^{t},D_{i}^{t},I_{i}^{t},e_{i}^{t}), (19)

until it is admitted, with executable closure, a passing component suite, and a recorded source repository, commit, and license, or excluded. A security hold set is applied when the library is loaded and saved, and because each entry records its source repository, same-repository donors can be excluded per target (Table 40).

Retrieval and Activation. The construction context 𝒞t\mathcal{C}_{t} holds the repository state, the constructed components with their recorded interfaces and dependencies, the decisions of earlier rounds, and the accumulated diagnostics. LEGO decomposes the request and activates primitives:

Πt=(r1,…,rK)=DECOMPOSE⁡(q,𝒞t),𝒜t=MATCH⁡(Πt,{ℱk}k=1K,{(si,ui)})⊆⋃k{i:Pi∈ℱk}.\Pi_{t}=(r_{1},\ldots,r_{K})=\operatorname{DECOMPOSE}(q,\mathcal{C}_{t}),\qquad\mathcal{A}_{t}=\operatorname{MATCH}\bigl(\Pi_{t},\{\mathcal{F}_{k}\}_{k=1}^{K},\{(s_{i},u_{i})\}\bigr)\subseteq\textstyle\bigcup_{k}\{i:P_{i}\in\mathcal{F}_{k}\}. (20)

Each requirement rkr_{k} names a capability with the interface it must expose and the dependencies it may assume. Retrieval runs outside the LLM, by embedding and reranking a query built from these constraints, and returns |ℱk|=m|\mathcal{F}_{k}|=m candidates, with m=2m=2. MATCH weighs coverage of Πt\Pi_{t} and compatibility with the target interfaces, the other selected primitives, and the existing repository. It activates the smallest mutually compatible set for the round, and a requirement that no suitable primitive covers goes to task-specific code gtg_{t}.

Primitive Adaptation and Collaboration. Round tt instantiates ADAPT as

(P~i,μi)=Miadapt​(Pi,rk⁡(i),𝒞t∪μ→i),i∈𝒜t,(\widetilde{P}_{i},\;\mu_{i})=M_{i}^{\mathrm{adapt}}\bigl(P_{i},\;r_{k(i)},\;\mathcal{C}_{t}\cup\mu_{\to i}\bigr),\qquad i\in\mathcal{A}_{t}, (21)

with k⁡(i)k(i) the capability that PiP_{i} was selected to cover and μ→i={μj→i:j∈𝒜t}\mu_{\to i}=\{\mu_{j\to i}:j\in\mathcal{A}_{t}\} the requirements addressed to it. A requirement μi→j\mu_{i\to j}, such as a changed signature, representation, dependency, or shared behavioural assumption, reaches its consumer in 𝒜t\mathcal{A}_{t} within the same round, along the dependency edges that Πt\Pi_{t} records, and the consumer adapts its own implementation; no primitive edits another’s component.

Editing, Execution, and Diagnosis. Repository Editing combines the adapted primitives with integration code into 𝒮t=INTEGRATE⁡({P~i}i∈𝒜t,gt)\mathcal{S}_{t}=\operatorname{INTEGRATE}(\{\widetilde{P}_{i}\}_{i\in\mathcal{A}_{t}},\,g_{t}) and resolves the composition constraints across primitive boundaries,

Γ⁡({P~i}i∈𝒜t)={Γapi,Γtype,Γdep,Γconfig},\Gamma(\{\widetilde{P}_{i}\}_{i\in\mathcal{A}_{t}})=\{\Gamma_{\mathrm{api}},\Gamma_{\mathrm{type}},\Gamma_{\mathrm{dep}},\Gamma_{\mathrm{config}}\}, (22)

namely API bindings, shared data representations and types, package dependencies, and configuration; the harness, not diagnosis, evaluates Γ\Gamma. Execution Feedback runs the target’s build checks and tests together with unit and integration tests synthesized from Πt\Pi_{t} and records ot=EXECUTE⁡(𝒮t)o_{t}=\operatorname{EXECUTE}(\mathcal{S}_{t}): build status, test outcomes and failing cases, runtime errors, and traces. Each task runs in a separate environment; suites share a 900-second timeout, and each test has a 180-second limit, tightened to 45 seconds inside repair after a timed-out round. Verification and Diagnosis computes

(vt,ϕt)=DIAGNOSE⁡(q,Πt,𝒮t,ot),vt∈{pass,fail},ϕt=(et,ct,ut),(v_{t},\phi_{t})=\operatorname{DIAGNOSE}(q,\Pi_{t},\mathcal{S}_{t},o_{t}),\qquad v_{t}\in\{\textup{{pass}},\textup{{fail}}\},\quad\phi_{t}=(e_{t},c_{t},u_{t}), (23)

on task completion, build success, test pass rate, interface consistency, and code quality. Build success and test pass rate come from execution, so vt=failv_{t}=\textup{{fail}} whenever the build or a required test fails. Diagnosis ties each observed failure in ete_{t} to execution evidence, finds the smallest set of components ct⊆𝒜tc_{t}\subseteq\mathcal{A}_{t} or interactions that explains it, classifies it among seven types, from an incorrect implementation or a missing capability to an integration failure, and gives each implicated component a revision objective in utu_{t}. It modifies no file and uses no held-out grading outcomes, original implementations, or floor and ceiling counts.

Revision. On failure, 𝒞t+1=𝒞t∪{ϕt}\mathcal{C}_{t+1}=\mathcal{C}_{t}\cup\{\phi_{t}\}, and the primitives in ctc_{t} are reactivated for another round of Eq. (21), while components that the new evidence does not contradict are preserved. The context accumulates diagnostics and is never truncated within a task. Πt\Pi_{t} is recomputed each round, so a requirement unmatched in round tt can be matched once neighbouring interfaces settle, and additional primitives are reserved for capabilities or dependencies that the evidence shows to be missing. A run stops when vt=passv_{t}=\textup{{pass}}, after b=5b=5 rounds per module, after two consecutive rounds without an additional passing test, or after two timeout rounds, and it returns the updated repository and its patch.

Controls. Configurations are named by their active stages: retrieval (R), primitive adaptation (A), execution feedback (V), and diagnosis (D). Each stage ablation is one substitution. Without D, revision runs on the raw execution evidence oto_{t} in place of ϕt\phi_{t}; without A, the retrieved PiP_{i} is integrated in place of P~i\widetilde{P}_{i}; and without R, 𝒜t\mathcal{A}_{t} is empty. Scoped generic editing (E) replaces primitive adaptation over the same retrieved components and differs from a primitive in the prompt contract above: the editor receives none of the primitive’s carried tests, metadata, or execution state. Vendor-and-invoke (I) copies the selected primitive unchanged into a vendored package and calls it, and read-only context (C) places its implementation, contract, and carried tests in the repository-level prompt without delivering its files. The independently developed agents run their own released harnesses with default scaffolding, tools, and stopping rules. A task adapter presents each LEGO-REPO task in the input format that the agent expects, and no agent receives the frozen test identifiers, the floor and ceiling counts, or any CodeFace entry.

Implementation. GPT-5.6 Terra is the default backbone, adaptation model, and diagnosis model, and one adaptation model instantiates all MiM_{i}; the study sweeps 13 backbones. The harness runs 10 concurrent model calls with at most 9,000 interface characters per module, top-2 retrieval, and b=5b=5. A task uses on average 856k input and 48k output tokens for repository-level construction, 11k input and 2.3k output tokens per adaptation over 7.4 successful adaptations, and 18k input and 2.6k output tokens per diagnosis round, and embedding and reranking cost a fixed $0.011. Priced at the hosted rates of the evaluated deployments, recorded calls cost $1.55 per task for execution feedback and $2.08 for LEGO with GPT-5.6 Terra.

Model Allocation. Table 27 varies the models in the backbone, adaptation, and diagnosis positions. Under a GPT-5.6 Terra backbone, GPT-OSS-20B in adaptation and diagnosis yields 0.4880 at $1.58 per task, above feedback with diagnosis at 0.3469 and $1.79, whereas a DeepSeek-V3.2 backbone with GPT-5.6 Terra in the other two positions reaches 0.2471 at $0.79.

Worked Adaptation. CodeFace entry cf-0412/schema-coercion, mined from marshmallow, spans 261 lines across 2 files, exports a field-coercion dispatcher and its error type, and carries 14 tests. Reconstructing pandera, LEGO required it to coerce untyped input to declared field types and to collect per-field errors, each with a location path, into one report. The adaptation replaced the donor’s exception-per-field control flow with an accumulating error collector, renamed the exported error type to the target’s contract, and moved the location path from a string to the target’s tuple representation. It dropped 3 tests that asserted on marshmallow’s message formatting, rewrote 5, and kept 6, and the 11 retained tests passed before repository-level composition bound the component to 4 sibling modules. A generic editor can produce the same rewrite but performs no carried-test check.

Construction Ladder. Figure 6(a) plots the ten configurations of Table 5 as a ladder of delivery: execution feedback adds 0.1008 to single-shot generation, unadapted retrieval 0.0172 to feedback, and retrieval with primitive adaptation 0.1665 to feedback with diagnosis. Panel (b) gives the relative gain over execution feedback by band, and the gap between the curves with and without same-repository donors at D4 and D5 is the part of the gain that those donors account for.

Primitive Fields. Table 28 locates LEGO’s 0.1041 margin over generic editing in the fields of PiP_{i}. A scoped generic editor over the retrieved components scores 0.4093, and adding the carried tests ViV_{i}, then the interface contract and provenance Ii,XiI_{i},X_{i}, then the dependency closure DiD_{i} raises it to 0.4431, 0.4818, and 0.5039. Added in this order, the fields recover 0.0946 of the margin, and the residual 0.0095 has a 95% interval of [−0.0071,+0.0148][-0.0071,+0.0148] with Wilcoxon p=0.49p=0.49. Withholding the carried tests from an otherwise complete primitive lowers delivery to 0.4796, a loss of 0.0338 that equals their forward increment [45].

Mapping to the Method. Within the method of Section 3, ADAPT returns P~i\widetilde{P}_{i} as the result of Eq. (2) and μi\mu_{i} as its messages, Repository Editing and Execution Feedback together form EXECUTE, DIAGNOSE is VERIFY, and admission into CodeFace is LEGO’s validation and publishing step, Eq. (7).

B.3.  Math Primitives: Self-Advertised Method Selection

A Math Primitive stores a proof method as a Method Contract, with the method’s required conditions, intended action, and residual obligations, and self-advertised method selection lets each contract propose its own use on a goal [46]. We give the full method and its experimental settings in that study’s notation. Figure 7 follows an illustrative Cauchy–Schwarz goal through the three stages of the method: the library whose selection sides the selector reads, self-advertisement with its commitment gate and tiered ranking, and proving under Lean compilation.

Problem and Contracts. Let gg be a Lean goal with local context Γ\Gamma, and let 𝒞\mathcal{C} be a finite library of Method Contracts. A contract cc has parameters xcx_{c}, a selection-facing description, required conditions Prec⁡(xc)\operatorname{Pre}_{c}(x_{c}), a target statement Gc​(xc)G_{c}(x_{c}) with an intended action, an execution scaffold ScS_{c}, and a list of residual obligations Oblc⁡(xc)\operatorname{Obl}_{c}(x_{c}). The action reduces the target to the required conditions and the obligations: once Prec⁡(θ)\operatorname{Pre}_{c}(\theta) and Oblc⁡(θ)\operatorname{Obl}_{c}(\theta) are proved for a binding θ\theta of xcx_{c}, the action yields Gc​(θ)G_{c}(\theta). A selector receives gg, Γ\Gamma, and the contract descriptions and returns an ordered list π⁡(g)=(c1,…,c|𝒞|)\pi(g)=(c_{1},\dots,c_{|\mathcal{C}|}) of the whole library. A contract is applicable to gg if some correct proof of gg contains a step that instantiates it. The experiments measure against a nonempty set A⁡(g)A(g) of annotated reference contracts. Correct annotations are applicable, and other proofs may use other methods, so agreement with A⁡(g)A(g) understates how often a shortlist contains a usable method.

Selection and Execution Sides. The selection side, which is what a selector reads, states the method, its typical target, when it applies and when not, and a manifest naming the verified material of the execution side without its Lean code. The execution side, which is supplied to the prover, holds a Lean scaffold over xcx_{c}, a compiled worked instance, the Mathlib declarations it relies on, Prec\operatorname{Pre}_{c} as Lean hypotheses, Oblc\operatorname{Obl}_{c}, GcG_{c}, and a verification record.

Self-Advertisement. One batched model call reads gg, Γ\Gamma, and the selection sides of all contracts and returns a proposal for each, so similarity plays no part in ranking or filtering the candidates. The proposal of cc makes a commitment that can be checked against the goal: a target tct_{c}, which instantiates Gc​(θ^)G_{c}(\hat{\theta}) in the goal’s own objects at a proposed binding θ^\hat{\theta}; an action aca_{c}; and the required facts Pre^c\widehat{\operatorname{Pre}}_{c}, which instantiate Prec⁡(θ^)\operatorname{Pre}_{c}(\hat{\theta}). It also cites verified material σc\sigma_{c} from the contract and records whether the contract offers itself (oco_{c}), its role ρc∈{main,support}\rho_{c}\in\{\text{main},\text{support}\}, and an integer applicability score s^c\hat{s}_{c}. A main nomination must pass the commitment gate

Gate⁡(c)=oc∧Spec⁡(tc)∧Spec⁡(ac)∧(σc≠∅),\operatorname{Gate}(c)=o_{c}\wedge\operatorname{Spec}(t_{c})\wedge\operatorname{Spec}(a_{c})\wedge(\sigma_{c}\neq\varnothing), (24)

where Spec\operatorname{Spec} holds when a target or action names a concrete object of the goal; a main nomination that fails the gate is demoted to a supporting role with its score unchanged. The tiered ranking orders contracts lexicographically by (τc,−s^c)(\tau_{c},-\hat{s}_{c}), where τc=1\tau_{c}=1 for main nominations that pass the gate, τc=2\tau_{c}=2 for other contracts that offer themselves, and τc=3\tau_{c}=3 otherwise. Ties are broken by contract identifier, so the ranking is deterministic given the model outputs.

Runoff. A prover that receives one contract depends on hit@1, and integer scores often leave the leading proposals close or tied. The optional runoff re-ranks the top qq contracts in one top-down pass of q−1q-1 calls: each call sees a contract, the contract above it, and that contract’s earlier proposal, writes a proposal for the lower contract, and swaps the two when that proposal fits the proof better. Contracts outside the window keep their order. The runoff uses the selector’s own backbone, so any gain it brings comes from direct comparison, and q=10q=10 matches the rerankers’ candidate count.

Conditional Scaffold Soundness. The study’s first result states what a checked scaffold establishes.

Proposition B.1 (Conditional scaffold soundness [46]).

Suppose a contract provides a Lean-checked term with no sorry or admitted proof holes, of type

Sc:∀xc,Prec⁡(xc)→Oblc,1⁡(xc)→⋯→Oblc,r⁡(xc)→Gc​(xc).S_{c}:\ \forall x_{c},\ \operatorname{Pre}_{c}(x_{c})\to\operatorname{Obl}_{c,1}(x_{c})\to\cdots\to\operatorname{Obl}_{c,r}(x_{c})\to G_{c}(x_{c}). (25)

For any binding θ\theta whose required conditions and obligations have checked proofs, applying ScS_{c} yields a checked proof of the target Gc​(θ)G_{c}(\theta).

Proof sketch.

Instantiate the checked term at θ\theta and apply it to the checked proofs of its premises. Lean checks that the resulting term proves Gc​(θ)G_{c}(\theta). ∎

The proposition applies to scaffolds checked in this parameterized form; a compiled example certifies that one example, not arbitrary new bindings. It concerns reuse, not discovery: a proposal identifies the remaining work for the new goal, Prec⁡(θ^)\operatorname{Pre}_{c}(\hat{\theta}) and Oblc⁡(θ^)\operatorname{Obl}_{c}(\hat{\theta}), without discharging it.

Similarity and Coverage. Let X=(g,Γ,contract descriptions)X=(g,\Gamma,\text{contract descriptions}) be the selector’s input, with A=A⁡(g)A=A(g) random given XX, and let T=ϕ⁡(X)T=\phi(X) be the features available to a similarity-only selector. With information FF, the best achievable expected hit@kk is Vk​(F)=𝔼⁡[maxS⊆𝒞,|S|=k⁡Pr⁡(S∩A≠∅∣F)]V_{k}(F)=\mathbb{E}\bigl[\max_{S\subseteq\mathcal{C},\,|S|=k}\Pr(S\cap A\neq\varnothing\mid F)\bigr]. Proposition 3.3 restates the study’s information bound, Vk​(X)≥Vk​(T)V_{k}(X)\geq V_{k}(T); its candidate-pool ceiling for a selector that reorders the similarity top-mm pool Pm​(g)P_{m}(g) and places the other contracts after it; and its multi-method coverage result, under which Hx​(S)=Pr⁡(S∩A≠∅∣X=x)H_{x}(S)=\Pr(S\cap A\neq\varnothing\mid X=x) is monotone and submodular, so greedy selection with the true marginal gains attains at least 1−1/e1-1/e of the best size-kk coverage [189]. The proofs of all three are in Appendix A.

Ranking Regret. With wc(x)=𝔼[𝟏[c∈A]/|A||X=x]w_{c}(x)=\mathbb{E}\bigl[\mathbf{1}[c\in A]/|A|\bigm|X=x\bigr] for a fixed input X=xX=x, a shortlist SS has expected recall@kk equal to Rx​(S)=∑c∈Swc​(x)R_{x}(S)=\sum_{c\in S}w_{c}(x), and self-advertisement can be read as estimating, from each contract’s proposal, the ordering by wc​(x)w_{c}(x) that maximizes it.

Proposition B.2 (Top-kk ranking regret [46]).

Let Sk∗S_{k}^{*} contain the kk contracts with the largest wc​(x)w_{c}(x), let S^k\widehat{S}_{k} contain the kk contracts with the largest scores s^c\hat{s}_{c}, and suppose there is a strictly increasing map ff such that |f⁡(s^c)−wc​(x)|≤ϵ|f(\hat{s}_{c})-w_{c}(x)|\leq\epsilon for every c∈Sk∗∪S^kc\in S_{k}^{*}\cup\widehat{S}_{k}. Then

Rx​(Sk∗)−Rx​(S^k)≤2​k​ϵ.R_{x}(S_{k}^{*})-R_{x}(\widehat{S}_{k})\leq 2k\epsilon.

Estimation errors affect the shortlist when they fall on contracts that are, or appear to be, among the top kk. The gate moves contracts that appear to be among the top kk but cannot state a checkable use below all supported nominations, and the runoff compares the leading proposals directly, since absolute scores from different contracts need not lie on the common scale that the premise requires.

Selection and Proof Success. For the event EkE_{k} that the first kk positions contain an annotated contract and the event ZBZ_{B} that the prover completes a Lean proof within BB compile calls, any prover satisfies Pr⁡(ZB)=Pr⁡(ZB∣¬Ek)+Pr⁡(Ek)​Δk\Pr(Z_{B})=\Pr(Z_{B}\mid\neg E_{k})+\Pr(E_{k})\,\Delta_{k} with Δk=Pr⁡(ZB∣Ek)−Pr⁡(ZB∣¬Ek)\Delta_{k}=\Pr(Z_{B}\mid E_{k})-\Pr(Z_{B}\mid\neg E_{k}). Selection controls Pr⁡(Ek)\Pr(E_{k}), while Δk\Delta_{k} depends on the contract’s execution guidance and residual obligations; the contract arm of Table 8 is the case k=1k=1, B=10B=10.

Contract Library. The 82 contracts are built once, offline, in three steps from solutions to Putnam 2000–2014 problems, none of them an evaluation problem. GPT-5.6 Sol extracts the methods used in the reference solutions and proposes merges between methods that play the same role in different problems, and the authors review each extracted method and each proposed merge. The model then drafts both sides of each contract from its source solutions, and each execution-side Lean artifact is compiled with Lean v4.27.0 and Mathlib at commit a3a10db. All 82 contracts pass, each with a scaffold stated for arbitrary parameters and a compiled worked instance. Construction and proving share this environment, so a scaffold that compiled at construction stays valid for the prover, as Proposition B.1 requires, and the runner exits at startup if the library’s recorded Mathlib revision differs from the environment’s Lake manifest.

Experimental Configuration. The selection baselines are random ordering, BM25 [161], TF-IDF cosine [162], OpenAI’s text-embedding-3-small and text-embedding-3-large [163], Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B [164], and a listwise LLM reranker over the top 10 candidates of each embedding model [123]. All LLM-based selectors run with DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash [171], GPT-5.6 Luna [170], and GPT-5.6 Terra, one backbone per block of Table 7. With πk​(g)={c1,…,ck}\pi_{k}(g)=\{c_{1},\dots,c_{k}\} and rank⁡(g)=min⁡{i:ci∈A⁡(g)}\operatorname{rank}(g)=\min\{i:c_{i}\in A(g)\}, the metrics over the NN problems of a benchmark are

hit@k=1N∑g𝟏[πk(g)∩A(g)≠∅],recall@k=1N∑g|πk​(g)∩A⁡(g)||A⁡(g)|,\displaystyle\text{hit@}k=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{g}\mathbf{1}\bigl[\pi_{k}(g)\cap A(g)\neq\varnothing\bigr],\qquad\text{recall@}k=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{g}\frac{|\pi_{k}(g)\cap A(g)|}{|A(g)|},
MRR=1N​∑g1rank⁡(g).\displaystyle\text{MRR}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{g}\frac{1}{\operatorname{rank}(g)}.

For proving, GPT-5.6 Luna runs a whole-proof repair loop with a budget of B=10B=10 Lean compilations per problem. Base is one attempt without retrieval; pass@20 draws 20 independent samples and so has twice the budget; APOLLO alternates generation with Lean-guided repair [117]; AxProverBase, Ax-Prover run without contracts under the same budget, is the direct control [118]; and the contract arm adds the top-ranked self-advertised contract to AxProverBase’s initial prompt.

Mapping to the Method. Within the method of Section 3, the selection side of a contract is its interface did_{i}, and a proposal is the relevance assessment of Eq. (3): the score s^c\hat{s}_{c} plays the role of sis_{i}, and the target, action, and required facts form the proposed use uiu_{i}.

B.4.  Knowledge Primitives: Source Learning

Each Knowledge Primitive owns a source model, an explicit and persistent state that holds the understanding of one authoritative source while remaining grounded in it. SourceLearn [47] is the framework that develops this model through repeated study and use of the source, and we describe it in its own notation: MM is a source model, FF the task solver, BB a token budget, R⁡(D,q)R(D,q) the source context of a task qq and RR alone a source region, and Π0\Pi_{0} and Π1\Pi_{1} are instructions on how to represent a source. Initial construction builds a provisional source model M0M_{0} from the source DD, Self-Directed and Task-Guided Source Learning refine it into MSM_{S} and then MTM_{T} through grounded source reconstruction, and at test time the solver receives the activated MTM_{T} beside the retrieved evidence (Figure 8).

Problem. A persistent authoritative source DD grounds recurring tasks (q,y)∼𝒫D(q,y)\sim\mathcal{P}_{D}, where yy is the desired outcome of qq. Knowledge access, source learning, and the use of the learned understanding are

y^=F⁡(q,R⁡(D,q)),Mt=Learn⁡(D,Ht),y^=F⁡(q,R⁡(D,q),Mt),\hat{y}=F\big(q,R(D,q)\big),\qquad M_{t}=\operatorname{Learn}(D,H_{t}),\qquad\hat{y}=F\big(q,R(D,q),M_{t}\big), (26)

where RR may be retrieval, long-context access, or a structured source representation, and HtH_{t} is the accumulated study and task experience. Repeated access alone can leave reusable knowledge fragmented or in need of reconstruction for each task. Source learning therefore faces two questions: what source knowledge to learn before future tasks are known, and how task feedback can improve source-specific competence beyond the task that produced it, since retaining an observed answer or correction risks learning the task rather than the source. Self-Directed Source Learning addresses the first question and Task-Guided Source Learning the second:

M0=Construct⁡(D),MS=SelfLearn⁡(D,M0),MT=TaskLearn⁡(D,MS,𝒢),M_{0}=\operatorname{Construct}(D),\qquad M_{S}=\operatorname{SelfLearn}(D,M_{0}),\qquad M_{T}=\operatorname{TaskLearn}(D,M_{S};\mathcal{G}), (27)

where 𝒢={(qt,yt)}t=1T\mathcal{G}=\{(q_{t},y_{t})\}_{t=1}^{T} holds guidance tasks grounded in the same source, with reference outcomes yty_{t}.

Source Model. MM is organized around source entities ee, each with a reusable representation mem_{e} of its properties, mechanisms, governing conditions, procedures, exceptions, distinctions, and relations to other entities, and higher-level structure organizes dependencies across entities. Each unit makes one reusable semantic commitment and cites the source elements it rests on; facts that a reader can look up stay in DD. Construct\operatorname{Construct} reads the source entity by entity within coherent regions, such as code modules or document sections, under a generic modeling instruction Π0\Pi_{0} that favors major entities, relations, procedures, and governing conditions over redundant low-level content. The resulting M0M_{0} is deliberately provisional.

Grounded Source Reconstruction. All later updates follow one principle: learning signals determine what should be reconsidered, while persistent knowledge is reconstructed from the authoritative source. For an affected source region RR and a learning signal ξ\xi,

OR=Inspect⁡(DR,MR,ξ),M′=GroundApply⁡(M,Reconstruct⁡(MR,OR),DR),O_{R}=\operatorname{Inspect}(D_{R},M_{R};\xi),\qquad M^{\prime}=\operatorname{GroundApply}\big(M,\operatorname{Reconstruct}(M_{R},O_{R});D_{R}\big), (28)

where the temporary observations ORO_{R}, gathered by rereading the region’s source content against the current model, are never copied into MM. Each proposed unit passes through the grounding gate, which judges a statement supported when its cited excerpts entail it and a negative claim supported when an excerpt states the denial; any other unit counts as unsupported. The region rewrite is committed if the preservation check finds each previously supported meaning still stated, entailed, or covered by a broader unit, and withheld otherwise.

Source-Model Activation. At task time, the solver receives at most B=24B=24k tokens of MM in addition to the evidence retrieved for the query:

AB​(M,q)={M,tok⁡(M)≤B,ActivateRegions⁡(M,q,B),tok⁡(M)>B,y^=F⁡(q,R⁡(D,q),AB​(M,q)),A_{B}(M,q)=\begin{cases}M,&\operatorname{tok}(M)\leq B,\\ \operatorname{ActivateRegions}(M,q;B),&\operatorname{tok}(M)>B,\end{cases}\qquad\hat{y}=F\big(q,R(D,q),A_{B}(M,q)\big), (29)

where activation selects task-relevant regions among those established during construction and preserves the internal structure of each region it selects.

Self-Directed Source Learning. Before future task requirements are known, one Inspect–Study–Consolidate cycle decides what deserves deeper study:

O=Inspect⁡(D,M),O+=Study⁡(D,M,O),M′=Consolidate⁡(D,M,O+).O=\operatorname{Inspect}(D,M),\qquad O^{+}=\operatorname{Study}(D,M,O),\qquad M^{\prime}=\operatorname{Consolidate}(D,M,O^{+}). (30)

Model-conditioned source inspection rereads the source content SeS_{e} of each entity against its representation, Oe=Observe⁡(Se,me)O_{e}=\operatorname{Observe}(S_{e},m_{e}), and records what the representation still fails to explain well; observations do not modify MM. Adaptive source study then selects, at planning round bb, study actions from the current model, the accumulated observations O¯b\overline{O}_{b}, and the study history H<bH_{<b}:

Γb=PlanStudy⁡(M,O¯b,H<b),Γb⊆{Deepen​(e,qstudy),Connect​(ei,ej,qstudy)}.\Gamma_{b}=\operatorname{PlanStudy}(M,\overline{O}_{b},H_{<b}),\qquad\Gamma_{b}\subseteq\bigl\{\textsc{Deepen}(e,q^{\mathrm{study}}),\ \textsc{Connect}(e_{i},e_{j},q^{\mathrm{study}})\bigr\}. (31)

Deepen investigates an unresolved aspect of one entity, and Connect jointly studies two entities whose dependency remains insufficiently understood. The temporary study question qstudyq^{\mathrm{study}} of each action guides retrieval and renewed reading and is not stored. Evidence consolidation then applies Eq. (28) once, a read-many, write-once pattern, and turns M0M_{0} into MSM_{S}.

Task-Guided Source Learning. In one pass over 𝒢\mathcal{G}, SourceLearn first returns to the source for each guidance task:

E~t=RetrieveGuide⁡(D,qt,yt),(Et∗,Ct)=Diagnose⁡(qt,yt,E~t),\widetilde{E}_{t}=\operatorname{RetrieveGuide}(D,q_{t},y_{t}),\qquad(E_{t}^{*},C_{t})=\operatorname{Diagnose}(q_{t},y_{t},\widetilde{E}_{t}), (32)

where Et∗E_{t}^{*} is the source evidence that supports the reference outcome and CtC_{t} the source requirements of the task. No other step of source learning directly observes yty_{t}, and neither yty_{t} nor Et∗E_{t}^{*} is stored as persistent knowledge. The task is then answered through Eq. (29); when the answer y^t\hat{y}_{t} is wrong, failure-guided local refinement rereads from DD the region behind the requirements that the model does not represent and revises it through Eq. (28):

Ct−={c∈Ct:c​ is not represented in ​Mt},Mt+1=Refine⁡(D,Mt,Ct−).C_{t}^{-}=\{c\in C_{t}:c\text{ is not represented in }M_{t}\},\qquad M_{t+1}=\operatorname{Refine}(D,M_{t};C_{t}^{-}). (33)

Requirements that MtM_{t} represents trigger no writing, which separates a representational deficiency from an error made although the required understanding is available. The pass yields the locally refined model MlocalM_{\mathrm{local}}. Cross-task representation learning draws from each guidance task at most one lesson about how, not what, to represent, and aggregates the recurring lessons with Π0\Pi_{0} into a representation policy Π1\Pi_{1}, which introduces no source knowledge:

ℓt=Lesson⁡(qt,Ct,Mt,y^t),Π1=Aggregate⁡(Π0,{ℓt}t=1T).\ell_{t}=\operatorname{Lesson}(q_{t},C_{t},M_{t},\hat{y}_{t}),\qquad\Pi_{1}=\operatorname{Aggregate}\big(\Pi_{0},\{\ell_{t}\}_{t=1}^{T}\big). (34)

Recalibration then revisits the source under Π1\Pi_{1} and incorporates structure that is missing or represented at an inappropriate granularity through Eq. (28):

MT=Recalibrate⁡(D,Mlocal,Π1).M_{T}=\operatorname{Recalibrate}(D,M_{\mathrm{local}};\Pi_{1}). (35)

MTM_{T} stays fixed for the test tasks.

Sources and Counterparts. MultiDoc2Dial contributes four government domains, DMV, SSA, StudentAid, and VA, each a source of 92–149 documents with 60 questions. NarrativeQA contributes 12 stories of its official test split, six movie scripts and six books with 27–30 questions each, read in full. SWE-QA contributes six of its fifteen repositories, streamlink, sphinx, xarray, pytest, flask, and conan, each a source at its pinned commit with 48 questions. APIBench has one source per model hub, TorchHub with 186 instructions and HuggingFace and TensorFlow Hub with 100 each, whose accuracies are averaged; a prompt that exceeds a backend’s context window counts as a failure. AppWorld’s API documentation, 457 API specifications across nine simulated apps, is a single source. RAPTOR [21] runs its official implementation with default settings (100-token chunks, recursive clustering, and collapsed-tree retrieval of the top 10 nodes within 3,500 tokens). HippoRAG 2 [98] runs its official package in its reproduction setting and passes its top 8 passages, matching the evidence budget of Hybrid RAG. AWM [25] induces workflows from the successful guidance-task experiences of each source and split and places them in the prompt of each test task of that split, beside the same Hybrid RAG evidence that SourceLearn receives.

Implementation. GPT-5.6 Luna [170] and GPT-OSS-120B [172] run at medium reasoning effort, and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash [171] at high effort on the QA benchmarks and medium effort on APIBench and AppWorld; all methods embed with text-embedding-3-large. M0M_{0} is constructed once per source and backend. Self-Directed Source Learning runs one cycle with K=20K=20 study actions, and its MSM_{S} is shared by the three splits. Hybrid RAG, which supplies R⁡(D,q)R(D,q), splits documents into sections and code into files and symbol-level units, fuses the top 30 elements by BM25 [161] and by dense retrieval [87] by reciprocal rank fusion, and passes the top 8 to the solver. On AppWorld, the ReAct-style code agent [1] runs for at most 50 steps, its documentation calls answered by a channel that returns each method’s own source context, with the built-in documentation app removed. The three 30%/70% splits of the QA benchmarks and APIBench keep related tasks on the same side, and AppWorld’s 90 training and 168 test-normal tasks serve as guidance and test tasks. The QA judge, GPT-5.6 Luna at medium reasoning effort, accepts an answer that makes the key claims of the reference without contradicting it, and accuracy is macro-averaged over sources and then averaged over splits; APIBench uses its AST-based evaluator, and AppWorld reports task goal completion. The ablations in Figure 9 use two sources per QA benchmark, SSA and VA, pytest and conan, and the scripts of All About Eve and The Breakfast Club, with the guidance and test splits of the main results. Removing Self-Directed Source Learning starts task-guided learning from M0M_{0}, removing Task-Guided Source Learning leaves MSM_{S}, removing cross-task representation learning leaves MlocalM_{\mathrm{local}}, and removing failure-guided local refinement recalibrates MSM_{S} under Π1\Pi_{1}.

Additional Results. The activated source model gives the solver more task-time context than the native retrieval baselines receive. We therefore give each retrieval baseline the per-question context budget of SourceLearn, which it fills by reading further down its own ranking without changing its ranking or index (Table 29). SourceLearn remains the best on three of the four sources and second on Sphinx, so task-time context alone does not explain its performance. The remaining analyses also use GPT-5.6 Luna with the sources, splits, and judge of the main results. On the QA benchmarks, the gain over Hybrid RAG is 14.9 pp on source regions that guidance tasks touched and 12.1 pp on regions that none touched (Table 45), so the learned understanding carries over to parts of the source that no guidance task exposed. On MultiDoc2Dial, the source model alone, with no retrieved evidence, performs comparably to Hybrid RAG with all eight retrieved elements, and removing the gold document costs Hybrid RAG about 25 pp but SourceLearn about 8 pp (Figure 18). The audits of Tables 44 and 44 cover StudentAid, pytest, and HuggingFace: at most 1% of the sampled units of M0M_{0}, MSM_{S}, and MTM_{T} are contradicted by their cited source elements, and 93.3% to 100% of the claims that a learning stage removed remain represented. Some Task-Guided units on the document and code sources are partially supported or unsupported; on StudentAid, the fully supported share falls from 79.2% in M0M_{0} to 63.3% in MTM_{T}, with 13.3% unsupported. The learned model therefore complements the source with reusable understanding, and the source stays authoritative and directly accessible through R⁡(D,q)R(D,q).

Mapping to the Method. As in Section 3.4, each source model is the resource of one Knowledge Primitive, source-model activation specializes COMPOSE, and grounded source reconstruction realizes VALIDATE on the publishing path of Eq. (7), along which the two learning stages improve each source model apart from the test tasks.

B.5.  Agent Primitives: Reusable Latent Building Blocks

Agent Primitives [48] address two limitations of existing multi-agent systems (MAS): they lack a reusable, task-agnostic abstraction for organizing multi-agent computation, so their complexity scales with task complexity, and they communicate in natural language, which degrades in long contexts and under accumulated noise. Drawing on neural network design, where complex models are built from reusable blocks such as residual blocks and attention heads [191], the study decomposes existing MAS architectures into a few recurring, minimal computation patterns, such as iterative review, multi-agent consensus, and plan–execute decomposition, and instantiates three representative primitives that communicate via key–value (KV) cache. Latent communication methods mainly improve how information passes between agents [135, 136, 137]; Agent Primitives use KV cache communication to implement the computation structure of each primitive. For each query, an LLM Organizer selects and composes the primitives into a primitive-based MAS, guided by a lightweight Knowledge Pool (Figure 10).

Latent Communication. For a Transformer decoder of LL layers [191], the KV cache after nn positions is 𝒵n={(Knℓ,Vnℓ)}ℓ=1L\mathcal{Z}_{n}=\{(K_{n}^{\ell},V_{n}^{\ell})\}_{\ell=1}^{L}, and decoding step tt appends its key and value, Ktℓ=[Kt−1ℓ;𝐤tℓ]K_{t}^{\ell}=[K_{t-1}^{\ell};\mathbf{k}_{t}^{\ell}] and Vtℓ=[Vt−1ℓ;𝐯tℓ]V_{t}^{\ell}=[V_{t-1}^{\ell};\mathbf{v}_{t}^{\ell}]. Latent communication is stated for two agents AA and BB for simplicity; the Selector of Voting and Selection reads the caches of all its Solvers. The input prompt xA1:nAx^{A}_{1:n_{A}} of AA holds its system prompt and the user query. After processing its full sequence sA=[x1:nAA;ynA+1:nA+mAA]s^{A}=[x^{A}_{1:n_{A}};y^{A}_{n_{A}+1:n_{A}+m_{A}}] of length TA=nA+mAT_{A}=n_{A}+m_{A}, AA holds the final KV cache 𝒵TAA\mathcal{Z}^{A}_{T_{A}}, a latent representation of sAs^{A}, and the fixed system prompt xB1:nBx^{B}_{1:n_{B}} of BB, processed alone, yields the system-level cache 𝒵nBB\mathcal{Z}^{B}_{n_{B}}:

𝒵TAA={(KTAA,ℓ,VTAA,ℓ)}ℓ=1L,𝒵nBB={(KnBB,ℓ,VnBB,ℓ)}ℓ=1L.\mathcal{Z}^{A}_{T_{A}}=\{(K^{A,\ell}_{T_{A}},V^{A,\ell}_{T_{A}})\}_{\ell=1}^{L},\qquad\mathcal{Z}^{B}_{n_{B}}=\{(K^{B,\ell}_{n_{B}},V^{B,\ell}_{n_{B}})\}_{\ell=1}^{L}. (36)

A combined KV cache concatenates the latent states of AA and the system prompt of BB at each layer:

K~B,ℓ=[KnBB,ℓ;KTAA,ℓ],V~B,ℓ=[VnBB,ℓ;VTAA,ℓ].\tilde{K}^{B,\ell}=[K^{B,\ell}_{n_{B}};K^{A,\ell}_{T_{A}}],\qquad\tilde{V}^{B,\ell}=[V^{B,\ell}_{n_{B}};V^{A,\ell}_{T_{A}}]. (37)

The resulting cache 𝒵~B={(K~B,ℓ,V~B,ℓ)}ℓ=1L\tilde{\mathcal{Z}}_{B}=\{(\tilde{K}^{B,\ell},\tilde{V}^{B,\ell})\}_{\ell=1}^{L} replaces the KV cache of BB, which then decodes autoregressively without natural-language communication from AA.

Input-Output Alignment Assumption. KV cache communication assumes that the decoder conditions future tokens on its accumulated key–value states alone, so that conditioning on 𝒵A\mathcal{Z}^{A} is distributionally equivalent to conditioning on the token sequence sAs^{A}:

p(y∣𝒵A,x1:nBB)≈p(y∣sA,x1:nBB).p(y\mid\mathcal{Z}^{A},x^{B}_{1:n_{B}})\approx p(y\mid s^{A},x^{B}_{1:n_{B}}). (38)

The approximation holds when both agents share the same model parameters and positional encoding scheme, so all agents use the same LLM, and all evaluations stay within one model architecture.

KV Cache Positional Re-encoding. Rotary positional encoding (RoPE) [139] rotates the key at position tt as RoPE⁡(Ktℓ)=R⁡(t)​Ktℓ\mathrm{RoPE}(K_{t}^{\ell})=R(t)K_{t}^{\ell}, where R⁡(t)R(t) is a deterministic block-diagonal rotation operator whose 2D rotation angles are linear in tt. The concatenated cache is treated as one continuous sequence, in which the system prompt of BB occupies positions 11 to nBn_{B} and the cache of AA positions 11 to TAT_{A}. To preserve RoPE semantics, the KV states of AA are re-indexed by the offset nBn_{B}, for each layer ℓ\ell and t∈{1,…,TA}t\in\{1,\dots,T_{A}\},

RoPE⁡(KtA,ℓ)→R⁡(t+nB)​KtA,ℓ,\mathrm{RoPE}(K_{t}^{A,\ell})\rightarrow R(t+n_{B})K_{t}^{A,\ell}, (39)

so that the concatenated cache can be used directly in standard decoding.

Communication Bottleneck. Two stress tests with Qwen3-8B [169] motivate KV cache as the medium. In long-context task injection, an auxiliary instruction is injected at the beginning, midpoint, or end of the long contexts of 351 En.QA examples from InfiniteBench. Without injection, natural-language communication reaches 51.6% accuracy and KV cache communication 61.3%. At the midpoint, injection compliance falls to 15.6% for natural language, against 73.3% for KV cache, while accuracy stays stable across positions, so the degradation stems from communication failure. In communication noise, 100 correctly solved GSM8K [153] traces, truncated to 6,000 tokens, are continued by another Qwen3-8B within 5,000 tokens while 0 to 25 sentences of unrelated reasoning are injected. With one and three noise sentences, natural language solves 91% and 73% of the problems and KV cache all of them; with 10 and 25, 47% and 40% against 93% and 77%.

Primitive Design. Internal coordination runs exclusively through latent KV cache exchange, so a primitive’s behavior is independent of text-level message passing, and each primitive can serve as a drop-in replacement for a single agent. The role system prompts fix role boundaries independently of task-specific content and encode no explicit problem-solving strategy. Review, an iterative self-critique operator, connects a Solver AA and a Critic BB through a latent feedback channel: BB consumes the KV cache of AA to generate corrective feedback, and the modified latent representation returns to AA for refinement until a stopping condition derived from the intermediate latent states holds, which gives adaptive depth of refinement. The Critic provides evaluative signals and neither revises the solution nor answers. In Voting and Selection, a consensus operator, parallel Solvers produce latent candidates independently, and a Selector votes and selects over these candidates directly in latent space, computing an aggregated latent state that produces the output; it judges correctness, consistency, and overall solution quality without introducing reasoning beyond the candidates. In Planning and Execution, a latent decomposition operator, a Planner PP produces a latent plan that decomposes the task into intermediate steps or subgoals without solving it, and an Executor EE follows the plan without modifying it to generate the output.

Primitive-Based MAS. A primitive-based MAS is a composition graph of primitives, which an LLM Organizer, GPT-5.2 by default, builds per query. The Organizer’s prompt supplies the query, the three primitives, and the Knowledge Pool, and instructs it to analyze the task requirements and complexity, to select primitives, and to determine their execution order and composition structure. The Organizer reasons at the level of primitives, designs no task-specific roles or natural-language protocols, and does not solve the task. Its primitive composition plan specifies (i) the primitives to instantiate and (ii) their execution structure in code, at 200–400 output tokens per query. The lightweight Knowledge Pool holds 45 previously observed queries paired with effective MAS structures from frameworks including Multi-Agent Debate [131], DyLAN [133], Self-Refine [140], AFlow [29], and MAS-GPT [134]. The Organizer retrieves entries by the input query as structural guidance and abstracts them into primitive compositions, replacing task-specific agents with Agent Primitives. The system then executes the plan, coordinating within and across primitives through KV cache, and externally behaves like a standard MAS.

Implementation. The study runs five worker backbones, Qwen3-4B, Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-14B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B, and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-70B, of which Table 10 reports three. With Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-14B, the primitive-based MAS reaches 69.6% and 77.6% average accuracy, against 55.7% and 65.5% for a single agent. LatentMAS [137] runs in its sequential configuration with m=40m=40, its best setting, and four agents, so TextMAS and the single-primitive baselines use four as well: two rounds for Review, three Solvers and one Selector for Voting and Selection, and one Planner with three Executors for Planning and Execution. In the primitive-based MAS, the Organizer sets the number of agents per query. The metrics are accuracy, token usage, and average inference time per query.

RoPE Re-indexing. Table 30 disables the re-indexing of Eq. (39) while the backbones and primitives stay unchanged. With Qwen3-8B, the composed MAS loses 13.3 pp on AIME25 and at most 2.7 pp on HumanEval+ and MedQA. With R1/Llama-70B, each primitive and the composed MAS lose between 26.7 and 59.7 pp, so positional re-encoding is critical for stable KV cache communication, most of all on the Llama-based backbone.

Further Results. Table 48 prices the methods of Table 11 per query at market output-token prices of $1.75 per million tokens for Llama-3-70B-Instruct and $14 per million for GPT-5.2, and divides accuracy by cost. With the same Llama-3-70B-Instruct workers, Claude-4 as Organizer reaches 72.8%, 93.2%, 81.1%, and 53.6% on MATH, GSM8K, HumanEval+, and GPQA, Qwen3-32B 71.3%, 89.8%, 78.6%, and 49.1%, and Llama-3-70B-Instruct itself, the iso-model setting, 72.0%, 91.8%, 81.0%, and 52.2%, so the framework does not rely solely on a proprietary Organizer. Over 100 examples per task category, Review accounts for 15%, 22%, and 48% of the selected primitives on MATH, HumanEval, and MedQA, Voting and Selection for 52%, 18%, and 35%, and Planning and Execution for 33%, 60%, and 17%, with 3.4, 2.8, and 2.5 primitives per query, so the Organizer adapts its composition to the task. On ARC-Challenge, which has no entry in the Knowledge Pool, the Organizer without the pool outperforms a single agent by 2.5 and 2.3 pp with Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B and random structure selection by 1.9 and 1.1 pp, and the pool adds a further 1.2 pp on average.

Mapping to the Method. The Organizer realizes COMPOSE (Eq. (4)), with the Knowledge Pool as the structural guidance it reads, and its primitive composition plan is the plan of that equation. Along the plan’s dependencies, agents that share one LLM pass the combined cache of Eq. (37). The Critic and the Selector judge results inside their primitives, the Review loop is the family’s revision, and the primitives and the pool stay fixed across queries.

B.6.  Dev-Primitives: Activation, Collaboration, Execution, and Diagnosis

Dev-Primitives are modular executable interfaces that turn repository components into active participants in software engineering [49]. HERMES, the harness engineering framework that instantiates them, consists of an activation module, a dynamically activated set of Dev-Primitives, an executable environment, and a diagnosis module. Dynamic activation and bug diagnosis, both implemented by prompting an LLM, are the two mechanisms that it supplies beyond the Dev-Primitive abstraction. Figure 11 gives the general workflow, in which bug diagnosis maps the observed failure back to the components that must be revised and the next round reactivates them. In one SWE-bench Verified trajectory with Qwen3-8B, six activated Dev-Primitives exchange 15 directed messages, and the issue is resolved in the first round.

Dev-Primitives. A repository consists of NN software components ℛ={ai}i=1N\mathcal{R}=\{a_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N}, and each component aia_{i} is associated with a Dev-Primitive PiP_{i} instantiated with an LLM ℳ\mathcal{M}:

(ai′,mi)=Pi​(ai,xi,𝒞i)=ℳ⁡([ai;xi;𝒞i]),(a_{i}^{\prime},\,m_{i})=P_{i}(a_{i},\,x_{i},\,\mathcal{C}_{i})=\mathcal{M}\bigl([\,a_{i};\ x_{i};\ \mathcal{C}_{i}\,]\bigr), (40)

where xix_{i} is the local objective assigned to PiP_{i}, 𝒞i\mathcal{C}_{i} the communication context of messages received from other Dev-Primitives, ai′a_{i}^{\prime} the optionally modified artifact (ai′=aia_{i}^{\prime}=a_{i} when no modification is required), and mim_{i} a natural-language message with task-relevant information or requirements for other components. In local modification, the primitive reasons over and edits its own artifact. In inter-primitive communication, it sends requirements such as interface changes, dependency updates, or testing requirements to the components that its local reasoning implicates, in practice its callers, callees, configurations, and tests. Each message is placed verbatim into its target’s communication context, and no central agent interprets, filters, or rewrites it. Participation does not imply modification: a primitive may contribute information while leaving its artifact unchanged.

State and Granularity. A Dev-Primitive persists across the revision rounds of a task with its current artifact and the communication accumulated during the trajectory; model hidden states are not preserved across calls. A new persistent file that an active Dev-Primitive creates is registered as a Dev-Primitive, while temporary outputs, caches, and logs are environment observations. Files are the default granularity, and on Terminal-Bench the components are the persistent filesystem artifacts, such as shell scripts, configuration files, and service definitions.

Dynamic Primitive Activation. The activation module converts the issue qq into a plan over repository components,

Π=ACTIVATE⁡(q,ℛ)={(i,xi)}i∈𝒜,𝒫𝒜={Pi∣i∈𝒜},\Pi=\operatorname{ACTIVATE}(q,\mathcal{R})=\{(i,x_{i})\}_{i\in\mathcal{A}},\qquad\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{A}}=\{P_{i}\mid i\in\mathcal{A}\}, (41)

where 𝒜⊆{1,…,N}\mathcal{A}\subseteq\{1,\ldots,N\} indexes the selected components; HERMES instantiates 𝒫𝒜\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{A}}, and inactive components receive no model calls. Activation is a single LLM call chain of issue analysis, component localization, dependency analysis, task decomposition, and edit planning. Here ℛ\mathcal{R} denotes access to the repository, not its concatenation into one context: the module retrieves candidate files and expands along dependencies by reading them, without a precomputed call graph. For each activated component, the plan gives an objective, dependencies, communication targets, and an expected action (inspect, modify, or validate), followed by an execution plan.

Collaboration and Execution. The activated primitives operate as one round, and HERMES applies their edits:

{ai′}i∈𝒜←Collaborate​({Pi}i∈𝒜,{xi}i∈𝒜),ℛ′←UpdateRepository​(ℛ,{ai′}i∈𝒜).\{a_{i}^{\prime}\}_{i\in\mathcal{A}}\leftarrow\textsc{Collaborate}\bigl(\{P_{i}\}_{i\in\mathcal{A}},\,\{x_{i}\}_{i\in\mathcal{A}}\bigr),\qquad\mathcal{R}^{\prime}\leftarrow\textsc{UpdateRepository}\bigl(\mathcal{R},\,\{a_{i}^{\prime}\}_{i\in\mathcal{A}}\bigr). (42)

Communication is interleaved with local modification and follows the repository dependencies encountered during execution, so a recipient may revise its modification after receiving a requirement within the round. The modified repository is executed in the benchmark-provided environment,

o=EXECUTE⁡(ℛ′)=(oshell,otest,oruntime,otrace),o=\operatorname{EXECUTE}(\mathcal{R}^{\prime})=\bigl(o_{\mathrm{shell}},\,o_{\mathrm{test}},\,o_{\mathrm{runtime}},\,o_{\mathrm{trace}}\bigr), (43)

which records shell commands, outputs, exit codes, and build status; test results; runtime behaviour and exceptions; and logs and stack traces. During solving, all modules use task-visible checks, such as repository tests, build commands, linters, and reproduction scripts written while solving. Held-out evaluation tests, such as the FAIL_TO_PASS and PASS_TO_PASS tests of SWE-bench Verified, are withheld until HERMES terminates.

Bug Diagnosis and Revision. Given the issue, the plan, the modified repository, and the execution observation, one LLM call returns the verdict

v=DIAGNOSE⁡(q,Π,ℛ′,o)∈{pass,fail},v=\operatorname{DIAGNOSE}(q,\Pi,\mathcal{R}^{\prime},o)\in\{\textup{{pass}},\textup{{fail}}\}, (44)

and, on fail, structured feedback ϕ=(e,c,u)\phi=(e,c,u): the observed failure ee, the suspected root cause cc together with the components implicated by the evidence, including components that activation may have missed, and revision guidance uu for each component. Diagnosis does not modify artifacts and cannot override deterministic execution failures: a trajectory with failing task-visible tests or unsuccessful compilation cannot be marked pass on model judgment alone. Activation then revises the plan,

Π′=ACTIVATE⁡(q,ℛ′,Π,ϕ),\Pi^{\prime}=\operatorname{ACTIVATE}(q,\mathcal{R}^{\prime},\Pi,\phi), (45)

retaining the modifications that new execution evidence does not contradict, updating objectives, removing components that are no longer relevant, and activating newly implicated Dev-Primitives. HERMES returns ℛ′\mathcal{R}^{\prime} on pass and a structured failure report FailureReport​(q,ℛ′,o)\textsc{FailureReport}(q,\mathcal{R}^{\prime},o) once the budget BB is spent. BB counts the revision rounds after the initial plan–collaborate–execute–diagnose round, so B=0B=0 performs that round without revision.

Implementation. Each Dev-Primitive is instantiated with its own LLM, which may differ from the activation and diagnosis models (Table 50). The primary backbones are GPT-5.6 Sol, Terra, and Luna, Claude Sonnet 5, Claude Opus 5, DeepSeek-V4, and Qwen3-8B [169]. Reasoning effort is medium where configurable unless a table states otherwise, and B=3B=3. Qwen3-8B is served locally with Ollama on NVIDIA A40 GPUs, with its default sampling parameters (temperature 0.6, top-pp 0.95, top-kk 20) and Ollama’s 32K context window; all other models are accessed through their official APIs. SWE-bench Verified uses the official snapshots, SWE Refactor Bench its composite score, Terminal-Bench 4.0 five runs per task, and DevOps-Gym the unweighted average of its build and configuration, monitoring, issue-resolving, and test-generation categories. Token counts and costs include all activation, Dev-Primitive, and diagnosis calls. Baseline results come from the benchmark leaderboard or published evaluation where the model, harness, reasoning effort, and benchmark version are reported, and are otherwise run under the same snapshot and protocol as HERMES. On SWE Refactor Bench, each configuration runs on all 20 migration tasks, and the Claude and GPT-5.6 models are evaluated at medium and high effort (Table 31).

Component Selection. Selection is measured against a target component set 𝒢\mathcal{G}, with 𝒜\mathcal{A} the Dev-Primitives activated across all rounds: recall is |𝒜∩𝒢|/|𝒢||\mathcal{A}\cap\mathcal{G}|/|\mathcal{G}| and precision |𝒜∩𝒢|/|𝒜||\mathcal{A}\cap\mathcal{G}|/|\mathcal{A}|, micro-averaged within each benchmark. Where a reference patch exists, 𝒢\mathcal{G} holds the files that it modifies, and otherwise the components that benchmark-specific supervision implicates; DevOps-Gym’s monitoring tasks are excluded. With GPT-5.6 Sol, recall is 95.4% on SWE-bench Verified, 83.3% on SWE Refactor Bench, 84.5% on Terminal-Bench 4.0, and 85.7% on DevOps-Gym, precision ranges from 64.9% to 72.6%, and 4.7 to 12.6 Dev-Primitives are activated per task. Solved tasks exceed failed tasks in recall by 16.5 to 24.7 points, where a SWE Refactor Bench task counts as solved when its composite score is non-zero.

Revision Budget. Raising BB from 0 to 3 adds 12.5 points on SWE Refactor Bench, 12.1 on Terminal-Bench, 9.50 on DevOps-Gym, and 4.8 on SWE-bench Verified, while raising it from 3 to 5 adds at most 0.9, which makes B=3B=3 the default.

Controls and Ablations. Table 32 separates the Dev-Primitives from the choice of components on Terminal-Bench 4.0. The single editor keeps GPT-5.6 Sol, the activation-selected components, the environment, the diagnosis module, and the revision budget, and replaces the Dev-Primitives and their messages by one editor that receives the whole plan with the contents of all selected components and modifies them jointly. Across the four benchmarks, it uses 10–14% fewer tokens and 11–16% lower cost than HERMES. On Terminal-Bench 4.0, it resolves 38.8% of the tasks against 51.8% for HERMES. Its compute-matched variant generates several candidate revisions per round, evaluated with the same environment and diagnosis, until tokens and cost approximately match, 6.7B against 6.8B tokens, and reaches 45.5%. Over the same components, the editor also loses 3.6 pp on SWE-bench Verified, 14.2 pp on SWE Refactor Bench, and 11.20 pp on DevOps-Gym, so on all benchmarks except SWE-bench Verified the replacement costs more than removing any single mechanism. Among the single-mechanism removals of Table 15, removing inter-primitive communication keeps each Dev-Primitive’s local reasoning and editing but exchanges no messages, and lowers SWE-bench Verified from 97.0% to 94.2%. Without on-demand activation, all Dev-Primitives identified in the initial task analysis stay active through all rounds, and primitive calls per SWE-bench Verified task rise from 9.6 to 28.7 (Table 52). Without execution feedback, diagnosis judges the repository by static inspection alone, and Terminal-Bench resolution falls to 43.6%. Without diagnosis feedback, the raw execution outputs remain available and later rounds proceed, but no structured diagnosis or guidance is produced. Three repetitions of the default configuration on SWE Refactor Bench give composite scores of 29.5%, 32.0%, and 31.5%, that is, 31.0±1.331.0\pm 1.3.

Related Frameworks. A Dev-Primitive is defined by the artifact it owns, so the set of primitives is induced by the repository, whereas the libraries of Agent and Tool Primitives are built ahead of their tasks [48, 44]. MAGIS and CodeTeam instead assign work to designer-specified roles or centrally coordinated file-level developers [77, 78], skill-based methods encapsulate reusable, task-agnostic behaviours [73], and context-management methods reorganize information within one centralized trajectory [84, 85]. In their original evaluation settings, MAGIS reports 13.9% resolution on SWE-bench against 36.6% for HERMES with GPT-5.6 Luna, and CodeTeam reports average test pass rates of 34.6% and 42.3% on NL2Repo-Bench [81] for its prompting and supervised fine-tuning variants, against 44.9% for HERMES.

Relation to the Method. Dynamic Primitive Activation (Eq. (41)) realizes COMPOSE (Eq. (4)), and Dev-Primitive Collaboration (Eq. (42)) the act step of Eq. (5). Execution and Bug Diagnosis (Eqs. (43) and (44)) realize EXECUTE and VERIFY, with ϕ=(e,c,u)\phi=(e,c,u) as the feedback ϕt\phi_{t}, and the re-planned activation of Eq. (45) is the revision of Eq. (6). The repository induces the library, which grows by the persistent files that active Dev-Primitives create.

B.7.  Navigation Primitives: Need-Conditioned Coordination

Navigation Primitives are scope-specialized workers, each searching one territory of an information space, and ANTMAN [50], an adaptive coordination framework, decides which of them search for a query. ANTMAN answers a query qq from an information space ℐ\mathcal{I} whose available information can grow large while the information that qq requires stays comparatively small. Newly encountered information can change the searcher’s understanding of the problem and redirect the search [187], so ANTMAN makes evolving unresolved information needs the runtime control state for coordination, which lets worker activation and search decisions adapt as those needs change. The method has three parts, shown in Figure 12: a static substrate map, a revisable Need Graph, and need-conditioned coordination and recovery.

Static Substrate Map. The map describes where ANTMAN can search. A substrate-specific partitioning procedure PP deterministically splits ℐ\mathcal{I} into MM territories, bounded searchable regions, and each territory receives a WorkerCard, lightweight metadata that summarizes its scope and content:

𝒯=P⁡(ℐ)={τ1,…,τM},ci=Card⁡(τi),𝒞={c1,…,cM}.\mathcal{T}=P(\mathcal{I})=\{\tau_{1},\ldots,\tau_{M}\},\qquad c_{i}=\mathrm{Card}(\tau_{i}),\qquad\mathcal{C}=\{c_{1},\ldots,c_{M}\}. (46)

The worker wiw_{i} of territory τi\tau_{i} is scope-specialized: ANTMAN requires no distinct model architectures, tool sets, or personas, and within a substrate all workers share one interface for searching, inspecting, and returning evidence. Eq. (46) defines the workers that are available, not those that must participate in a query, and the map stays fixed during execution.

Revisable Need Graph. The Need Graph describes what remains unresolved. The coordinator initializes G0=InitializeNeedGraph⁡(q)G_{0}=\mathrm{InitializeNeedGraph}(q) and maintains the runtime state

Gt=(Nt,Δt),zt​(n)=(st​(n),ℰt​(n),ℋt​(n),pt​(n)),G_{t}=(N_{t},\Delta_{t}),\qquad z_{t}(n)=\bigl(s_{t}(n),\,\mathcal{E}_{t}(n),\,\mathcal{H}_{t}(n),\,p_{t}(n)\bigr), (47)

where NtN_{t} is the set of information needs at step tt, Δt\Delta_{t} holds their dependencies, and each need nn carries its resolution status st​(n)s_{t}(n), accumulated evidence ℰt​(n)\mathcal{E}_{t}(n), attempt history ℋt​(n)\mathcal{H}_{t}(n), and progress state pt​(n)p_{t}(n). The unresolved needs form 𝒰t={n∈Nt∣st​(n)≠resolved}\mathcal{U}_{t}=\{n\in N_{t}\mid s_{t}(n)\neq\mathrm{resolved}\}; resolved needs stay in NtN_{t}, and final synthesis reads their evidence. After each report rtr_{t}, the task-local update Gt+1=U⁡(Gt,rt)G_{t+1}=U(G_{t},r_{t}) may resolve a need, keep it unresolved, reframe it into n′n^{\prime}, or add requirements and dependencies that new evidence reveals, so needs may branch during execution. Within UU, evidence selection keeps the evidence most relevant to the query and discards redundant or unsupported material, and need-resolution assessment judges the need resolved, partial, or unresolved: a resolved need is closed, a partial need is replaced or refined into a more specific unresolved requirement, and an unresolved need stays active. Need Graph consolidation adds each proposed need as a new requirement, attaches it to an existing dependency, merges it with an overlapping need, subsumes it under an existing one, or discards it if redundant.

Need-Conditioned Coordination and Recovery. At step tt, ANTMAN selects an unresolved need, routes it with the Need Graph and the WorkerCards, and invokes the corresponding territory-backed worker:

nt=Select⁡(Gt),it=Route⁡(nt,Gt,𝒞),rt=Exec⁡(wit,nt,τit),n_{t}=\mathrm{Select}(G_{t}),\qquad i_{t}=\mathrm{Route}(n_{t},G_{t},\mathcal{C}),\qquad r_{t}=\mathrm{Exec}(w_{i_{t}},n_{t},\tau_{i_{t}}), (48)

where it∈{1,…,M}i_{t}\in\{1,\ldots,M\} identifies the selected worker. Route has two stages: a non-LLM retrieval stage ranks the WorkerCards by sparse lexical, exact-term, and dense matching, combined by reciprocal-rank fusion, into a bounded candidate set, and the orchestrator then decides from GtG_{t} whether and where to dispatch the need, respecting the dependencies between needs. Retrieval bounds the WorkerCard information within one routing decision, while the Need Graph governs the sequence of decisions and when search ends. The dispatched worker plans a bounded sequence of actions with its substrate’s tools, searches its own territory, and returns a report rtr_{t} of evidence, progress, and remaining uncertainty; global state remains in GtG_{t}. If repeated attempts make no progress, Stuck⁡(nt,Gt+1)\mathrm{Stuck}(n_{t},G_{t+1}) holds and Recover\mathrm{Recover} returns Reframe\mathrm{Reframe}, Reroute\mathrm{Reroute} to another territory, or Fallback\mathrm{Fallback} to an alternative resolution path, leaving the workers and the map unchanged. When the required needs are resolved or the execution budget BB is spent, ANTMAN synthesizes the answer from the evidence of resolved needs, which completes the execution procedure of Algorithm 2.

Runtime Coordination Demand. Because the graph is revised, the needs realized over a query can outnumber the initial set N0N_{0}:

ℋ⁡(q)=⋃t=0TqNt,H⁡(q)=|ℋ⁡(q)|,\mathcal{H}(q)=\bigcup_{t=0}^{T_{q}}N_{t},\qquad H(q)=|\mathcal{H}(q)|, (49)

where TqT_{q} is the final coordination step and a reframed or newly introduced need counts as new. A need nn receives a⁡(n)≤ρa(n)\leq\rho routing attempts, its initial routing and any reroutes, and the worker-dispatch events and distinct activated workers are

K⁡(q)=∑n∈ℋ⁡(q)a⁡(n),𝒜⁡(q)=⋃t=0Tq−1{it}.K(q)=\sum_{n\in\mathcal{H}(q)}a(n),\qquad\mathcal{A}(q)=\bigcup_{t=0}^{T_{q}-1}\{i_{t}\}. (50)

Each routing decision at Line 7 of Algorithm 2 concerns one need and activates at most one worker, so |𝒜⁡(q)|≤K⁡(q)≤ρ​H​(q)|\mathcal{A}(q)|\leq K(q)\leq\rho H(q), and with |𝒜⁡(q)|≤M|\mathcal{A}(q)|\leq M this gives ANTMAN’s Proposition 1, |𝒜⁡(q)|≤min⁡{M,ρ​H​(q)}|\mathcal{A}(q)|\leq\min\{M,\rho H(q)\}, which Proposition 3.1 restates in the notation of Section 3 and Appendix A proves together with its corollary. A partition-driven method that activates a constant fraction of its MM partitions instead has |𝒜partition​(q)|=Θ⁡(M)|\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{partition}}(q)|=\Theta(M). A larger space enlarges the candidate pool, which stays passive until the Need Graph creates demand for it.

Implementation. ANTMAN runs all components on GPT-4.1, and ANTMAN-H keeps the GPT-4.1 orchestrator and runs all non-orchestrator components on Qwen3-8B [169]. The information-access layer adapts to each substrate, while the Need Graph, the worker organization, and the coordination procedure stay the same. In the controlled long-context setting, workers use lexical and semantic retrieval with bounded reading of selected document regions; repository navigation adds structural navigation over symbols, imports, references, inheritance, and call relations. GAIA-Text-103 uses a single territory-backed worker with web search, backed by Tavily, webpage text extraction, and isolated Python execution, an interface that all methods on GAIA share. Agentic methods on RepoProbe-Python and all ablation variants run under at most 100 LLM calls per query, and the iterative sparse retrieval baseline allows up to three lexical retrieval rounds, in which the LLM judges whether the accumulated evidence suffices and reformulates the query.

Evaluation Settings. Multi-document QA scores 30 questions from each of HotpotQA [93], 2WikiMultiHopQA [157], and MuSiQue [158] for nine methods, 810 predictions in all, with one frozen answer-extraction and evaluation pipeline, and its baselines also run on GPT-4.1. In the space intervention, each per-length entry averages 30 evaluations, ten questions with evidence at early, middle, and late positions. The demand study uses ten matched 512K base contexts, each with 16 planted evidence records over a fixed pool of eight territories; documents, distractors, evidence locations, territory assignment, and WorkerCards stay fixed across demand levels, while the query and its gold answer change with the level. Each record holds an independently generated value ei∈{0,…,7}e_{i}\in\{0,\ldots,7\}, and at level k∈{1,4,16}k\in\{1,4,16\} the answer is yk=(∑ei∈Dkei)mod8y_{k}=\bigl(\sum_{e_{i}\in D_{k}}e_{i}\bigr)\bmod 8 over nested required-evidence sets D1⊂D4⊂D16D_{1}\subset D_{4}\subset D_{16}, so omitting any required unit leaves the answer ambiguous over all eight classes. Runs are capped at ten coordination rounds, answers are scored by exact match, and Complete Evidence counts a unit as recovered when its content is extracted, rather than when its document is accessed. The ablations use the 512K condition, a 40-question SWE-QA-Pro subset sampled with seed 42, and a fixed 40-question GAIA subset. Their variants keep the territories, WorkerCards, models, tools, execution budget, and synthesis procedure, and the Need-Graph variants also share the initial decomposition and Need Graph. Graph-free Adaptive receives the same query, WorkerCards, accumulated evidence, and interaction history but no explicit Need Graph; w/o Need Revision prevents changes to the graph’s structure or formulation, w/o Adaptive Rerouting fixes each need’s worker after its initial routing, and w/o Recovery disables stuck detection, reframing, and fallback.

Additional Results. On multi-document QA (Table 33), ANTMAN’s macro average of 0.711 EM and 0.814 F1 leads the specialized S2G-RAG [108], at 0.700 and 0.799, so need-driven coordination preserves answer quality on standard tasks, and ANTMAN-H, at 0.622 and 0.763, is above all baselines except S2G-RAG. Across the lengths of the space intervention, ANTMAN keeps its active coordination nearly constant and its F1 stable, while the active coordination of LongAgent and CoA grows with the space (Figure 13 and Table 53). Because it narrows the context searched for each unresolved need, ANTMAN is also robust to evidence position: averaged over the 32K to 128K contexts, its Middle F1 minus the mean of its Early and Late F1 is +0.015+0.015, against −0.181-0.181 for direct full-context inference, which shows the lost-in-the-middle pattern [39]. Under growing demand, the trajectory-level split of worker activity traces the dip in active coordination to exploration at low demand: at one unit, 4.1 of 5.0 worker activities are unrelated to the required evidence (Table 54).

Mapping to the Method. Within the method of Section 3, a territory τi\tau_{i} is the resource aia_{i} of a Navigation Primitive, and its WorkerCard cic_{i} is the interface did_{i}. Select and the two-stage Route realize COMPOSE one need at a time, the need-resolution assessment inside UU plays the role of VERIFY, and recovery is the revision step of Eq. (6).

B.8.  Harness Primitives: Composing Task-Specific Harnesses

Harness Primitives are reusable harness mechanisms with a clear application scope and composition contract, mined from failed task trajectories [51].
