Based on them, STITCH Selects suitable primitives given Task Information and compiles them into Task-speCific Harnesses at test time, keeping the development of Harness Primitives separate from their composition into each task’s harness. In Figure 14, development turns a recurring failure, checks that fail without triggering repair, into a validated repair primitive, and test-time composition selects and wires different primitives from the same library for each of three tasks. We state the framework below in STITCH’s own notation.

Problem. Let xx be a task instruction and cxc_{x} an execution specification that describes the task-solving language model, the actor, its interaction interface, and the task environment setup. A harness HH is the control program that mediates the actor’s interaction with the environment, and for the resulting trajectory τ\tau, Rx​(τ)∈{0,1}R_{x}(\tau)\in\{0,1\} indicates task success. With the actor model and the environment fixed, a construction procedure FF maps the task information to a harness Hx=F⁡(x,cx)H_{x}=F(x,c_{x}), and the goal is

Hx⋆∈arg⁡maxH∈ℋ⁡(cx)𝔼τ∼p(⋅∣x,cx,H)[Rx(τ)],H_{x}^{\star}\in\underset{H\in\mathcal{H}(c_{x})}{\arg\max}\;\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim p(\cdot\mid x,c_{x},H)}\bigl[R_{x}(\tau)\bigr], (51)

where ℋ⁡(cx)\mathcal{H}(c_{x}) is the set of compatible harnesses and p(⋅∣x,cx,H)p(\cdot\mid x,c_{x},H) the induced trajectory distribution.

Primitives and Harness Graphs. The library 𝒫={p1,…,pM}\mathcal{P}=\{p_{1},\dots,p_{M}\} holds implemented, reusable control operations. A primitive’s application scope describes when it is expected to facilitate the task and when its overhead or behavior may be undesirable, according to its success on the evaluated tasks; its composition contract specifies its inputs, outputs, required environment setup, and dependencies. Scopes guide the harness composer, and contracts guide the implementation of the harness compiler. A harness is a directed graph G=(V,E)G=(V,E) whose nodes are control operations, each invoking a primitive, and whose edges specify execution order and conditional branches; the operations communicate through shared execution state, which holds the interaction history and intermediate results. The seed harness HseedH_{\mathrm{seed}} is abstracted as a graph GseedG_{\mathrm{seed}}, and the task-specific graph GxG_{x} represents HxH_{x}.

State Guard. State Guard, one of the five Terminal-Bench primitives, addresses a recurring failure in which actor actions destroy inputs needed later. It blocks recognized direct writes, restores files that an action changes, and reports the affected paths in a failed-action observation. Its scope selects it when local inputs are irreplaceable, actions plausibly risk modifying them, and outputs are separate, and it excludes files that the task requires editing in place. Its contract has the source paths to protect and the declared output paths as inputs, mutation reports and integrity-check results as outputs, file access and storage for recoverable copies as setup, and as dependencies a snapshot before the first actor action, a check after each action, violation feedback to the next actor request, and the final integrity check for completion logic.

Primitive Development. A development agent, distinct in role from the actor, runs the actor under HseedH_{\mathrm{seed}} on a development set 𝒟dev\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{dev}} and analyzes the failed attempts (Rx​(τ)=0R_{x}(\tau)=0) for recurring deficiencies. For each deficiency, it proposes a mechanism, specifies when it should activate and which subsequent actor decision it should influence, and implements it. Mechanism tests check that the operation activates and that its output changes the relevant request, action, or control-flow decision, and matched development runs with and without the candidate measure its benefit to Rx​(τ)R_{x}(\tau). This evidence drives iterative revision and library acceptance: only primitives with a positive effect are accepted, development ends once the number of valid primitives passes a threshold θ\theta, and each accepted primitive then receives its scope and contract. The seed harness is mini-SWE-agent 2.4.6 [8], the development model GPT-5.6 Sol, and the actor during development GPT-5.6 Luna; the 100 SWE-bench and 44 Terminal-Bench development tasks are sampled at random and disjoint from the evaluation samples. For an actor model or a task domain not used in development, implementations and contracts stay unchanged, and the scopes are adjusted on development tasks.

Test-Time Composition. Before the first actor request, the composer π\pi, which shares the actor’s backbone (GPT-5.6 Luna at medium reasoning effort), reads the task, cxc_{x}, the budget, a compact description of GseedG_{\mathrm{seed}}, and the whole primitive catalog in one initial_single_pass prompt. It applies each primitive’s choose_only_if criteria literally and returns should_mutate, a rationale, and an intent. With should_mutate=false and intent=null, it keeps the seed graph when no other primitive fully qualifies; otherwise the composition intent IxI_{x} names primitive instances with their parameters at a design level, without generating their implementation code or handling their integration. The deterministic compiler KK then builds the candidate graph

Ix=π⁡(x,cx,Gseed,𝒫),G~x=K⁡(Gseed,Ix,𝒫,cx),I_{x}=\pi\bigl(x,c_{x};\,G_{\mathrm{seed}},\mathcal{P}\bigr),\qquad\widetilde{G}_{x}=K\bigl(G_{\mathrm{seed}},I_{x};\,\mathcal{P},c_{x}\bigr), (52)

connecting the selected primitives to the seed graph and supplying the dependencies that their contracts require; selecting a repository map, for instance, also inserts the map into the actor’s request. The candidate is checked for supported primitives, compatibility with cxc_{x}, valid connections, reachable termination, and bounded loops. The diagnostics of an invalid candidate return to the composer for bounded correction, the seed harness is retained if correction fails, and KK builds the valid graph into Hx=F⁡(x,cx)H_{x}=F(x,c_{x}), as summarized in Algorithm 3. During the run, the structure of GxG_{x} stays fixed while its conditional branches respond to observations, and selected verification and repair primitives return a failed check to the actor for repair. We record whether each selected primitive is activated and executed without runtime errors, and the benchmark scores Rx​(τ)R_{x}(\tau) after the run.

Comparison with Code Generation. STITCH’s analysis assigns zero utility to invalid harnesses: with V⁡(H)∈{0,1}V(H)\in\{0,1\} indicating the absence of the modeled implementation failures and R⁡(x,H)R(x,H) the success probability given valid execution, a harness earns J⁡(x,H)=V⁡(H)​R​(x,H)J(x,H)=V(H)R(x,H). Proposition 3.2 restates STITCH’s Proposition 1 and part 1 of its Proposition 2, and part 2 compares composition with raw code generation. With Ωi\Omega_{i} the application scope of pip_{i} and μi\mu_{i} its task prevalence (Section 3.5), let k⁡(x)=∑i=1M𝟏​(x∈Ωi)k(x)=\sum_{i=1}^{M}\mathbf{1}(x\in\Omega_{i}) be the number of oracle-selected mechanisms, generated in one attempt without repair. If, conditional on xx, each mechanism fails independently with probability ϵ∈(0,1)\epsilon\in(0,1) and the harness is valid if and only if none of these failures occurs, then ℙ⁡(V⁡(Hgen)=1∣x)=(1−ϵ)k⁡(x)\mathbb{P}(V(H_{\mathrm{gen}})=1\mid x)=(1-\epsilon)^{k(x)}, while compositions of validated primitives by the deterministic compiler are assumed to execute validly, V⁡(Hcomp)=1V(H_{\mathrm{comp}})=1. Let k¯=𝔼x​[k⁡(x)]=∑i=1Mμi\bar{k}=\mathbb{E}_{x}[k(x)]=\sum_{i=1}^{M}\mu_{i}, assume k⁡(x)=k¯k(x)=\bar{k} for all tasks, although the selected mechanisms may differ across tasks, and suppose that valid generated harnesses attain the performance R​(x,𝐚∗​(x))R(x,\mathbf{a}^{*}(x)) of the oracle activation ai∗​(x)=𝟏​(x∈Ωi)a_{i}^{*}(x)=\mathbf{1}(x\in\Omega_{i}). If 𝔼⁡[J⁡(x,Hcomp)]>0\mathbb{E}[J(x,H_{\mathrm{comp}})]>0, composition outperforms this oracle generator if and only if

k¯>k∗=ln⁡(𝔼⁡[R⁡(x,𝐚∗​(x))]/𝔼⁡[J⁡(x,Hcomp)])−ln⁡(1−ϵ)≈1ϵ​ln⁡𝔼⁡[R⁡(x,𝐚∗​(x))]𝔼⁡[J⁡(x,Hcomp)],\bar{k}>k^{*}=\frac{\ln\bigl(\mathbb{E}[R(x,\mathbf{a}^{*}(x))]\,/\,\mathbb{E}[J(x,H_{\mathrm{comp}})]\bigr)}{-\ln(1-\epsilon)}\approx\frac{1}{\epsilon}\ln\frac{\mathbb{E}[R(x,\mathbf{a}^{*}(x))]}{\mathbb{E}[J(x,H_{\mathrm{comp}})]}, (53)

where the approximation holds for small ϵ\epsilon. With A=𝔼x​[R⁡(x,𝐚∗​(x))]A=\mathbb{E}_{x}[R(x,\mathbf{a}^{*}(x))] and B=𝔼⁡[J⁡(x,Hcomp)]B=\mathbb{E}[J(x,H_{\mathrm{comp}})], the failure model gives 𝔼⁡[J⁡(x,Hgen)]=𝔼x​[(1−ϵ)k⁡(x)​R​(x,𝐚∗​(x))]=(1−ϵ)k¯​A\mathbb{E}[J(x,H_{\mathrm{gen}})]=\mathbb{E}_{x}[(1-\epsilon)^{k(x)}R(x,\mathbf{a}^{*}(x))]=(1-\epsilon)^{\bar{k}}A. Since 0<B≤A0<B\leq A, the inequality B>(1−ϵ)k¯​AB>(1-\epsilon)^{\bar{k}}A holds if and only if k¯>ln⁡(A/B)/(−ln⁡(1−ϵ))\bar{k}>\ln(A/B)/(-\ln(1-\epsilon)), and the approximation follows from −ln⁡(1−ϵ)=ϵ+O⁡(ϵ2)-\ln(1-\epsilon)=\epsilon+O(\epsilon^{2}). Part 2 thus characterizes a reliability trade-off under a constant mechanism count and independent implementation failures.

Baselines and Settings. Each fixed-primitive baseline evaluates a fixed harness configuration that contains one designated focused control mechanism, its required dependencies, and shared supporting operations, which together form a minimal compatible set of operations handled by the compiler. The harness optimizers MemoHarness [144] and MetaHarness [143] start from the same mini-SWE-agent seed and use GPT-5.6 Sol as their development model. The actors not used in development are GPT-5.6 Terra with medium reasoning, DeepSeek-V4-Flash without reasoning, and Claude-4.5-Haiku. Appendix C reports the transfer of primitives across task domains and the composer’s selection patterns: the composer keeps the seed harness for about half of the tasks and otherwise mostly selects a single primitive.

Additional Results. On SWE-bench Verified with the three actors not used in development (Table 34), STITCH has the best average on all three metrics and the best scores with DeepSeek-V4-Flash and Claude-4.5-Haiku, while Codex leads with GPT-5.6 Terra, at 88.0% against 86.5% Pass@1; each fixed primitive exceeds the seed on the average.

As the test-time library grows along a single order of addition (Figure 15), Pass@1 rises from 73.0% for the seed harness (size 0) to 80.5% at size 8 on SWE-bench Verified and from 60.0% to 72.2% at size 6 on Terminal-Bench 2.0, ending above Codex on both benchmarks.

The activation rate is 100% for each selected primitive (Figure 16), which supports part 2, the comparison with raw code generation: free of the reliability risk of generated harness code, the selected primitives take effect during the actor’s execution. Composition costs 4.3% of one actor attempt on SWE-bench Verified and 2.7% on Terminal-Bench 2.0, whereas the output-token lower bound for an oracle that writes the complete harness, with no input, reasoning, or debugging cost, is 23.35 and 17.23 actor attempts, about 543×543\times and 638×638\times the cost of composition.

Relation to the Method. The compiled graph GxG_{x} is the plan of Eq. (4): the composition intent IxI_{x} names its primitive instances and their parameters, and the compiler adds the dependencies along which results flow; the shared execution state is the context of Eq. (5), and primitive development is STITCH’s form of the validation and publishing of Section 3.3 (Eq. (7)).

Appendix C Additional Experimental Results

This appendix completes the experimental record of the eight primitive families, in the order of Section 4. Each subsection extends the family’s subsection there with complete benchmark breakdowns, retrieval and verification diagnostics, model allocations, provenance and budget controls, grounding audits, scaling trajectories, or selection patterns, and it names the mechanism of the family that its material bears on. Appendix B states each family’s full method in its own notation, and all values are copied from the eight companion studies, whose settings and evidence Appendix D records. The tables of this appendix follow the table convention of Section 4.1.

C.1.  Tool Primitives: Breakdowns, Retrieval, and Validation

Section 4.2 compares HEART with the reference systems of ToolBench, NESTFUL, and τ2\tau^{2}-Bench and removes one component at a time, a harness mechanism or ToolFace with its Tool Primitives (Tables 1, 2, 3, and 4); the controls at a matched backbone and tool catalogue and at a matched call budget accompany the framework in Appendix B.1 (Tables 25 and 26). This subsection adds the diagnostics of retrieval, validation, and revision. HEART is evaluated on five benchmarks [44]. ToolBench covers large-scale API invocation [6], NESTFUL nested call sequences, and τ2\tau^{2}-Bench interactive dual-control execution [32, 31]. ACEBench targets fine-grained multi-tool workflows, and BFCLv4 agentic web search and memory function calling [58, 20]. The ACEBench and BFCLv4 results, which Section 4.2 summarizes, appear in full in the companion study’s own tables. Three further suites are related benchmarks: StableToolBench, which replaces ToolBench’s live APIs with deterministic virtual servers [56], HammerBench [192], and ToolSandbox [33]. Each benchmark table follows its benchmark’s own protocol.

The ToolBench reference rows include Vicuna [176], Alpaca [177], and GPT-4 [178]. The NESTFUL comparison also lists Granite’s function-calling model [179], Llama 3.1 [174], Mixtral [180], DeepSeek-V3 [181], and GPT-4o [182]. Their configurations and scores follow the companion study. NESTFUL’s own metrics are F1 for function and parameter names, partial and full sequence accuracy, and win rate.

The last three tables concern how HEART’s harness finds Tool Primitives and judges their results. Table 36 measures how often semantic retrieval over the 25,519 schema descriptors returns the gold tools. A plan step can invoke only a tool that retrieval returns, the containment behind the candidate-pool ceiling of Proposition 3.3(ii), and validation-triggered revision recovers part of the first-pass misses by reformulating the tool query. Table 36 compares result validation, which judges every step’s result on four criteria, with human labels. HEART audits validation because its recovery loop is conditioned on it: most false passes fall on the task-completion criterion for partially satisfied objectives, fewer than 3% of trajectories end on a false pass, false fails cost redundant revision rounds without changing outcomes, and the plateau at B=3B=3 indicates that the loop terminates because validation converges (Appendix B.1). Table 37 varies HEART’s maximum revision budget BB; B=0B=0 disables revision.

Section 4.3 compares LEGO with construction paradigms, consumption and field controls, and model allocations (Tables 5, 6, 28, and 27). The tables below break delivery down by band and domain, restrict donor provenance, fix the attempt budget, give the uncertainty over decoding seeds and paired tasks, and report the independently developed agents by band with their cost. Table 38 breaks LEGO-REPO delivery down by difficulty band and domain. Across the five bands, the absolute gain over feedback stays between +0.161 and +0.209, so the larger relative gains on harder bands come mostly from a falling feedback score. Its coverage column measures offline reachability in the library. These are measured library variants, and the gain over feedback stays positive under every restriction. The restrictions are possible because every CodeFace entry is admitted with a recorded source repository, commit, and license (Section 3.3). Table 40 fixes the same integer attempt limit for both configurations; at every reported limit from 1 to 8, the library configuration stays above feedback alone [45].

Table 41 evaluates four configurations over three decoding seeds and gives paired contrasts on seed 1, with bootstrap intervals over the 522 tasks. LEGO averages 0.5116±0.00240.5116\pm 0.0024 over the seeds, and its paired gain over feedback with diagnosis is +0.1665+0.1665, with 95% interval [+0.1503,+0.1847][+0.1503,+0.1847] [45].

Table 42 gives the four independently developed repository agents of Section 4.3 by difficulty band, with their recorded cost per task. OpenHands and Claude Code cost $2.41 and $2.16 per task, against $2.08 for LEGO, and SWE-agent and Agentless cost $1.86 and $0.94. C.3.  Math Primitives: Per-Problem Method Ranks

Section 4.4 compares self-advertisement with similarity retrieval and reranking (Table 7) and reports downstream proof completion (Table 8). Figure 17 shows where the coverage gains of Table 7 come from [46]. Each dot is one problem, placed by the rank of its highest-ranked annotated method under self-advertisement and by that method’s rank under one similarity retriever. Dots in the shaded region are methods that similarity ranks outside its top five but self-advertisement places inside. Many of them lie outside the top ten of their panel’s retriever. In the three embedding panels, this places them outside the pool of the reranker built on that retriever; BM25 has no reranker. This is the candidate-pool ceiling of Proposition 3.3(ii) at work: no reranking backbone can recover a method that its pool omits, whereas self-advertisement judges every contract from its proposal.

C.4.  Knowledge Primitives: Grounding, Preservation, and Transfer

Section 4.5 compares SourceLearn with retrieval and memory baselines on five benchmarks and at a matched context budget (Tables 9 and 29). The material below audits the learned source models, splits the gains by region, and reduces the evidence. Tables 44 and 44 are SourceLearn’s post-hoc audits of grounding and source authority, the principle that learning signals determine what is reconsidered while persistent updates are reconstructed from the authoritative source (Eq. (28)) [47]. The first judges sampled units of M0M_{0}, MSM_{S}, and MTM_{T} against their cited source elements, and the second checks whether units removed by learning remain represented in the revised model. Table 45 splits test questions by whether their source regions overlapped the guidance tasks, for GPT-5.6 Luna. The gain over Hybrid RAG on unseen regions shows that the benefit of the learned source model extends beyond the regions that the guidance tasks touched.

Figure 18 reduces the retrieved evidence or removes the gold document on MultiDoc2Dial. SourceLearn degrades more slowly than Hybrid RAG, so the source model supplies source understanding when task-local retrieval is incomplete. Figure 19 reports what the source model holds at each learning stage and the share of units with an explicit condition. It also reports how much of the test questions’ required content is represented, and the association between represented content and accuracy (Appendix D).

C.5.  Agent Primitives: Structure Selection and Cost

Section 4.6 compares the primitive-based MAS with a single agent, text-based and latent MAS, and each single primitive applied to every query, and it removes positional re-encoding (Tables 10 and 30). The eight benchmarks of Table 10 combine mathematical problem solving in AIME, MATH, and GSM8K [150, 151, 152, 153]; executable code evaluation through HumanEval+ and MBPP+, the stricter test suites built on HumanEval and MBPP [183, 184, 154]; and medical and graduate-level question answering [155, 156]. The benchmark mean therefore aggregates heterogeneous evaluation procedures, and the individual columns report each of them.

Tables 47 and 47 hold the Organizer ablations [48]. They replace the GPT-5.2 Organizer by Claude-4 [175] or by random selection of structures from the Knowledge Pool, and they remove the Knowledge Pool. They thus vary the model and the information behind the Organizer’s choice of primitives, down to a random choice, and the study concludes that the main benefit comes from problem-aware structure selection rather than from a specific Organizer model. Table 11 compares the primitive-based MAS with eight independently designed MAS methods and two single-model prompting baselines on Llama-3-70B-Instruct [174], separately from the backbones of Table 10. The prompting baselines are Chain-of-Thought [165] and Self-Consistency [166]; the MAS methods include Self-Refine [140], a Quality-Diversity comparator [185], and SPP [186]. Table 48 adds the cost accounting for the same methods. Its row for a Llama-3-70B Organizer repeats the GPT-5.2 accuracies, an inconsistency of the Agent Primitives study that Appendix D records. Table 49 gives the output tokens behind these costs. With either Organizer, the primitive-based MAS uses fewer tokens than every MAS method on each benchmark: 3,301 per query on average with the GPT-5.2 Organizer, against 8,252 for MAS-GPT, 2.5×2.5\times fewer.

C.6.  Dev-Primitives: Model Allocation and On-Demand Activation

Section 4.7 compares HERMES with same-backbone harnesses, with a single editor over the same components, and with variants that remove one mechanism at a time (Tables 12, 13, 32, 15, and 14). Table 50 assigns models independently to activation, the Dev-Primitives, and diagnosis; its values in parentheses are improvements, in pp, over the homogeneous Qwen3-8B configuration [49]. With Qwen3-8B Dev-Primitives, a stronger diagnosis model alone raises Terminal-Bench resolution from 27.6% to between 44.5% and 47.9%. A stronger activation model alone reaches at most 38.2%. Table 52 adds the Terminal-Bench 4.0 inference cost of five of these configurations. Table 52 counts primitive calls with and without on-demand activation on all four benchmarks, which shows how much instantiating only the activated Dev-Primitives 𝒫𝒜\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{A}} saves within one task (Section 3.3). Its ablation keeps every component found by the initial analysis active for the whole trajectory. Repeated calls of one primitive after messages or revisions make the call counts exceed the number of distinct active components.

C.7.  Navigation Primitives: Scaling and Activity Diagnostics

Section 4.8 reports ANTMAN in structured information spaces, under a growing space and a growing demand, and with its need tracking, rerouting, or recovery removed (Tables 16, 17, 18, and 19). The structured-navigation comparison in Table 16 includes RepoDistill [168]. Table 53 gives every space size and baseline row of the controlled intervention from 32K to 512K, which examines the behaviour that Proposition 3.1 predicts at approximately fixed demand [50]. It reports active coordination, calls and cost per query, and answer quality (EM and F1) for each space size. Table 54 decomposes trajectory-level worker activity under growing demand, measured by required evidence in place of H⁡(q)H(q), into activity that contributes required evidence and activity that does not. This decomposition explains why active coordination dips from 5.0 to 4.3 workers between one and four required units: at one unit, most activity is exploration that finds no required evidence. Worker activity is a trajectory-level count and differs from the number of distinct workers in Table 18.

C.8.  Harness Primitives: Catalogs, Transfer, and Selection

Section 4.9 compares STITCH’s task-conditioned composition with the seed harness and with fixed and random compositions, and it repeats the comparison with actors not used in development (Tables 20, 21, and 34). MemoHarness [144] is a harness-optimization comparator in Tables 20 and 21, evaluated with the same mini-SWE-agent seed as STITCH [51]. The test-time libraries hold eight and six entries (Appendix D).

Figure 20 evaluates each benchmark with only the primitives developed on the other one. Implementations and contracts are kept, and scopes are adjusted on development tasks. With these out-of-domain primitives, STITCH’s Pass@1 stays below its in-domain result but above the seed on both benchmarks. Its Pass@2 and Pass2 also stay above the seed, and on Terminal-Bench 2.0 its Pass@2 exceeds the in-domain run. Figure 21 shows how many primitives the composer selects per task and which combinations it selects. The composer keeps the seed graph for about half of the tasks and otherwise mostly selects one primitive. This sparse selection complements the selection and activation rates of Figure 16.

Appendix D Study Settings and Evidence Ledger

The quantitative record of this paper is the eight companion manuscripts. For each study, this appendix records its primitive in the study’s own terms, its evaluated settings, the evidence that Sections 4 and 5 use, and the scope of that evidence. Each subsection carries the identifier (S01–S08) of the companion manuscript’s source snapshot from which its values are copied, the same identifier that the bibliography uses; because the identifiers name manuscripts, they do not follow the family order. The subsections follow the family order of Section 4.

D.1.  S02: Tool Primitives

Primitive. A Tool Primitive is an LLM-based wrapper that encapsulates one ToolFace schema–function pair (si,fi)(s_{i},f_{i}), 𝒫i​(x,c)=ℳ⁡([si;c;x])\mathcal{P}_{i}(x;c)=\mathcal{M}([s_{i};c;x]), and all Tool Primitives share one Qwen3-8B backbone [44]. HEART’s harness has three mechanisms: request decomposition plans the task, value resolution grounds each step’s values, and result validation judges every step’s result. On a failed validation, the structured feedback enriches the context, and targeted revision re-plans for at most B=3B=3 rounds. ToolFace contains 25,519 tools, built by collecting tools and manually authoring their schemas, and the set of Tool Primitives is induced by ToolFace and grows with it.

Controls. The matched-backbone table fixes Qwen3-8B and ToolFace (Table 25). ToolBench pass rates for ReAct, retrieval-only, planner–executor, DFSDT, and HEART are 33.5, 41.0, 52.6, 55.8, and 75.1%, and their NESTFUL full accuracies are 0.08, 0.10, 0.19, 0.13, and 0.44. The budget-matched self-refinement control without Tool Primitives reaches 34.2% and 0.15 (Table 26). Removing result validation gives 47.6% and 0.15 in the component ablation (Table 4).

Scope. The matched-backbone comparison holds Qwen3-8B and ToolFace fixed to isolate the harness (Section 4.2), so it separates HEART from its backbone and catalogue. In the τ2\tau^{2}-Bench airline domain, where the reference systems run on their own backbones, HEART succeeds in all four trials on 0.63 of the tasks against 0.50 for Claude-4.6-Sonnet (Table 3). The primitive-specific controls are the budget-matched control and the removal of ToolFace and the Tool Primitives, which leaves 16.1%. The audit of result validation samples 200 decisions from ToolBench and NESTFUL trajectories (Table 36). HEART’s robustness study injects a malicious tool document into the retrieved candidates to manipulate tool selection, following ToolHijacker [190], and reports a 0.0% attack-success rate on ToolBench, because tool schemas stay in each primitive’s own prompt and never enter the caller’s [44].

D.2.  S04: Code Primitives

Primitive. A Code Primitive is a reusable executable software component equipped with a resident LLM, Pi=(Ci,Ii,Di,Vi,Xi,Mi)P_{i}=(C_{i},I_{i},D_{i},V_{i},X_{i},M_{i}): the implementation, the exposed interface and behavioural contract, the dependency closure, the carried validation tests, supporting context and provenance, and the resident LLM [45]. One adaptation model instantiates every MiM_{i}. The resident LLM assesses the component’s relevance to a requirement and, once the primitive is selected, adapts the component and reruns ViV_{i} on it. CodeFace contains 1,424 entries, 871 mined, 343 harvested from verified construction runs, and 210 web-sourced, each admitted with executable closure, a passing component suite, and a recorded source repository, commit, and license.

Benchmark. LEGO-REPO contains 522 frozen reconstruction tasks from installable Python repositories, spanning seven domains, 22 capability tracks, and five difficulty bands. The benchmark removes an implementation while retaining its task interfaces, tests, and environment. Native passing-test counts are normalized between a floor and the original implementation’s ceiling and clipped to [0,1][0,1], so a delivery score is not binary task success. A score counts only for an admissible run, in which execution completes, provenance confirms that the tests exercised the generated code, and the span between floor and ceiling is at least five tests; any other run scores zero (Eq. (11)).

Controls and Costs. Feedback, feedback plus diagnosis, context-only reuse, unchanged import-and-call, structured-schema adaptation, and LEGO score 0.3180, 0.3469, 0.3544, 0.3430, 0.4974, and 0.5134 (Tables 5 and 6). With GPT-5.6 Terra in every model position, LEGO costs $2.08 per task; with GPT-OSS-20B in the adaptation and diagnosis positions, it costs $1.58 and scores 0.4880 (Table 27). The DeepSeek-V3.2 row of Table 27 is one configuration of the study’s sweep over thirteen backbones, in which adaptation and diagnosis stay on GPT-5.6 Terra.

Scope. Frozen native tests supply the acceptance specification. The field controls of Table 28 add fields cumulatively in one order, so their gains are increments in that order. In a model allocation, only the adaptation position belongs to the primitive. The study reports source-repository exclusion and corpus-disjoint controls.

D.3.  S05: Math Primitives

Primitive. The library holds 82 Method Contracts, one per reusable proof method extracted from Putnam 2000–2014 solutions, and each pairs a selection side, which the selector reads, with an execution side, which goes only to the prover [46]. The execution side holds a Lean scaffold stated for arbitrary parameters, a compiled worked instance, and Mathlib anchors. It also states the contract’s required conditions Prec\operatorname{Pre}_{c} as Lean hypotheses and the residual obligations Oblc\operatorname{Obl}_{c} left after the method’s step. Lean provides the proof language and kernel [10], and Mathlib provides the reusable mathematical library [11]. GPT-5.6 Sol extracts the methods and proposes merges, all of which the authors review, and then drafts both sides of each contract. Every execution-side Lean artifact is compiled in Lean 4.27.0 with Mathlib commit a3a10db, the third of the three construction steps, and all 82 contracts pass. One batched call of a shared backbone writes, for each contract, a target, an action, required facts, cited verified material, an offer flag, a role, and a score. Residual obligations follow from the contract and its binding and are not proposal fields.

Evaluation. Method selection uses 120 Putnam 2015–2025 problems and 60 IMO ProofBench problems. Reference methods are annotated from official solutions with model assistance and human checking, and fixed before selector evaluation. Each reranker reorders the top 10 contracts of an embedding ranking with the same backbone. For GPT-5.6 Luna, self-advertisement reaches Putnam hit@5 of 0.950, against 0.842 for Qwen3 with reranking, whose hit@1 is 0.683 (Table 7). OpenAI-large with reranking has the best hit@1, 0.692, at hit@5 0.825, and self-advertisement’s hit@1 is 0.658. IMO ProofBench hit@5 is 0.883 for these rerankers and 0.917 for self-advertisement. Adding the top-ranked contract to the prompt of AxProverBase under ten Lean compilations changes its proof rates from 5.8 to 12.5% on Putnam and from 10.0 to 15.0% on IMO ProofBench (Table 8); pass@20 receives twice that budget.

Scope. Hits are scored against the annotated reference methods. A checked scaffold leaves its residual obligations to the prover, which completes 12.5% of Putnam and 15.0% of IMO ProofBench proofs with the contract within ten compilations (Table 8). The downstream comparison adds contract content as well as selection. The coverage gain belongs to self-advertisement as a whole, commitment gate included. The study traces much of it to annotated methods that similarity ranks outside its top five (Figure 17). Ranking improvements depend on the criterion, and an additional runoff raises some metrics and lowers others.

D.4.  S06: Knowledge Primitives

Primitive. A Knowledge Primitive is SourceLearn’s persistent, revisable source model MM of one authoritative source DD, organized around source entities, whose representations capture properties, mechanisms, governing conditions, procedures, exceptions, distinctions, and relations to other entities, and whose units cite the source elements they rest on [47]. At task time, source-model activation AB​(M,q)A_{B}(M,q) supplies the whole model, or its task-relevant regions within B=24B=24k tokens, to the task solver beside the Hybrid RAG evidence R⁡(D,q)R(D,q). The model changes only in the offline learning stages before test tasks, and every update after construction follows grounded source reconstruction: every proposed unit passes the grounding gate, which requires its cited source excerpts to entail it, and a region rewrite is committed only if the preservation check finds no previously supported meaning lost, unless a stronger statement subsumes it.

Evaluation. Five benchmarks are MultiDoc2Dial, NarrativeQA, SWE-QA, APIBench, and AppWorld, and three backends yield fifteen settings. All methods share the backend, the embedding model, and the answer or agent prompt, including the AppWorld scaffold. SourceLearn and AWM receive the same Hybrid RAG evidence, whereas RAPTOR and HippoRAG 2 use their own retrieval. Guidance and evaluation use fixed disjoint splits, with AppWorld using its official train/test-normal partition. SourceLearn improves over Hybrid RAG in fourteen settings and leads all evaluated methods in thirteen (Table 9). The one setting without improvement is GPT-OSS-120B on AppWorld, from 30.4 to 27.4. On GPT-OSS-120B SWE-QA, SourceLearn improves on Hybrid RAG, but HippoRAG 2 leads with 56.7 against 53.4.

Scope. All QA results use one LLM judge, GPT-5.6 Luna, which is also an evaluated backend. Grounding measures support by the cited source. Learned units enter only through grounded source reconstruction, whose grounding gate is itself a model judgment. In the grounding audit, contradicted units stay at or below 1%, but some Task-Guided units on the document and code sources are only partially supported or unsupported: full support of StudentAid units falls from 79.2% in M0M_{0} to 75.0% in MSM_{S} and 63.3% in MTM_{T} (Table 44). The learned model is therefore not a replacement for the source, which stays authoritative and directly accessible through R⁡(D,q)R(D,q). SourceLearn also receives more source context than Hybrid RAG; at matched budgets it leads on three of the four sources (Table 29). Figure 19(d) reports accuracy by the coverage of a question’s required claims, an association across test questions.

D.5.  S01: Agent Primitives

Primitive. Review, Voting and Selection, and Planning and Execution each encapsulate a recurring multi-agent computation pattern as a reusable latent operator behind the external interface of a standard LLM agent; their internal agents follow task-agnostic role system prompts and coordinate exclusively through KV cache exchange [48]. The study’s Input-Output Alignment Assumption states that conditioning on a sender’s KV cache approximates conditioning on its token sequence when the agents share model parameters and positional encoding, and the study re-indexes transferred keys under RoPE. An Organizer, GPT-5.2 by default, composes the three primitives per query, guided by the entries it retrieves from a Knowledge Pool of 45 MAS structures, and the system executes the selected primitives according to the composition plan.

Evaluation and Extracted Evidence. The main table reports average accuracy over AIME25, AIME24, MATH, GSM8K, HumanEval+, MBPP+, MedQA, and GPQA-Diamond (Table 10). From the single agent to the composed MAS, average accuracy rises from 58.8% to 75.3% with Qwen3-8B, from 71.0% to 77.6% with DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B, and from 70.1% to 76.4% with DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-70B.

Scope. The Organizer’s backbone and its variable structure and agent count are part of the evaluated pipeline. Internal communication runs between agents that share one backbone. The study also compares text with cache communication in two stress tests, an auxiliary instruction injected into a long context and unrelated reasoning sentences injected as noise, which Section 4.6 summarizes. On DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-70B, the LatentMAS baseline reaches 60.0% average accuracy, below the single agent’s 70.1%, which the study attributes to its aggressive chunking of latent reasoning steps, in contrast to the conservative latent communication of Agent Primitives. Table 48 reproduces an inconsistency of the study. Its Llama-3-70B Organizer row repeats the GPT-5.2 accuracies, 72.4, 93.8, 82.3, and 53.2%, and derives its efficiencies from them and its own costs, whereas the study’s Organizer-sensitivity table reports 72.0, 91.8, 81.0, and 52.2% for that Organizer. The cost table prices the methods of the MAS comparison (Table 11).

D.6.  S03: Dev-Primitives

Primitive. Each component aia_{i} of the repository ℛ={ai}i=1N\mathcal{R}=\{a_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N}, a file by default, is associated with a Dev-Primitive PiP_{i} that wraps it with a resident LLM; given its local objective xix_{i} and the communication context 𝒞i\mathcal{C}_{i} of directed messages, it returns the optionally modified artifact and its messages [49]. The set of primitives is induced by the repository, a persistent file that an active Dev-Primitive creates is registered as a new Dev-Primitive, and each persists across the revision rounds of a task. Bug diagnosis is one LLM call over the executed repository that returns pass or fail and, on fail, the structured feedback ϕ=(e,c,u)\phi=(e,c,u). The revision Π′=ACTIVATE⁡(q,ℛ′,Π,ϕ)\Pi^{\prime}=\operatorname{ACTIVATE}(q,\mathcal{R}^{\prime},\Pi,\phi) reactivates only the implicated primitives, within B=3B=3 revision rounds after the initial round by default.

Evaluation and Extracted Evidence. SWE-bench Verified uses 500 instances. With GPT-5.6 Sol, the mini-SWE-agent comparator reaches 96.20±0.8696.20\pm 0.86% and HERMES 97.00±0.7697.00\pm 0.76%, reported as mean and standard error (Table 12). Recorded cost is $1.15 versus $1.80, and latency 182.37 versus 205.34 seconds. The DevOps-Gym comparison to Codex uses the same backbone and reports a four-stage average of 49.89 versus 55.41 (Table 14). On Terminal-Bench 4.0, over five runs of the 66 tasks with GPT-5.6 Sol, HERMES resolves 51.8% against 33.0% under Codex at medium effort and 55.5% against 37.3% at maximum effort (Table 13). On the 20 SWE Refactor Bench migrations, the composite rises with GPT-5.6 Sol at medium effort from 6.5% under Codex to 31.0%.

Scope. The four-stage average is the unweighted mean of the stage success rates (Table 14), and task settings and repeated-run procedures vary across the benchmarks. In the backbone-scaling study (Table 50), only the configuration that keeps GPT-5.6 Sol for activation and diagnosis changes the Dev-Primitive model alone; it reaches 50.6% against 51.8% on Terminal-Bench. The configuration at 49.7% also moves diagnosis to GPT-5.5. HERMES’s Terminal-Bench version and task set differ from those of S08.

D.7.  S07: Navigation Primitives

Primitive. A Navigation Primitive is a territory-backed worker of ANTMAN’s static substrate map, and ANTMAN coordinates these scope-specialized workers by the information needs that remain unresolved [50]. A deterministic, substrate-specific partitioning procedure splits the query’s information space into MM territories, each with a WorkerCard that summarizes its scope and content, and within a substrate the workers share one search interface and, in each configuration, one backbone. The revisable Need Graph records each need’s status, evidence, attempt history, and progress, and it controls worker selection, routing, and recovery. The substrate map stays fixed during execution, and what carries across queries is the partitioning procedure, the worker interface, and the coordination policy.

Evaluation. ANTMAN and all baselines use GPT-4.1; ANTMAN-H keeps the GPT-4.1 orchestrator with Qwen3-8B elsewhere. The structured-navigation comparison covers 108 RepoProbe questions across eight repositories, a frozen 80-question SWE-QA-Pro set, and GAIA-Text-103 (Table 16). ANTMAN’s scores are 38.21, 79.78, and 58.3; GAIA iterative sparse retrieval scores 45.6 under the shared tool interface. GAIA uses a single territory-backed worker, so the coordination mechanisms it tests are need tracking and recovery. The controlled distractor-space intervention keeps the underlying needs approximately fixed while increasing space from 32K to 512K. Under it, active coordination grows 1.23×1.23\times, against 15.29×15.29\times for LongAgent and 15.33×15.33\times for CoA (Table 17). A separate demand intervention fixes 512K and increases required evidence from one to four to sixteen units. Multi-document QA scores 30 questions from each of HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, and MuSiQue for nine methods with one frozen answer-extraction and evaluation pipeline.

Scope. The demand intervention’s calls are 35.5, 43.6, and 86.2 and costs $0.107, $0.111, and $0.293 per query. The space intervention uses ten questions with evidence at early, middle, and late positions, and the demand intervention ten matched 512K contexts at each of its three demand levels [50]. Full ANTMAN scores 60.00% on the 40-question GAIA subset and 81.43 on the 40-question SWE-QA-Pro subset, sampled with seed 42, of Table 19, against 58.3% on GAIA-Text-103 and 79.78 on the 80-question SWE-QA-Pro set (Table 16). Methods run in ANTMAN’s evaluation harness share its question sets and model setting, and all GAIA methods share the tool interface.

D.8.  S08: Harness Primitives

Primitive. A Harness Primitive is an implemented, reusable control operation with an application scope and a composition contract [51]. Before the actor’s first request, a harness composer on the actor’s backbone selects primitives in a composition intent. A deterministic compiler connects them to the seed graph and supplies the dependencies that their contracts require, and the candidate is checked for supported primitives, compatibility with the execution specification cxc_{x}, valid connections, reachable termination, and bounded loops. An invalid candidate returns diagnostics to the composer for bounded correction, and if correction fails, the seed harness is retained. A primitive is accepted into the library after mechanism tests and a positive matched-run effect on development tasks.

Evaluation. SWE-bench Verified uses a 100-task evaluation subset and Terminal-Bench 2.0 a 45-task subset, each with two attempts per task and development tasks disjoint from evaluation. The actor and selector is GPT-5.6 Luna, and the development model is GPT-5.6 Sol. On SWE-bench Verified, seed and STITCH Pass@1 are 73.0 and 80.5%; Pass@2 is 78.0 and 85.0%; and success on both attempts is 68.0 and 76.0% (Table 20). On Terminal-Bench 2.0, seed and STITCH Pass@1 are 60.0 and 72.2%; Pass@2 68.9 and 77.8%; and success on both attempts 51.1 and 66.7% (Table 21). Codex reaches 79.0% Pass@1 on SWE-bench Verified and 56.7% on Terminal-Bench 2.0.

Scope. These are sampled subsets and differ from S03’s settings. The catalogs and fixed baselines cover six SWE-bench Verified and five Terminal-Bench 2.0 primitives, and the library-size curves of Figure 15 extend to test-time libraries of eight and six entries. The cross-actor evaluation (Table 34, SWE-bench Verified only) uses actors held out from primitive development and adjusts the application scopes on development tasks. The 543- and 638-fold cost comparisons on SWE-bench Verified and Terminal-Bench 2.0 use an optimistic lower bound that counts only the output tokens of the generated implementation and excludes input, reasoning, and debugging costs.

Appendix E Evaluation Protocol for Cross-Family Composition

This appendix specifies an evaluation of HEELO as one system that composes primitives of several families. Its experiments measure what the three results of Section 3.5 predict, namely activation against realized demand (Proposition 3.1), the gap between task-conditioned and fixed composition (Proposition 3.2), and the reach of a retrieval stage (Proposition 3.3), together with the reliability of the verification that each family brings. The companion studies measure these quantities within a single family: ANTMAN grows space and demand separately, STITCH compares fixed, random, and task-conditioned harnesses, and the study of self-advertised method selection compares self-advertisement with reranking of a similarity pool. The protocol specifies their measurement for compositions that span families.

E.1.  Primary Hypothesis and Task Construction

The primary hypothesis is that composing primitives through HEELO improves task success or total cost at a fixed evaluation standard, relative to comparable access to the same underlying assets. A benchmark should therefore contain requests that need at least two families and a task-level evaluation that cannot be replaced by adding the families’ own scores. Suitable task templates include documented API migrations with repository regression tests, source-grounded workflows with mocked external actions, and formalized transformations that need both method selection and a Lean-checked proof of the selected method’s required conditions and residual obligations.

Tasks should use frozen artifacts and environments, with separate development, library-validation, and held-out request sets. Library construction must not use held-out outcomes. Donor provenance, any overlap between donors and task repositories, and possible public benchmark exposure should be documented. Reference outcomes of guidance tasks should not enter persistent state directly: as in SourceLearn, they serve only to locate source evidence and derive source requirements; updates are reconstructed from the source. A task’s success criteria and its grading process must be fixed before systems are compared. During a run, verification may use only the tests, builds, and evidence available in the task’s environment, as in LEGO and HERMES, while held-out tests and grading outcomes are reserved for final scoring, and revision (Eq. (6)) changes the plan but not the criteria.

E.2.  Comparators and Controlled Changes

  1. 1.

    Monolithic Execution: one task-level agent uses the same underlying assets and authorized tools.

  2. 2.

    Retrieved Context: the same components, source material, and method descriptions are available as context, without primitive-local execution or adaptation.

  3. 3.

    Executable Reuse: components are invocable, but a task-level script manages selection, dependencies, evidence, and revision.

  4. 4.

    Fixed Composition: the best fixed subset of primitives, chosen on development tasks and applied to all tasks, which plays the role of the best static harness Hfixed∗H^{*}_{\mathrm{fixed}} of Proposition 3.2.

  5. 5.

    Full HEELO: library selection and composition and evidence-based execution and improvement as described in Section 3.3, with each family’s own mechanisms for selection, verification, and revision (Section 4) and each primitive’s permissions enforced where it runs.

  6. 6.

    Mechanism Ablations: remove one mechanism at a time, such as relevance assessment, the passing of requirements between primitives, verification, or revision, while keeping the underlying assets fixed and grading each run by the preregistered task-level evaluation.

The evaluation should hold the backbone, tool access, underlying assets, and total inference budget fixed, and add quality–cost curves for allocation strategies that one matched budget cannot represent fairly. An oracle selection condition, which activates on each task the primitives whose single-primitive runs improve it, approximates the oracle task-conditioned activation 𝐳∗​(q)\mathbf{z}^{*}(q) of Proposition 3.2; it estimates how much error is attributable to selection and is reported separately from deployable performance. Besides the shared assets, all comparators receive the same tests and source evidence.

E.3.  Measurements

The primary quality measure is end-to-end task success under the preregistered task-level evaluation. The verdicts of each family’s own verification should be reported beside it, together with the runs that end because the revision budget BB is spent. Most of these verdicts are pass or fail, such as those of HEART’s result validation, of LEGO’s and HERMES’s diagnosis, of Lean’s compilation, and of STITCH’s validity check of each candidate graph. ANTMAN’s need-resolution assessment is three-valued (resolved, partial, or unresolved), and its runs end in a synthesized answer that the benchmark grades (Section 4.8). Hidden checks stronger than the task-level evaluation, run on the composed system’s own task distribution, should measure how often each verification passes a wrong result. HEART’s audit of result validation on 200 sampled decisions measures this reliability within one family (Table 36), and SourceLearn’s grounding and preservation audits measure how well the stored units of its source models are supported by their cited source and preserve earlier meaning (Tables 44 and 44). A composed system can route harder requests to a check than the check’s own study did, so its rates must be measured under the composed distribution. False passes matter most, because they separate a more reliable system from one that reports success more often by weakening a check.

For Proposition 3.2, single-primitive arms, which apply one focused primitive with its required dependencies and shared supporting operations to all tasks, as STITCH’s fixed arms do, estimate each primitive’s effect Δi​(q)\Delta_{i}(q) against the arm without primitives. These estimates give the prevalence μi\mu_{i} of the primitive’s application scope, its mean in-scope gain g¯i\bar{g}_{i}, and its mean out-of-scope penalty κ¯i\bar{\kappa}_{i}, and the final activations under Full HEELO give the rates αi\alpha_{i} and βi\beta_{i}. Together they predict Γfixed\Gamma_{\mathrm{fixed}} and the utility-weighted selection loss of Full HEELO (Eq. (9)). Comparing the predictions with the measured gaps between the oracle selection condition, Fixed Composition, and Full HEELO tests the additive model on compositions that span families, where primitives of different families can help only together or interfere.

Library-size experiments should vary the number of irrelevant primitives in the library independently of task demand and relevant coverage, as ANTMAN’s space intervention enlarges the distractor space at approximately fixed demand. They should measure candidate recall, assessment cost, the number of distinct active primitives against realized demand, and task quality. Where COMPOSE activates a primitive only by routing one unresolved need to it, as ANTMAN does, the routing count K⁡(q)K(q) and the realized demand D⁡(q)D(q) are observable, so each run can be checked against Eq. (8); elsewhere, required evidence can stand in for demand, as in ANTMAN’s demand intervention. This separates selective execution, which Proposition 3.1 bounds, from discovery cost, which can grow with the library. For Proposition 3.3, each retrieval stage should report its own hit@mm and recall@mm beside the final hit@kk and recall@kk, which Eq. (10) bounds for every k≤mk\leq m. This separates misses of retrieval from misses of assessment, as Figure 17 does for Math Primitives and Table 36 does for the retrieval stage of Tool Primitives.

Costs should include library construction and validation, indexing, relevance assessment, adaptation, execution, retries, final checks, hosting, and revalidation after updates. Model calls and tokens should be reported as well as any monetary values, with the recorded pricing convention and model labels. Latency should include queueing and p50/p95 values, together with cancellation and timeout rates. Cross-request reuse should report the one-time cost of building and validating the library separately from the per-task costs, together with the number of tasks that share it, as STITCH separates the offline development of its primitives from a composition cost of a few percent of one actor attempt.

Diagnostic measurements should distinguish observed failures from causal attribution. Injected or independently verified defects can measure whether diagnosis implicates the primitives that own them, the set ℐt\mathcal{I}_{t} of Eq. (5), and whether revision then reactivates only those primitives, as LEGO and HERMES do.

E.4.  Stress Conditions and Statistical Analysis

Concurrency experiments should run concurrent tasks over one shared library, which no task changes (Section 3.3), with conflicting and disjoint edits. In LEGO and HERMES, a primitive edits only the component it owns and passes cross-component requirements, within the same round, to the primitives that must satisfy them; conflicting edits test this ownership when primitives of different families touch the same artifact. Drift experiments should revise API schemas, source documentation, runtime dependencies, and model compatibility while measuring invalidation and revalidation. Fault experiments should include unavailable dependencies, stale dependency records such as a Code Primitive’s dependency closure DiD_{i} or a Harness Primitive’s composition contract, wrong relevance assessments, truncated evidence, malicious tool output, and uncertain external completion in a mock environment. These interventions test each family’s own checks without irreversible real-world effects.

Task runs should be paired across conditions, with repeated seeds or attempts where the system is stochastic. Confidence intervals should come from task-level outcomes with an appropriate paired resampling or test, not from unpaired, rounded table means. Software task families and source groups may require clustered resampling. Sample size and stopping rules should rest on a prespecified, practically meaningful effect and a pilot variance estimate.

An evaluation supports the integrated system only if its task-level outcome and complete cost accounting justify composing primitives through HEELO. A failure of interoperability or economics is reported as a specific finding about the system, separately from the overall average.
